LYNCHED IN ILLINOIS.
A Negro who Assaulted a Woman Strung Up to a Tree.
A Negro who Assaulted a Woman Strung Up to a Tree.

PINCKNEYVILLE, Ill., Feb. 14.—There was vigorous rapping on the big wooden door of the jail at 2 o'clock this morning. Sheriff Penwarden and the jailer who live on the upper floor saw below them six masked men who carried two shotguns and four revolvers. The Sheriff in his night dress and nightcap began to harangue the men, who declared that they had come from St. John's to lynch Alonzo Holly, a negro, who assaulted a white woman two months ago. The longer the Sheriff talked the more impatient the vigilantes became. Finally one of the men pointed the barrel of his shotgun at the window.

The white figure of the Sheriff disappeared in an instant, and the next instant the keys to all the cells in the jail were turned over to the mob, which numbered about fifty men. Without another word the masked men fell upon Holly, who was crouched in one corner of his cell. The prisoner cried and chattered all the time he was being bound, and begged his executioners to spare his life. A rope was quickly tightened around the man's neck and a rush was made for the door.

Holly now pleaded for two minutes to pray, and this being refused, he asked a fellow prisoner to pray for him. At the front door he endeavored to halt, and was jerked forward upon his face, and was thus dragged about fifty feet to a maple tree, where he was hanged to a limb about eight feet from the ground.

As soon as the lynchers dispersed, the Sheriff and jailer started out to give the alarm. When only a few feet from their door they came upon the negro, hanging almost across the sidewalk. He was dead. When daylight came the Coroner cut the body down with a corn knife. The vigilantes are not known.

From the time they entered the jail until the negro was jerked up to the ice-covered limb not a word was spoken to the cringing victim. The day after the crime Holly was brought here and placed in jail. That night a mob came from St. John's to lynch him, but the officers had taken him to Belleville. He was left there until he became so troublesome that the officials refused to keep him longer, and last Saturday he was brought back here.

Holly said two days ago that he would rather be hanged than stay in the Belleville jail. It was thought that the excitement had subsided, and therefore no trouble was anticipated. Holly's crime was particularly brutal. He cut the clothing from his victim with a razor, and then held the blade to her throat.

WAUSAU, Wis., Feb. 16 — The saloon-keepers and gambling-house keepers in this city, who are being warred upon by the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, have decided upon a novel way of defending themselves. CRIMES AND CRIMINALS.
A Small Mob Attacks a Jail, and Take a Prisoner Out and Lynch Him.
PINCKNEYVILLE, Ill., February 14.—[Special.]—At 3 o'clock this morning the first lynching that ever occurred in Perry county took place. The victim was Alonzo Holly, a negro, who was confined in the county jail upon the charge of ontraging a white woman, between Dugoin and St. Johns, some time last December. Sheriff Renwarden boards with the jailer, Jeff King, and they were the only men about the premises last night, except the prisoner. The first intimation they had of the mob was about 2 o'clock in the morning, when a knock was heard at the front door. Mr. King answered the knock, but on opening the door he slammed it shut, and went and awakened the sheriff. Mr. Renwarden opened a window, but was promptly covered with shotguns. He explained to the crowd that he merely wanted to argue the matter with them. After talking for some time, and failing to convince them they ought to let the law take its course with the negro, they began to batter the door down.

The jailer, in the meantime, had viewed the situation from all the windows of the building and found the house premises securely guarded, so he concluded the best thing to do was to save the door by unlocking it. Once inside the building, the six men demanded the keys to the cage in which the cells are located, adding emphasis to the demand by covering the two men with four revolvers and two shotguns. The keys were delivered and the cage quickly opened. One of the prisoners told the mob in which cell the negro was to be found. He was dragged forth from under the bed, where he had endeavored to hide, his hands were tied behind him and an inch rope was placed about his neck. He was then led out. He begged for two minutes in which to pray, and that being refused, he asked one of the prisoners, John Eaton, who is awaiting trial upon the same charge as that for which the negro was hanged, to pray for him.

In going from the cell to the front door of the building he called on the jailer for help, but just at that time the jailer was busy looking into the business end of a shotgun. At the door the negro pulled back and was jerked forward upon his face, and in this position dragged about fifty feet to a large maple tree. The rope was thrown over a limb about eight feet from the ground and the negro jerked into space. The rope was then tied around the tree and the mob dispersed, though it is supposed some of them stayed in the vicinity until they were satisfied that life had left the negro.

Holly, in his death struggles, caused the rope to slip several inches nearer the body of the tree on the limb, and when found his toes were touching the ground.

After the mob left the sheriff and jailer started out to alarm the town, and they found the negro within a few feet of the jail still warm. The victim was cut down about five o'clock. It is supposed the mob came from St. Johns, but how none seem to know. They were well drilled, and no one outside of the jail knew they were here until after they left. They departed in different directions.

An inquest was held today and a verdict of hanging by unknown parties was returned. An attempt was made to hang Holly about one month ago, but he was run off to Beeleville by the officers. He became so troublesome that they refused to keep him there and last Saturday he was brought back here. He had served a term in the penitentiary, and was a bad negro generally. He leaves a white wife about twice his own age.

A WISCONSIN TRAGEDY.
The Little Village of Kickapoo the Scene.
FOUR PEOPLE MURDERED.
An Old Man, His Wife and Two Grandchildren the Victims----Northwest News.
Special to the Globe.
LA Crosgrain Wia
LA Crosse, Wis., May 25.—A horrible murder occurred in the town of Kickapoo, Vernon county, to-day, four persons being slain—Reuben Drake and wife and two children of James Dupee, their grandchildren, who were visiting at his house. The Drake family occupy a farm four miles from the little settlement of Readstown and fifteen miles from Viroqua. They were past middle life and moderately well-to-do. This morning a neighbor went to Drake's house on an errand, knocked, but getting no answer and the door being partly open, entered. A most horrible sight confronted him. There on the floor lay Drake and wife, face downwards, the head and face of each mangled by shotgun wounds, and the floor swimming in blood. In the next room lay two children on a bed, with their throats

CUT FROM EAR TO EAR.

One of the children was yet alive, but unable to make any communication, and died in a very short time. The neighborhood, and, in fact, the whole county, was notified within the next few hours and hundreds of people gathered in the vicinity. Officers are actively tracing out clues to the perpetrators of the horrible deed. The house had been completely ransacked, showing that search had been made for valuables. Foot marks could be seen leading East from the house and road, but as yet no clue has been found. The nearest neighbor woman heard three shots fired in the direction of Drake's house at 11 o'clock last night, but supposed it to be some hunter returning home late. Another woman tells of meeting a stranger who avoided her and hid in the brush alongside of the road. Drake was known to have obtained some pension money a month ago, and it is supposed the murderers were after that, which would indicate the deed was done by somebody in the neighborhood.
andrew-grandstaff-viroqua-1888-06-01.A3:
LYNCHED BY A MOB. A THOUSAND MEN HANG A MURDERER IN WISCONSIN. The Slayer of the Drake Family Taken For. o'bly From Prison and Suspended From a Tree—The Culprit Bogs Precusively for Mercy—The Foul Crime Convicted.
VIROQUA, Wis, June 2—2. a. m.—Soon after midnight a thousand determined men surrounded the jail in which Andrew Grandstaff, charged with the brutal murder of Reuben Drake and family on the night of May 21, was confined. They demanded the prisoner, but the authorities refused to give him up. The barricades were then broken down and the officers overpowered. An hour was spent in breaking down the steel cage and then the prisoner fought with desperate fury with the mob. The struggle did not last long and he was taken out, bound hand and foot, led to the porch below and there preparations were made to hang him. The appearance of the prisoner was shocking, as he was covered with blood from wounds received while the steel cage was being battered. A rope was placed around his neck and the prisoner was asked what he had to say. He protested that he was innocent, but it was known that he had made a full confession in the afternoon, and he was not believed. He pleaded pleitously for his life, but his entreaties were out short by a pull at the rope that had been thrown over a limb of a tree and he struggled in the air. Then he was let down and given another chance to confess. After a second elevation he made a statement that he, Frank and Elisha Carey had the murder concocted and that they had the deed accomplished before he arrived at the house. None of the above is thought to be true.

Grandstaff hung for eleven minutes before life was extinct. His remains will not be cut down before morning.

THE MURDERER'S CONFESSION.

The substance of the confession made by Grandstaff to the detectives yesterday is as follows:

He went to Drake's house shortly after dark and knocked at the door. He was admitted by the old gentleman [Drake]. He asked for a drink of water, which was given him. Grandstaff then says: "I asked him if he had money and he said he did not. Then I drew a revolver and told him I wanted his money. He said he did not have any, but was expecting some soon. When he said this I shot him. When I went into the house Mrs. Drake was putting the two grandchildren to bed. She went into the bedroom to go to bed before I shot Mr. Drake. Just after I shot she came out with the Winchester rifle. I think I had then shot the old man twice and he had fallen. As Mrs. Drake came out the bedroom door I shot her twice. I think I looked into everything, but found no money. The children were then awake and looking at me. I thought I would have to kill them, for they knew me and would tell on me. Then I cut their throats—the little girl's first. She was on the front side of the bed. The boy was upon his elbow when I took hold of him and I struggled. I cut his throat, but do not remember of stabbing him."

The murderer then described his return to Jennings' house, where he was afterwards arrested.

andrew-grandstaff-viroqua-1888-06-01.A10:
FOUGHT LIKE A TIGER.
HOW GRANDSTAFF HELD THE VIRO- QUA MOB AT BAY.
With a Club He Defends Himslf for Over an Hour—He Dies Declaring Himself Innocent, but the Authorities Have His Written Confession—His Account of the Terrible Crime.

VIROQUA, Wis., June 4.—The lynching of Andrew Grandstaff will be the talk of the town for months. The sheriff had a dozen deputies in the jail with him, and at first repulsed the infuriated mob that assaulted the jail Friday night, but they returned to the charge and overpowered the posse. Then the mob proceeded to Grandstaff's cell. A breach was quickly made in the cell door with a hammer, and then an awful struggle for life began upon the part of the prisoner. In some way he had secured a large club, and standing in the breach in the cell door with club in hand he kept the crowd of vigilantes at bay for more than an hour. Every attempt to enter or grapple him was met with blows, and many were the wounded assailants who retired from the front. The situation at this time is described as something terrible. It was a caged murderer fighting for his life, and it was thought at one time that he could only be secured by maiming him with a bullet. At last, however, the pressure was so great that a number of the mob rushed in and managed to grapple Grandstaff and he was soon secured. a rope thrown around his neck and wounded and bleeding he was led down-stairs to the howling multitude below. At the front entrance of the jail a halt was made and he was confronted by James Dupee, the father of the murdered children, who stood like an avenging Nemesis.

"I am the father of the little children. I want you to say if you took the lives of my two little angels."

Grandstaff with a dazed and wild look replied: "I was not there. I did not kill your children or know that they were there."

This the mob derided and proceeded to string him up and let him down twice to force a confession from him. He protested his innocence, and the third time he was allowed to strangle. Grandstaff made a confession to the officers who arrested him, which is as follows:

I am 24 years old and live in the town of Kickapoo, at Kickapoo Center. I left Jennings' place in the town of Liberty, about 8. a. m., May 24; went along the ridge through the woods and off the ridge at Newville, across the river at Gedder bridge, and across the Kickapoo bottom, and went on the ridge in the timber, and then along the ridge to the point above Reuben Drake's house. I got there, I think about, 4 o'clock in the afternoon of the same day; staid there until dark; then I went down into the bottom and up to the house; stopped and looked into the window, then knocked at the door. Drake said, "Come in." I went in and asked him for a drink of water; took the drink and spoke a few words to him. They called me by name. I asked him if he had any money. He said he had not. Then I drew a revolver and told him I wanted his money. He said he did not have any, but he was looking for some. I then shot him. When I first came in Mrs. Drake was putting the children to bed. She then went into her own bedroom to go to bed before I shot, and after she put the children to bed, just after I shot, she came in with the rifle. I think I shot the old man twice. He had fallen just as Mrs. Drake came out of the bedroom door. I shot her. Just as I shot her she left the rifle fall. I shot her twice, I think. I looked in the drawer and saw there was no money. The children were then awake and up on their arms in bed looking out in the sitting-room. I then thought I would have to kill them, for if I did not they would tell on me. Then I cut their throats. I cut the little girl's throat first. She lay on the front side. The boy was up on his elbow. When I took hold of him he struggled some. I cut his throat. Don't remember stabbing him. This is the knife I did the cutting with, and this is the revolver I did the shooting with. It is one I bought at Towner's in Viro qua some time last fall.

This confession was signed by Grandstaff and was witnessed and sworn to before a justice of the peace. It is believed that this statement is entirely true and that he was alone in committing the dreadful deed, although in his dying moments at the tree he denied his guilt.
andrew-grandstaff-viroqua-1888-06-01.A11:
THE KICKAPOO TRAGEDY.
The Murderer of the Drake Family Arrested at Viroqua-He Makes Confession of the Horrible Crime-Taken from the Jail and Hanged by a Mob.
RECHLAND CENTER, Wis., June 1.—Andrew Grandstaff, a young man of bad, repute, who owns forty acres adjoining the Drake place, was captured six miles from the scene of the late murder last night by Vernon County deputies and confessed to the awful crime of killing of old Reuben Drake, his wife and two grandchildren. He is now lodged in the Vernon County jail.

VIROQUA, Wis., June 1.—Great excitement prevails in this city this morning over the arrest of a young man named Andrew Grandstaff, supposed to be connected with the murder of the Drake family. The arrest was made about 9 o'clock last night, one week after the murder occurred. Grandstaff is 25 years of age and has borne an exceedingly hard reputation in the Kickapoo Valley. He has made it his headquarters for several years. Many depredations have been laid at his door, but he has never been arrested for them. During a school meeting at Kickapoo Center, in February, he was shot in the bowels with a charge of common shot, but owing to his strong constitution he recovered.

The arrest of Grandstaff was made by C. J. Farrell, of Pinkerton's Chicago force, who has done good work during the twenty-four hours he has been on the ground. Farrell was assisted by ex-Sheriffs Goodell and Morley. They brought the prisoner to this city, arriving here at 7 o'clock this morning. He was closeted in a room at a hotel with the officers until 10 o'clock, where it is rumored he made a full confession.

By 10 o'clock matters had worked to such a heat that a lynching party was assured had not better councils and cooler judgment prevailed.

Grandstaff was born in this county. He is an illegitimate child and is ignorant and daring. The detectives are earnestly at work and more interesting developments are almost sure to come to light within twenty-four hours.

Madison, Wis., June 1.—The sheriff of Vernon County has telegraphed the Governor that he has arrested the suspected murderer of the Drake family and that he cannot protect him from the wrathful populace without help. The Governor has taken no action about the matter as yet.

Viroqua, Wis., June 2.—Surrounded by a mob of fully 1,000 determined men, the murderer of Reuben Drake, his wife and their two innocent little grandchildren, found retribution on an improvised gallows in front of the jail at an early hour this morning. His name is Andrew Grandstaff. Being suddenly pounced upon by the authorities he made a full confession as to the atrocious quadruple butchery, and before night the men of the vicinity gathered in ominous fashion to mete out swift justice. Recognizing the necessity oi securing reinforcements if the life of the prisoner was to be preserved for the process of law, the sheriff wired Gov. Rusk to call out the militia. It was, of course, too late to comply immediately, as no trains would bring the nearest company of national guards to the scene this night, and so the governor telegraphed in reply that the sheriff should swear in all the special deputies he might require to protect the prisoner until he could get a company of militia to the place. Every man within a radius of twenty miles and more, however, was in sympathy with the fast multiplying mob and the authorities were unable to obtain any reinforcements worth mentioning. It is doubtful if even a company of militia could have saved the life of the prisoner, for Judge Lynch ruled supreme this night, and he had a thousand men to do his bidding and a reserve of a thousand more. The authorities suppressed the fact that Grandstaff had made a confession, knowing that the possibility of taking the life of an innocent man was the only thing that prevented the mob from making quick work with the murderer. Had they been absolutely sure of their man, Grandstaff would not have been alive at 10 o'clock to-night. There were rumors of a confession, but those who alone could substantiate the reports would not do so. The prisoner, however, was finally taken from the jail after a bloody struggle and hanged.
andrew-grandstaff-viroqua-1888-06-01.A13:
Lynching at Virequa.
An account was given last week of the brutal murder of Reuben Drake, his wife and two little grandchildren at their home in Vernon county, the evening of May 24. Last Friday the murderer was captured by a Pinkerton detective, and lodged in jail at Reads-town. A confession, made by him to the sheriff, which is supposed to be true. The next morning he was taken to Viroqua and talk of lynching became so general that the sheriff telegraphed for help to defend the prison, but it failed to reach him in time, and at 11:50 that night a band of about 100 men marched to the jail and demanded that Grandstaff should be given up. Every possible argument was used to prevent the lynching, but nothing would satisfy the enraged people, but what they considered just punishment for the cowardly and brutal crime. Another confession differing from the first was extorted from the doomed man, but his appeals for mercy were unheeded, and he was hanged to the limb of a tree in the court-yard. His last words implicated two young men, neighbors of the Drake's, but his story is not believed. Grandstaff comes of a bad lot. His illegitimate father is a brother of Jona Love, who is now serving a sentence at Waupun for the murder of Ole Olson, at Purdy, in this county, in February, 1887. His mother is dead. Grandistan was abought 20 years old, unmarried and a thorough young desparado.

It is probable, but not absolutely certain, that the right man was hanged in this case; but even so, that does not excuse the brutality, almost equal to his own, which moved the people to commit this deed of violence. It is the old spirit of "an eye for an eye." The precedent of lynch-law is a very dangerous one, and we are sorry that it has been resorted to in Wisconsin.

anschlag-garden-grove.A1:
MURDER MOST FOUL.
Terrible Tragedy Enacted Near Santa Ana.
A MAN AND HIS WIFE KILLED.
The Assassin Lynched by a Posse of Infuriated Citizens.
[Associated Press dispatches to the HERALD]
SANTA ANA, January 26.—Mr. Hitchcock, a prominent farmer of Garden Grove, five miles from Santa Ana, came to town last Monday evening with his wife, and acknowledged his property to a German named Anschlag, who had bought his ranch, and after that was not heard of. Suspicion was aroused last night, and investigation proves that Hitchcock and his wife returned home on Monday afternoon and delivered the deed to Anschlag who claimed that he paid them the balance in cash, viz: $8000, and brought them to Santa Ana before daylight on Tuesday morning to take the early train. They were not seen here and no such parties are known to have taken the train on that date. Search at the house proves that all their clothing, including three overcoats of Mr. Hitchcock and his wife's clothing, trunks and jewelry, including her gold watch, are all unmolested, or not even packed up and put away.

A GHASTLY DISCOVERY.

At 4:45 this afternoon one of the numerous parties of searchers, riding three miles southeast of the Hitchcock house, discovered fresh straw on the prarie. They commenced digging and soon discovered bodies. They soon unearthed them, and after taking the names of witnesses, lifted out the bodies of Chas. B. Hitchcock and his wife.

HOW THE DEED WAS DONE.

Hitchcock while attending to his team between 9 and 10 p. m. as usual, was waylaid in the barn by Anschlag with an axe, who followed this up by killing Mrs. Hitchcock, loading both bodies in the wagon, drawing them to this forsaken spot, burying them and starting to Santa Ana by daylight. Out of the horrible hole came several cans, probably of blood, gathered from the ground where the victims were killed. Next came two ropes which had been on the legs of the bodies to haul them around with. A party of lynchers quickly organized and started at once for Anschlag, but Marshal Insley had foreseen the trouble and started the prisoner for Anaheim.

IDENTITY OF THE DECEASED.

Mr. Hitchcock, was a handsome man, tall, broad, shouldered, and commanding of appearance; Mrs. Hitchcock, was likewise a handsome, refined lady highly accomplished. Both were leaders of social societies. He was one of the main leaders in the advancements of the Santa Ana valley and first in railroad movements, hotels, etc. Both were loved and honored by all who knew them. Mr. Hitchcock's father and mother are now tottering on the edge of their graves. Mrs. Hitchcock's father and mother are living at Compton, Illinois, with another son, Frank.

Anschlag is a middle sized man, dark brown eyes, smooth face, well dressed, speaks very little English. He has been here one year. He has a brother in Manchester, England. His mother lives in Germany.

LATEST—ANSCHLAG LYNCHED.

Information reached here at 8:30 P. M. that the lynching party overtook the officers a few miles south of Anaheim, near a bunch of trees, and finished by hanging the murderer. The courts will be petitioned to set aside the deed and allow the property to go to the heirs of the murdered instead of to those of the murderer.
anschlag-garden-grove.A2:
No doubt now remained in the minds of the populace but that Anschlag was the murderer, and the enraged citizens started out to lynch him. Constable Finley had removed him and the German who was arrested with him to Anaheim, whence he was followed by the infuriated mob, who broke into the jail, but did not find Anschlag to vent their rage upon, as he had been removed from the jail shortly before, and, it is stated, was hidden in a corn-bin. Yesterday both men were brought to the county jail in this city, where they will be safe for a time.

Drs. Kelly and Ball made a thorough post-mortem examination of the bodies, but had not sent in their report when our reporter left.

THE INQUEST.

Mr. O. Witham testified at the inquest as follows: I am a farmer and blacksmith residing at Garden Grove. On Thursday morning I went to Dr. John Chaffee, brother-in-law of the deceased, and had a conversation with him concerning the disappearance of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock, and from the facts I had learned I thought that perhaps a murder had been committed. I told him my suspicions and he stated that he thought that probably the two Germans had done the deed. Mrs. Chaffee told me that she had gone down to Mrs. Hitchcock's house and searched it. All the clothes were there except the dress that Mrs. Hitchcock had on. She asked Anschlag what sort of clothes Mrs. Hitchcock had on when he drove her and her husband up town. His statement did not compare with any clothes that the two deceased had. Anschlag also told Mrs. Chaffee that he drove them to Santa Ana, but he did not know whether they were going to Los Angeles or not when he left them. I then suggested that we commence the search for the bodies at once. I went to the barn of Mr. Hitchcock and took measurements of the horses' feet, also the width of the wheels apart and the breadth of the tiers. I examined the wagon and found blood on the floor of the wagon and on the cross-bar; this showed us that there had been foul play, and we started out for the store near Garden Grove and went westwards, examining the tracks of horses' feet and the wagon tracks. When we got near Dr. Head's residence we saw three men digging. We drove down and they told us that they had found Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock. They had dug as far as the corpses when we got there. Mr. Robinson was with me. They had thrown out the dirt and also a canvass frock, a pair of overalls and a hat Both bodies were severely bruised and cut about the head and neck. We took the bodies out, put them into a wagon and brought them to the undertaker's rooms at Santa Ana. The search for the bodies commenced on Thursday, after 1 'oclock P. M. We found no instruments, that had been used to commit the deed, in the barn. The hired German that was arrested with Anschlag came to his place on Tuesday, and the murder probably occurred on Monday night between 8 and 10 o'clock p. m. A social had been arranged on Sunday to take place on Wednesday evening at the house of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock."

Several papers, a bank bill, a powder or two, two pair of bloody overalls, and a half-burned letter were found in a clump of cane trees a short distance from where the murderer had buried his victims. The letter was in Mrs. Hitchcock's hand-writing, and had evidently been written on Sunday or Monday. The inquest was still in progress when the reporter left for this city.

THE PRISONER.

Upon learning that Fred Anschlag had been brought to this city, a representative of THE HERALD. visited the County Jail, and through the kindness of Jailer Russell was permitted to see and talk to the prisoner. He is a tall, slender, black-haired, smooth-faced, youngish-looking man, with high cheek bones, and was rather fashionably than otherwise attired. He could speak very little English, but said that he was not guilty of the murder of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock, and that the last he had seen of them was on Tuesday morning last, when he had left them in front of Mr. Taylor's house in Santa Aua. The first time he met Mr. Hitchcock was when he went to the office of W. A. Beckett in Santa Ana for the purpose of buying a ranch. Mr. Beckett had shown him property in several places, and among others that of Mr. Hitchcock, for which he was to pay $8000. In making preliminary arrangements for the purchase, the prisoner had engaged Mr. Taylor, a lawyer, who could speak German. On Wednesday, last week he agreed to buy the place and paid Mr. Hitchcock $95 on account, at the same time signing an agreement to purchase the same. After the agreement had been made he had gone to Anaheim and engaged Antone Decker to work for him and then went back to Santa Ana and stopped at the Taylor House until Saturday, when he went to the residence of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock and stayed until Tuesday. Mr. Hitchcock had obtained a deed and had taken it home with him. On Monday, Mr. and Mrs Hitchcock said they were coming to Los Angeles on the morning train. So on Tuesday morning he and the murdered people rose at 5 o'clock. Shortly afterward he paid Mr. Hitchcock the remainder of the $8,000 and received the deed in return. He then hitched the team to the wagon and all three started for Santa Ana, where Mr. Hitchcock expected to take the train for this city. They had reached Santa Ana about a quarter to seven o'clock on Tuesday morning and about a quarter of a mile from the depot, in front of the Taylor

The Santa Ana Avengers Fall to Catch
Murderer Anschlag.

The Santa Ana Avengers Fall to Catch Murderer Anschlag.

[Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]

SANTA ANA, January 27th.—As your reporter left the lynchers last night, at the residence of the deceased, they started in pursuit of the officers. The crowd arrived shortly at Anaheim and broke open the jail, not overtaking the officers, but found no prisoner. The half-frightened populace of Anaheim, believing they had succeeded in catching the murderers, telephoned the officers here to that effect.

The night was dark, and a very thick fog had arisen before 6 o'clock. It was impossible to see 100 yards ahead, and the officers, by turning at the first cross-road, easily evaded the mob, and, by lying out all night, reached Anaheim in safety and took the Southern Pacific train to Los Angeles and delivered the prisoners at the County Jail.

Constable Farley, in the discharge of his duty, is deserving of the greatest praise, as not only did he do his duty, but he was no doubt the means of saving the life of Antonio Decker, who as yet stands clear of all evidence of guilt, circumstantially or otherwise.

The bodies of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock were washed this forereon, and multitudes of people, reaching thousands in number, viewed the ghastly sight.

Mr. Hitchcock had been chopped in the back of the head by the stroke of the ax, and then chopped a second time as he turned around, this time over the right car and just below the crown of the head. His throat was then cut with a knife.

Mrs. Hitchcock had been chopped first in the right temple by one blow of the sharp ax, as she was, no doubt, approaching the murderer face to face, her every expression on her once beautiful, but now firm, countenance, showing she had evidently been coming to the protection of her beloved husband, thinking naught of herself and caring less for the dangers before her, her mind and her soul intently bent on the defense of her husband. No more touching picture of pure womanhood ever blessed the countenance of humanity than the firm and determined look on the corpse of Mrs. Louise Hitchcock to-day.

New and startling developments were made this morning at the residence of the murdered couple. The bloody ax which had done the fatal deed was a common ax well sharpened, and was found under the barn thoroughly besmeared with the blood of its victims, and a few moments later J. C. Gormley, reporter of the Los Angeles Tribune, discovered the connecting link of the tragedy in the form of Anschlag's well-known overalls thoroughly saturated and besmeared with the blood of the victims and the mud from their grave.

rowly Escaped Lynching.

Los ANGELES, Jan. 27.—The accounts published this morning about the lynching of the murderers of the Hitchcocks near Santa Ana last night are incorrect. The murderers were hidden in Anaheim over night to escape the mob and brought to jail in this city this morning.

Los ANGELES, Jan. 27.—A special from Anaheim to the Express says: Great excitement. prevailed among the citizens when the Hitchcock murderers were brought into town. The prisoners were secretly placed in the cellar of a store and kept there till morning. A body of men broke into the jail during the night, but failed to find the murderers. The men were brought to Los Angeles this morning and placed in the County Jail.
anschlag-garden-grove.A9:
THE WRONG MAN HUNG

California Vigilantes Lynch a Man Who Was Entirely Innocent.

The Real Murderer Is Arrested and Makes a Full Confession.

Citizens of Virginia Want the Hatfield-McCoy Vendetta Squelched.
The Indiana Election Law Conspirators Are Found Guilty.
Los ANGELES, Cal., Jan. 28.—Frederick Anschlag, the young German who was arrested with another man named Antoine Decker for the murder of Charles B. Hitchcock and wife near Garden Grove, made a full confession to-day. Anschlag says he left Garden Grove at 5 o'clock Tuesday morning in an open wagon with Hitchcock and wife to go to Santa Ana. He had previously concealed in the wagon a hatchet, and when in an unfrequented spot, about three miles from Hitchcock's home, he suddenly grasped the hatchet, arose in the rear of his victims and first attacked Mr. Hitchcock, killing him with a few blows. He then turned on the defenseless wife and struck her down, killing her with a single blow, which crushed the side of her face and head. Anschlag says he tied the hands and feet of each with ropes to keep them from swinging about with the motion of the wagon. Driving nearly a mile further away he dug a hole and put the bodies therein, covering the grave with straw. He then went back to the ranch house at Garden Grove, took off his clothes and hid them and washed the hatchet. Then he went to Santa Ana and got Decker and drove with him back to Garden Grove, when they took possession of the ranch and went quickly to work. Anschlag says he murdered Hitchcock to get the deed of the ranch and to get the owners out of the way without paying for the property. He states positively that Decker had nothing to do with the crime and knew nothing of it. The funeral of Hitchcock and wife took place at Garden Grove to-day and was attended by a great number of people, as the victims were among the leading people of the community. It will be remembered that Decker was lynched for the crime.
anschlag-garden-grove.A11:
FOUL PLAY.
A Prominent Farmer and His Wife Murdered for Money.
A German Suspected and Lynched for the Crime.
A Bold Penitentiary Outbreak Nipped in the Bud.
Forty-two Prisoners Determine to Cut their Way to Liberty.
SANTA ANA, Cal., Jan. 27.—S. B. Hitchcock, a prominent farmer, came to Santa Ana last Monday with his wife and acknowledged the deed to his property to a German named Anschlag. They returned home, but not having been seen thereafter, the neighbors grew suspicious of foul play and instituted a search. Their dead bodies were found yesterday a long ways from the house. Hitchcock and his wife were side by side in a hole in the ground, which had been covered over with earth and straw. Hitchcock's throat was cut from ear to ear and his wife's head was split open with a hatchet. It seemed evident that Anschlag had murdered them to retain the money he had paid them for the land. A lynching party was at once organized and started for Anschlag and he was lynched before officers could interfere.

LATER.
Los ANGELES, Cala., Jan. 27.—The accounts published this forenoon about the lynching of the murderer of the Hitchcocks, near Santa Anna, is incorrect. The murderer was hidden in Anahiem over night to escape the mob, and was brought to jail here this morning.

PRISONER'S PLAN OF ESCAPE.
* LOUISVILLE, Jan. 26.—A desperate plan of forty-two prisoners to escape from the Jeffersonville penitentiary was discovered yesterday by Warden Patten by accident. A man named Forbes who was in the plot was frightened into giving the scheme away. Every Thursday evening the men are taken out, one range at a time, into the hallway and shaved. One heavily armed guard is in charge and according to the plan as soon as the range was unpacked the forty-two prisoners were to overpower the guard, cut his throat and after locking his dead body in a cell they were to make a bold dash for the main corridor and liberty. It was expected that some of them would be killed but as nearly all of them are life prisoners or long term prisoners they agreed to take the risk. They were to arm themselves with iron bars, clubs, knives, etc., to be found on the way and kill every man who opposed them. Had the wardens vigilance not detected the plot there would have probably been many lives lost and one of the most extensive prison outbreaks ever heard of would have occured.

ACCUSED OF FRAUD.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., Jan. 25.—Indiana filed suit to-day in the circuit court at Jeffersonville against David M. Allen, who was steward of the Prison South during A. J. Hoard's administration as warden. The petition charges that Allen converted to his own use January 1st, 1875, and March 1st, 1877, provisions and goods to the value of $40,000, which it is sought to recover. It is also charged that Allen conspired with Howard, Captain Craig and others to defraud the state out of articles to the value of $150,000, for which judgment is also prayed. Other paragraphs charged that Mr. Allen, in the purchase of supplies for the prison, conspired with certain firms, whose name are given to defraud the state out of $100,000.

SENT UP FOR TWENTY YEARS.
KANSAS CITY, Jan. 25.—Frank Emerson was convicted of burglary in the criminal court here to-day, and was given a sentence of twenty years in the penitentiary, the heaviest punishment ever inflicted for that crime in this city.

LOSSES BY FIRE.
PITTSBURG, Pa., Jan. 26.—The fire which broke out in Dalzell & Co.'s warehouse resulted in a total destruction of the building, together with an adjoining structure on First avenue, occupied by the Anchor Paste company. Dalzell & Co. will lose $40,000 on the building and stock. The paste company's loss is $3,000; insured for $2,500. Wamhoff & Co., glass manufacturers, $2,000; Sheriff & Co., brass finishers, $2,000. The insurance will nearly cover the loss.

FOR THE DEFENDANTS.
CHICAGO, Jan. 26.—The suit for $20,000 damages, brought by Ulman, a Chicago grocer, against Colonial Litter, secretary of the National Dairy Association, City Butter Inspector Howe, and others, for illegal prosecution, was tried before a jury in Judge Algar's court to-day, and resulted in a verdict for the defendants. Ulman was one of some twenty local dealers who were prosecuted and fined for selling butterine for butter.

BROUGHT TO TRIAL.

CHICAGO, Jan. 26.—James W. Sykes, until recently a well-known seed merchant and proprietor of a large warehouse, was placed on trial to-day before a jury in Judge Horton's court, the charge being the issue of fraudulent receipts. The amount of money said to have been obtained by the crime is $110,000, of which $96,000 was from the Merchant Loan and Trust Company, and the remainder from the Hide and Leather Bank.

A NERVY SHERIFF.

ARKANSAS CITY, Jan. 26.—A Purcell, I. T., dispatch to the Republican-Traveler, says: Marshal Carr found John McGrew, the murderer of John Watkins, at noon to-day about twenty-five miles from the scene of the tragedy. Upon being commanded to throw up his hands he opened fire upon the marshal, and shot his horse from under him. Carr then opened fire upon McGrew, inflicting wounds from which he died soon afterwards.

BRINGS SUIT.

ST. PAUL, Minn., Jan. 26.—John A. Roeblings, Son & Co., wire cable manufacturers brought suit in the district court to-day against the New York Cable Construction Company and the St. Paul City Railway Company for $7,240, yet unpaid for the cable used in the road here, asking for a lien on all the property of the cable road, and that the same be sold to satisfy the above claim.

ANSCHLAG'S CASE
Set for Saturday-Scenes on the Street.
The case of John Henry Frederick Anschlag, the confessed murderer of Mr. and Mrs Hitchcock, of Garden Grove, was called in Judge Cheney's court yesterday morning at 10 o'clock. At this time there were as many people in the court-room as it could possibly ho'd, and the crowd even extended down the hallway to the sidewalk, showing that the murderer or his crime had not been forgotten. The case had been set, not for trial, but to give the defendant a chance to plea to the charges against him. When the case was called, Attorney Peyton ar se and stated that he desired to enter a motion to set aside the information on the ground that there were no papers on file showing that the defendant had ever been held by any committing magistrate, and that the District Attorney had no right to file an information without at the same time filing the evidence taken in the lower court. To substantiate the motion, his colleague, Mr. McGregor, then proceeded to read a long decision rendered some years ago by the Supreme Court of California in a case of Fresno county. District Attorney Dupuy answered, admitting that the testimony taken in the lower court had not yet been filed, but said that it was being transcribed from the shorthand reporter's notes as rapidly as possible. He also stated that he was present during the enire examination before Justice Austin, and heard every word of the testimony. Yet at the same time the filing of the information was per ectly legal. The gentleman had but just concluded his remarks, and the Court had continued the matter until 1:30 o'clock, when Court Reporter Rutan entered bearing the papers in question.

At half-past one o'clock the Court re-convened, and Judge Cheney overruled the motion to set aide the information. Anschlag then pleaded "Not guilty" to both charges.

District Attorney Dupuy then asked the Court to set the day for trial,
the court, after listening to all the arguments on both sides, announced that the case, No. 202, would be set for trial, whereupon Attorney McGregor arose and stated that according to the rules adopted by the Superior Court of this county in 1885, the case must of necessity go over for the session. Attorney Peyton then took up the fight for a delay, and stated that they desired to correspond with defendant's relatives in Europe in order to ascertain his peculiarities. e c., which would probably take about three months, and desired the case to go over for the session, at the same time informing the court that a German lawyer had entered into the court as an associate counsel, and had had no opportunity of consulting with the accused. The court, after listening to all the arguments on both sides, announced that the case, No. 202, would be set for trial Saturday, the 11th inst., at 10 a.m., and that in the attorneys for the defense could show any legal cause why the trial should not be proceeded with upon that date, they must bring affidavits to substantiate.

The courtroom was then cleared, by the crowd did not disperse. I collected several hundred strong around the doorway leading to the courtroom and waited for Anschlag's appearance. When he did come down, guarded by the deputy sheriff's and handcuffed to a man named O'Brien, the crowd pressed closely around him and followed him to the curb. As he was led across the street some one in the crowd set up a cry, "Let's hang him." This was followed by similar remarks, and the shouting was in the ears of the prisoner, quite ominous, for he started on a run for the stairway, for the start of the Herald building. The crowd, however, did not appear to be serious, but stood on the street and laughed at Anschlag's fear. He was so badly frightened, however, that he could hardly climb the hill to the Coun y Jail. The man who whom Anschlag was handcuffed was almost as badly frightened as Anschlag, and objected to being fastened to another man of so much notoriety.

GUILTY
Of Murder in the First Degree.
THE VERDICT OF THE JURY,
Which Agreed in Sixteen Minutes
—Sentence to be Passed on
Friday.
The previous announcement privately by the attorneys in the Anschlag case that yesterday would probably close the evidence, drew an unusually large crowd in and about the Court House. At 10 A. M. the defendant appeared, and the trial was resumed by Attorney Peyton, who asked that the jury might be allowed to retire, as he wished to make a motion which he considered it would not be proper for the jury to hear. The jury was ordered to retire, and Mr. Peyton asked that he be allowed to examine the jury as to whether they had knowledge of the decision of the jury called to investigate the sanity of Anschlag. The privilege was denied, and the case resumed by the calling of Dr. G. C. Kirkpatrick, on the part of the defense, who testified: I am a practicing physician, and have been engaged in my profession for nineteen years. I have had some experience in cases of insanity. Blows on the head not infrequently cause insanity. Dr. Kirkpatrick here interposed an objection, stating that if he was to be used as an expert he was entitled to and demanded his fee in advance. The Court assured the Doctor that if such fees were due, and there was a precedent for the claim, it would be allowed him. The fracture of the inner skull plate often produces insanity. The seat of the disease of insanity is usually in the cerrebellum. Hereditary insanity is generally believed in, among medical men. There is such a thing as homicidial insanity. There are many cases of mania or insanity in which at times the individuals come to such a state of mind that they do what they know to be wrong, having no power over their actions. Many persons so afflicted seek their friends at such times and request them to prevent their doing what they feel impelled to do.

Persons laboring under such insanity often commit crime and may afterwards readily confess their actions or on the other hand may carefully and shrewdly conceal the offense.

This kind of insanity is called emotional or moral insanity. A diseased brain is always coupled with insanity.

While waiting for the return of a subpoena for Dr. R. C. Kirkpatrick, the District Attorney stated to the Court that he wished to recall Mr. Decker which he had previously announced he would do.

ANTON DECKER

Testified: I live in Santa Ana, I have lived in America since 1865. I have known Anschlag. Met him first at Anaheim on the 18th of January. In the hotel at that place he employed me to work for him at $30 per month. He told me he would meet me at Santa Ana on Tuesday, which he did at 10 A. M. on that day. While at Anaheim I noticed that Anschlag always read German newspapers so I spoke to him and became acquainted.
He told me he had a ranch at Garden Grove and asked me if I could cook, plow, and care for a ranch. I said yes, and then he hired me for $30 per month. When I met him at Santa Anna he had a wagon and there was a plow, trunk, basket and several packages in it. We did not stop but drove direct to Garden Grove. We put up the horses and then had some lunch. I did not cook anything for there was plenty of grub on the table. There was mutton chops, plenty of pies, bread, milk &c. I noticed the bed in the bed room and it was made up and looked as if no one had slept on it. In the afternoon I washed the buggy and cleaned the horses off. They were very muddy and in a bad condition. Next day I got up early and prepared breakfast. Anschlag did not get up until 7 o'clock. That day we moved some hen-coops in the forenoon and hauled manure into the orchard in the afternoon. We were in the kitchen when arrested. A good many men watched us with shot guns and pistols. I remember that one gentleman asked him where he got the money to purchase the farm. He said, "Oh, I have plenty of money. I keep four or five thousand dollars in my satchel all the time." He said he got $2600 a few weeks ago.

MISS LUCIA HILL

being recalled by the District Attorney, testified: I know the handwriting of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock. (Papers partly burned, which were picked up at the pepper tree, near the grave of the Hitchcocks, were shown.) I recognize the writing as that of Mrs. Hitchcock. Witness pointed out the letters "Louis" and said that was the name of her aunt, her name being Louise.

"I also recognize among the fragments the writing of Mr. Hitchcock."

anschlag-garden-grove.A18:
ANSCHLAG'S REMAINS.
They Are Inspected By Many Curious People.
HIS ANTE-MORTEM STATEMENT.
Frank Fray Gave Him the Poison and Wolff Told Him How To Use It.
The sudden and unexpected release of Anschlag from the grip of the law by a dose of poison was the common topic of conversation on the streets yesterday. On every side were heard expressions of regret that the sentence could not be carried out. It will be remembered that when the crime was first discovered by the farmers about Garden Grove and the murder traced to Anschlag, he narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of an infuriated populace. When better counsel prevailed and the law was left to take its course, it was generally conceded that the case was so clear against the murderer that there could be no possible avenue open for his escape. The trial went its course to its end and it was evident that the man must surely hang. There was no possibility of a pardon from the Governor, and no other means of escape seemed to open before him. The chance of suicide seldom occurred to anyone, although it was known that poison had on several occasions been found in his possession. The fact that the man was such an arrant coward and that he was quite without friends who would be likely to send him any delicacies in the shape of strychnine or arsenic, made it quite improbable that he would ever manage to take his own life. The event therefore was a complete surprise, and was the occasion of profound disappointment to a good many people.

The body was taken from the jail yesterday morning about 3 o'clock, and carried to the undertaking rooms of Orr & Sutch, on Spring street, to await a Coroner's inquest. When the doors were opened at 6 o'clock a number of people were waiting to be admitted. Throughout the day a stream of curious men, women and children poured in and out of the undertaking rooms, passing around the body which lay upon a stretcher in a large room back of the office. The general verdict was that his face was quite as repulsive as it had been described to be, and the sentiment was frequently expressed that he would have looked better with a rope around his neck.
After the body was removed from the jail a more thorough search was made of his cell, and in the murderer's bed was found the statement on which he had been at work when he was seen by the reporter Wednesday evening. It was written in German, and the translation is as follows:

Every man, after reading these lines, will learn that the death sentence pronounced upon me did not terminate as it should, but that I have taken my own life. No doubt many persons who do not know me will say that I lacked the courage to suffer the penalty of the law, but that is not true. So far as I am concerned, I would have had courage enough; yes, even more than that—I would have shown to the many people who would have come to see me die that I was not afraid. When on the scaffold I would have reminded those who had strayed from the path of virtue and righteousness to again return to it. If they had violated the laws of God and had seen my ending in life, I would have told them not to continue to sin, but try and lead a pure and honest life; to discard the ways of the wicked and learn the bidding of God. I think that the death I have chosen is not an easy one, and it will cause me a great deal of pain and suffering. Certainly that shows I am not lacking in courage. No; the reason I did not wish to die on the gallows was an entirely different one. I come of a very respectable family and was reared in good society, and enjoyed the advantages of a gentleman's life. Therefore I have feeling and am ashamed of my disgrace, and am determined, as matters stand, to cut short my life in this way and not to end it on the gallows. First, I wanted to spare my relatives and friends the disgrace and humiliation of allowing myself to be hanged. Second, I did not wish to disgrace the whole of the German nation, which I hope will rightly understand my feelings. Therefore, it was the disgrace alone which prevented me from dying on the gallows. Although they have thoroughly searched and watched me, I have had the poison for six months. I did what I thought was for the best. I have made peace with my God and I feel that God has forgiven me. Although I have sunk so low and deep, He has, through Jesus Christ, washed my soul from all sins. And notwithstanding my poor lost soul, He will not judge me harshly, but will forgive me. Amen.

J. H. Fritz Anschlag.

Of course, had there been the least suspicion as to what the document contained it would have been very eagerly read by the jailors earlier in the evening, but as Anschlag has been writing much of the time of late it was allowed to pass unnoticed until he should be ready to send it away.

No new facts have been developed as to the source of the poison. Every possible precaution seems to have been taken by the jailors to prevent just what happened, but the craft of the murderer outwitted them. It is evident that he had had the poison concealed in the piece of tobacco for some time, and it can hardly be doubted that it is a part of the quantity which Frank Fray brought to the jail. The post mortem examination will be held this morning at 9 and the physicians of the city will probably be present en masse. The inquest will be held in the course of the day if a satisfactory time can be arranged by the Coroner.:

august-richards-halleck-1888-11-11.A1:
DASTARDLY OUTRAGE.
Robbery and Probably Murder.
Last night shortly after 10 o'clock Uncle Billy Hazeltine, who occupies the Murphy house at Halleck, went over from the hotel with the purpose of retiring. On entering the house he proceeded to the head of the stairway where he was assaulted by some one lying in wait. Mr. Hazeltine, who by the way is somewhat feeble, being about 70 years old, was knocked down, severely beaten and robbed of $45, all the money he had about him. Before the victim could give the alarm his assailant had made his escape. On examination it was found that the thief had ransacked the house, but had found nothing of value.

Ed Kelly, from whom we obtain the facts, came down on the early train this morning with the hope that the robber might possibly be found, but up to this writing there is no clue to his whereabouts. It is earnestly hoped that the wretch may be arrested and brought to speedy justice. In all probability if he had been caught before leaving Halleck the citizens of that town would have saved the county the expense of a trial, as Uncle Billy is esteemed almost as a father by a host of friends there and elsewhere in the county. Mr. Keily fears that the old gentleman will not recover from his truises, as he is seriously injured.
august-richards-halleck-1888-11-11.A2:
The Assassin Arrested.
August Richards, supposed to be the man who beat and robbed Uncle Billy Hazeltine at Halleck last Friday night, was arrested by W. J. Hanks last Saturday evening, between sun-down and dark, about three miles from Deeth where he was skulking in the sagebrush. The prisoner was taken to Deeth and turned over to Constable McAdams who brought him down yesterday afternoon and lodged him in jail. Having waived examination he will be kept in custody to await the action of the Grand Jury. Richards served a term in our county jail some time ago on conviction of malicious mischief committed at Sprucemont. During the past Summer he worked for M. Glaser, near Peko.

A reward of $50 was offered for the arrest of the culprit, and W. J. Hanks having made the arrest will receive the reward which he will turn over to Uncle Billy, the victim of the assassin.

Considerable excitement among the passengers on the train, and amusement for the citizens, was created when the train arrived at Halleck where an impromptu gallows was erected, to which was attached the rope with hangman's noose, and when the train stopped a delegation of five determined men entered the car and demanded the prisoner who, by the way, was almost frightened to death. After a palaver of a few minutes in which the Constable protested that he would guard the prisoner with his life and would kill the first man that laid hands on him, the would-be lynchers left the train, to the great relief of the culprit who was as white as a corpse, thinking his time had come.

Uncle Billy has so far recovered from his injuries as to be able to come down on yesterday's train for the purpose of serving as a witness at the preliminary examination, and hopes soon to be all right again. Our item in Saturday's issue with regard to the money taken was an error, as the robber got only $35; and $34 was found on the person of the prisoner when arrested.

betsy-clark-camden-1888-12-08.A1:
DIED TO SAVE HER HONOR.
A Woman Killed by a Negro who Met her on a Lonely Road.

COLUMBUS, S. C., Dec. 9.—On a lonely road in Kershaw county, Betsy Clark yesterday morning met Emanuel Gaskin, colored. The man insulted her and then attempted to assault her. The woman fought bravely, and Gaskin was getting the worst of it, when he suddenly drew a knife and stabbed her in the throat. Betsy turned and ran, but the negro followed and knocked down with a lightwood knot. He then severed her head from the body, and, placing the knife on her breast, left the body in the road.

When the murder was discovered a search was at once organized, and Gaskin was apparently among the most earnest in the hunt. He overdid the business, however, and a white man, noticing his excitement, charged him with the crime, which he furiously denied. He was taken before a Trial Justice, where blood was found on his clothing, and he confessed the whole thing. The crowd, principally negroes, was about to lynch Gaskin, but he was hurried away to jail.
betsy-clark-camden-1888-12-08.A2:
A Cool Murderer.
A Cool Murderer.

Emanuel Gaskins, a negro, stabbed Bessie Clark near Camden, S. C., and then deliberately severed her head from her body, and placing the knife on her breast coolly walked away. The murder was discovered later by a party of sportsmen, and a search was at once instituted for the murderer. Gaskins himself soon joined in the search, and was most vehement in denunciation of the crime. A spot of blood was discovered on his sleeve by one of the party, who promptly accused him of being the murderer. He at first denied the charge, but upon being taken before r magistrate he soon weakened and made a full concession. The crowd attempted to lynch him, but the Sheriff and his deputies rescued him and finally lodged him in jail at Camden.

TWO NEGROES LYNCHED.
Each One was Eager to Murder White People of the Neighborhood.
NEW ORLEANS, Jan. 4. A special from
People of the Neighborhood.

NEW ORLEANS, Jan. 4.—A special from Meridian, Miss., says: "In the neighborhood of the Robert's place, twelve miles northwest of this city, there has been great excitement since the Wednesday after Christmas. The trouble appears to have originated from bad feeling engendered among the negroes of that locality by the lynching of a negro who entered the house of Mr. Houston at midnight, and attempted to murder one of the inmates with an axe. The negro was recognized and afterwards hanged. Since that time the negroes have been making threats and there has been bad feeling generally. Just prior to the holidays an old negro man reported that a conspiracy was brewing to kill certain white men in that locality.

THE REPORT CORROBORATED.

"This report was corroborated by overhearing a conversation between a negro reporting the existence of a co spiracy and one Bud Spears, who, it was said, was the ringleader among the negroes. Satisfactory evidence being produced as to Spears' intention and his determination to carry out his threat, a party of masked men rode up to his house on Wednesday, Dec. 26, and riddled him with buckshot. Another negro who was at Spears' house was wounded in the hand, but made his escape. Since that time the white people of that section have been ferreting out the conspirators, and arresting negroes and trying them before a justice of the peace. Seven negroes were under arrest yesterday, and upon investigation were acquitted. A number of men are still under arms, but things are gradually quieting down."

Speedy Punishment Follows the Crime of a Negro in Halifax County, Va.

OF A Negro in Hallifax County, Va.
DANVILLE, VA., July 27.—In Hallifax County, near Meadsville, yesterday, Bruce Younger, colored, committed an assault upon Mrs. Robert Dodge, who was in a delicate condition. He was taken before a justice of the peace and sent to jail at Hallifax Court-House to await the action of the grand jury. THEY SWUNG HIM.
A DETERMINED BAND OF HALIFAX COUNTY LYNCHERS.
A Negro Paye the Penalty of Attempting
a Fiendish Crime—Quick
Work.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
SOUTH BOSTON VA. July 27—In

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

South Boston, VA. July 27.—In the neighborhood of Meadsville, a quiet little village about ten miles from Halifax Courthouse, lives the family of Mr. R. C. Dodd. He is held in high esteem by his neighbors and the community generally. Wednesday night the 25th instant he was absent at a neighbor's house, expecting to go to Charlotte next day. He left his wife and children at home. Mrs. Dodd retired early and was aroused from her sleep about 1 o'clock by the presence of a negro man in her bedroom. He had raised the window of the room and before she was awakened was on her bed attempting the fiendish purpose that controlled him. An awful struggle, took place, the lady all the time making heartrending screams for help. The man, who worked for Mr. Dodd, occupied an out-house on the lot, and with him that night were his brother and two other negroes. He left his companions in his night-clothes, and, as stated, entered the room through the window. Mrs. Dodd's struggles and screams were so prolonged and desperate that her assailant finally became frightened and ran out of the front door of the house, but came around to Mrs. Dodd's window and asked why she was screaming. The other negro men then came up.

THE ARREST.

Yesterday morning a negro named Bruce Younger was arrested for the crime. He was fully identified by Mrs. Dodd, and was immediately brought to Halifax Courthouse and put in jail. Late yesterday evening it was rumored on the streets here and at Halifax Courthouse that Younger would be lynched by indignant citizens from Meadsville and throughout the county.

The officials of the county, of course, heard of the rumor and at once began to consider how to prevent the proposed lynching. They were met by the troublesome fact that there was no place the prisoner could be securely confined in, and as their every movement was watched they feared to take the negro from the jail because he might be rescued by his friends and a terrible affray between
confined in, and as their every movement was watched they feared to take the negro from the jail because he might be rescued by his friends and a terrible affray between white and colored people he precipitated. It was therefore deemed best to place a guard at the jail, but in this also great difficulty was experienced.

WERE SCARCE.

All the young men of the village were said to be at a dance; at any rate none could be found. Indeed, all the men of the town seemed to have vanished. Finally, however, Sheriff Moore succeeded in pressing into service six or seven gentlemen, who could not escape him, and they waited at the jail for further developments.

AT MIDNIGHT.

At about midnight a party of horsemen reached the jail. They at once demanded the keys, which the sheriff refused. Every man of the party seemed to have a pistol in his hand flashing and glittering in the moonlight. The party then issued orders for the court-yard, in which the jail is situated, to be cleared, which was speedily done, the sheriff and his squad being completely helpless and overpowered. The men went about their work with great deliberation, for the yard was picketed all around with guards, while another force with a pick broke open the jail and commanded Younger to come out.

PROTESTED INNOCENCE.

The man refused and protested his innocence again and again. Pistols were placed at his breast and he then consented. Younger, with a handkerchief tied over his mouth, was finally brought out by his captors, who at once proceeded down towards Foot's creek, a few hundred yards from the town. Reaching there they told the man his last hour had come, and gave him five minutes in which to pray. Still protesting his innocence he knelt down upon the bank of the creek, and in the still, ghostly moonlight, the scene was one of intense awe and solemnity—the prisoner preparing to meet his terrible death, his executioners standing around grim, silent, and determined.

When the doomed man had finished his prayer a rope was placed around his neck and he was led upon the foot-bridge (about twelve feet high) that spans the creek. He was told that he must die and was urged to confess his guilt.

CONFESSION.

At the last moment he did so, saying that he was the guilty man, and that Mrs. Dodd's statement (which I have given above) was entirely correct. He said that while he had not accomplished the object of his assault he had entered Mrs. Dodd's room with that intention and had used every effort to succeed, and was only prevented by her struggles and screams and the fear that he would be discovered.

DROPPED OFF.

Everything being ready he was dropped from the bridge, but the fall being a very short one his neck was not broken.

MANY SHOTS.

The party then fired their pistols at him at short distance time and again, and the shots rang sharp and clear upon the midnight air. Younger's body hung from the bridge until this morning, when it was cut down and carried to the court-house room, where your correspondent saw it this morning.

The man's clothing was scorched and burned in several places from the fire of the pistols, and about twenty-five or thirty bullets took effect. His face was not disfigured. This is the first lynching that ever occurred in this county, and considering the circumstances it was the most quiet affair of the kind recently reported. Everybody, black as well as white, seems to think that the wretch met a deserved fate, and some of the severest denunciations of him I have heard have been from men of his own color.

LITTLE CONCEALMENT.

The party who did the work were not masked. Some slight attempts were made, but were very feeble. Very little attempt was made to conceal their features. It was made up of men from different parts of the county, and there was an entire absence of excitement or passion.

The act was but the swift vengeance of an outraged people. They met about two miles from Halifax Courthouse and held a full consultation, and it was determined that if the negro persisted in his innocence to the bitter end that the rope would be cut and he would be taken back to jail. He was only to be killed if he confessed.

Mrs. Dodd, at the time of the assault, was in a very delicate condition, and was terribly frightened and bruised and injured. At this writing it is feared she may not survive the shock. Indeed, it is reported that she died this morning.
danville-danville-1888-08-01.A5:
FROM HALIFAX COUNTY.
A Human Fiend Taken From Jail and Lynched—Death of an Estimable Man. [Special Carry-On Dedication]
[Special Correspondence.]
FAX COURTHOUSE VA. In

[Special Correspondence.]

HALIFAX COURTHOUSE, VA., July 27.—Editor Times: Early yesterday morning Bruce Younger (colored), was committed to jail charged with the hemious crime of rape upon Mrs. Robert Dodd, a white married lady, wife of a respectable farmer living near Meadsville. While the act was hellish enough, it was made doubly so by the ladies peculiar condition. Some time after midnight last night about one hundred men rode into town and secured their horses on the out side of the Court-house square, and proceeded to the jail. They were well organized and had a competent leader. After the men got over in the Courthouse square they threw out guards all around the jail. Not a man spoke a word, but the commands were given by signals. The jail keys were in the possession of the wife of the former jailor, and the lynchers could not obtain them, so they proceeded to batter down the doors, breaking locks, etc., when the cell was reached containing the prisoner they bound and gagged him, and at once proceeded to the place of execution, which was to a high footbridge near here across Toots Creek. Here I learn the man made a full confession of his crime, and he was allowed five minutes to pray. Then he was suspended between heaven and earth and his body riddled with bullets, after which the lynchers quietly departed. Mrs. Dodd is said to be in a critical condition, and a report reached here this morning that she is dead. I do not know whether the report is authentic. I do not believe in such work generally, but I do think this is a justifiable case. This is the first prisoner ever taken from jail in this county and executed.

Mr. W. A. Rogers, deputy clerk County Court, died on the 20th ultimo after a painful illness of eleven days. Mr. Rogers was connected with the clerk's offices of this county for the last twenty years. The deceased was a man of high character, was warm-hearted and generous. If the space could be spared I could fill the issue of your paper with deeds of charity and pleasing reminiscences of his office life, but nothing I could say would raise him in the estimation of the people of Halifax who knew him best, for we all loved him and had an exalted opinion of him. He leaves a devoted wife and two daughters to shed tears over his grave, and nothing I can say would wipe away or stay one of them. Peace to his ashes.

Saturday.
A black ravisher of a white married woman was captured and lynced at Danville, Va., yesterday.

Newton and Will Paris have been arrested at Tulip, Tex., for murdering two negroes in Indian territory.

The will of the late E. P. Roe, the author, leaves his property to his wife and to his family after her death.

Jacob Heem, Samuel Ditson and William Anderson were drowned while bathing at Omaha, Neb., last evening.

Patrick Burke and Henry Halverson lost their lives by suffocation while cleaning out a well near Crystal Falls, Mich.

At Pawnee City, Neb., last night an hotel cook stabbed and killed his sweetheart because she would not marry him.

Seven negroes and a white man were arrested at Bonham, Tex., yesterday, for robbing Texas & Pacific freight cars.

Cable communication was opened between New York and Hayti and San Domingi, West Indies, via Santiago de Cuba, yesterday.

The examination of Geo. A. Clark, the al leged dynamiter, was continued to August 2 by the defense, at Aurora, Ill., yesterday.

William Gill, of Richland township, Illinois, hanged himself yesterday, because two of his children had married against his wish.

Neil Costello, a brakeman on a 'Frisco train, was fatally shot by a tramp who was stealing a ride yesterday, near Springfield, Mo.

The Illinois Association of Expert Judges of Swine met at Decatur, Ill., yesterday, and elected H. O. Cowell, of Mechanicsburg, president.

Gov. Hill of New York has commuted the sentence of Chiara Cignerale, the Italian woman who killed her husband, to imprisonment for life.

Bill Miller, a white man of Hiseville, Ky., won a wager and 50 cents by biting off the head of a live adder which he had caught in the field.

Glass bottle blowers and the manufacturers held a conference at Pittsburg yesterday and amicably arranged a scale of wages for the ensuing year.
Dave Replogle, an enterprising stenographer of St. Joseph, Mo., hid himself in the ventilator of the opera house to hear the proceedings of a Brotherhood meeting, but was captured and the police judge imposed a fine.

Mary Dyehouse, aged 13, an inmate of the Princeton (Ind.) Orphans' home, made three unsuccessful attempts to burn the home yesterday because she had been whipped for thieving. She will be sent to the reform school.

The hearing of the Chicago, Kansas City and St. Paul railway case against the interstate commission at Dubuque, Io., was finished yesterday. The points to be decided are the application of the long and short haul clause, where there is competition with a water line, and the cutting of rates.

William L. Penny, jr., and Robert Barnett charged with "buncoing" William Murdock out of $10,000, were placed on trial at Pittsburg, Pa. WEST AND SOUTH.
REPRESENTATIVES of organized bodies of locomotive engineers and firemen and switchmen met in convention on the 24th at St. Joseph, Mo., to consider their common interests in general and the "Q" strike in particular.

At ten o'clock on the night of the 24th a rainbow was distinctly seen during a rainstorm at Princeton, Ind.

RICHARD AIKEN, aged thirty-five years, had both eyes blown out by the accidental discharge of a gun on the 24th near Versailles, Ky.

JOHN GRAYSON and Lillburn Trigg were fatally shot in a quarrel on the 24th at Abingdon, Va., and the mother of Trigg died from the shock caused by her son's death.

G. W. BLEWETT was on the 24th nominated for Congress by the Prohibitionists of the Second Indiana district.

The shoe factory of Krippendorf, Dittman & Co., at Cincinnati, was destroyed by fire on the 24th. Loss, $310,000.

PROHIBITIONISTS of the Tenth Illinois district on the 24th nominated J. H. Sedgwick for Congress.

In Virginia hail tell to the depth of five inches on the 25th, in some places completely destroying growing crops and gardens.

Brutal Assault Followed by Lynchling
DANVILLE, VA., July 27.—At an early hour yesterday morning, Bruce Younger, colored, met Mrs. Robert Dood, wife of a prominent Halifax county farmer, in the road near Meadsville, in that county, and by force and threats overpowered and criminally assaulted her. She dragged herself to her house and reported to her husband. In two hours Younger was arrested and sent to jail by a magistrate to await indictment by the grand jury. Last night a body of men, over one hundred in number, surrounded the jail at Halifax Court House, overpowered the jailor, took Younger out and hanged him to a bridge near the village. The body was found by early passers this morning. It had many bullet holes in it, and the clothing was partly burned, showing that the first intention was to burn the brute, and that, perhaps, appearing revolting, he was hanged, and, while swinging, was shot. Public sentiment endorsed the lynching.

An Incendiary's Confession. WORCESTER, Oct. 12.—James A. Cary, the confessed Spencer incendiary, set fire to the house of Leander Sibley, Oct. 2. Cary occupied the house himself, and carried considerable insurance on his furniture. In his confession he says that he lighted the fire in the basement and went to bed, thinking some one would see the blaze and arouse him. No one saw it, and it gained such headway that he was forced to jump from the window in order to save his life. In so doing he struck on his head, inflicting injuries from which he is only now recovering. He says that he set the fire to get the insurance. He is now in jail here. The occurrence was regarded as any similar calamity would be, until Mr. Stolfe recently gave some startling evidence of emotional insanity. In one of her fits she made mention of having drugged her boy and then hanged him to avoid suspicion, leaving a box near by, making it appear that he had used it to enable him to commit suicide.
