george-w-blanchard-washington-1888-01-17.A2:
BESSIE MORRISON'S STORY.
Lawyer Carrington Tells it to a Jury
while Bessie Sheds Tears of Sorrow.
To-day, in the Criminal Court, Judge Montgomery, the trial of Bessie, alias Elizabeth Morrison, a rather handsome girl, seventeen years old, for the larceny of $997 of Geo. W. Blanchard, alias D. W. Donaldson, at Richmond, Va., on the 6th instant, was commenced—Mr. Sheppard prosecuting, and Messrs. Campbell Carrington and T. C. Taylor for the defendant. During the pathetic opening address of Mr. Carrington the girl frequently shed tears. The latter said the questions before the trial ended would be not as to the guilt or innocence of this girl, but what should be done with the prosecuting witness. It was the same old touching story—a systematic piece of villainy, an experienced man of the world and unsophisticated country girl and ruin. He said that away off in the northwest part of Michigan, in June last, dwelt a family—a father of sixty-five, a mother of sixty, several daughters and a son, the defendant being the baby of the family. Handbills describing one of the "Greatest Shows on Earth," consisting of a few monkeys and monstrosities of nature, were distributed. One of these was taken to that home by the brother and read, and on a Thursday evening she rode with her brother to town and saw the show. This girl, then wearing short dresses, talked of the show with her neighbor, Nettie Banks, and with her went the show. There the proprietor feasted his eye upon her with an unholy purpose in his heart, and when the performance was over she was told that the proprietor wished to see her. She declined to go to him, and he came to the buggy in which she was about to return home. The result was that she was taken to a hotel, and she sent word home that she had gone to visit a friend, and next that she had left town. Then she found herself some hundreds of miles from her home and her ruin was accomplished by the man who represented himself as a single man. Mr. Carrington then described their travels, saying that they passed as husband and wife and occupied the same room; that he regarded what was in her possession as their mutual property, and that he promised to marry her. He claimed that the prosecuting witness had dropped the money, and he did not accuse her of taking the money until she had become tired of his closeness, and being in a delicate condition, proposed to return to her parents, and he then threatened that, before she should go, he would send her to the penitentiary.

BLANCHARD'S TESTIMONY.

The prosecuting witness, Geo. W. Blanchard, took the stand and testified that he missed the money ($697) in Richmond, Va., on December 14, but suspected others, who were arrested, and it was in Baltimore that he suspected her and caused her arrest. On cross-examination the witness denied seeing the girl in the buggy or taking her away from her home. He denied that he ever
caused the money to be given to the person who wanted it. The person who wanted it was a man named John Doe. John Doe was a man who was a man who was a
fair grounds, they roomed at the St. Charles Hotel.
After recess the defendant resumed the stand.
While in Richmond, she said, she learned that Blanchard was a married man. He ill-treated her and she took the money. She afterward told him that she had the money, and he said he was satisfied. She said he abused and assaulted her. She then asked him for her trunk, as she wanted to go home on account of the manner in which she had been treated and the condition she was in. He refused to give her the trunk unless the money was returned, which she refused to do, because she thought the money belonged to her on account of her life having been ruined by him. During the time she was with him he did not give her more than £5. She denied that she had acted improperly with any man since she left Ashland with the prosecuting witness.
Testimony was offered as to the defendant's condition and the defense closed its case.

A VERDICT OF NOT GUILTY.

The case was submitted without argument and with a brief charge, and in ten minutes a verdict of not guilty was rendered, which was received with suppressed applause.

THEY THREATENED LYNCHING.
An Exciting Scene at the End of Bessie Morrison's Trial.
Yesterday afternoon after the verdict of not guilty was rendered in the Criminal Court in the case of the young girl Bessie Morrison, who was charged with the larceny of $097 from George W. Blanchard, an itinerant showman, quite a scene took place in the court. On the entry of the verdict Mr. T. C. Taylor, who, with Mr. Carrington, appeared for the defendant, asked an order directing that the money be restored to the defendant, "to put it out of the way of Blanchard, who, he said, was mean enough to do anything to replevin it." This remark was received with applause, during which the foreman of the jury said it was their request that the money be given her. Assistant District Attorney Coyle, who had been sent for here appeared. He said it was customary when a defendant was acquitted to give him or her the property. This announcement was greeted with applause, during which the court made the order giving the money to the girl, and adjourned. The judge left the bench, and immediately the crowd, jurors included, flocked around the defendant, extending congratulations. Blanchard got into the crowd, and taking hold of her arm said: "I want to talk with you, Bessie." She pulled away and got behind Mr. Carrington. The latter asked if she wanted to talk to Blanchard, and she replied: "No, I never want to see him." Blanchard asked: "How about the money?" and Mr. Carrington replied: "Miss Bessie and myself will look after the money. You go home and look after your monkeys, and if you don't go quickly we'll string you up." At this point some one exclaimed: "Hang the d————!" Other cries were raised, and many in the crowd made for Blanchard, almost lifting him from his feet. Officer McTaggert and others seized him, however, and quickly hustled him from the room, saving him from the fury of the crowd. A large number of people escorted Miss Bessie and her counsel to police headquarters, where the money was returned to her. She left on an evening train for her home in Michigan.

KILLED BY A FALSE FRIEND.

Charles McKane Lured into the Mountains and Murdered by an Ex-Convict.
Mountains and Murdered by an Ex-Convict.

DENVER, Col., Nov. 3.—About a week ago George Wetherell induced Charles McKane, of Pueblo, to start with him for the mountains to visit a mining camp. Nothing more was heard of McKane until yesterday when his mutilated remains were found in Beaver creek. His head had almost been severed with an axe, while his body was shockingly mangled. Wetherell had murdered his victim while he slept. He then abstracted $238 from McKane's pocket, stole his team and drove to Denver. He could not satisfactorily account for the team and the police arrested him on suspicion of being a horse thief, but when a bloody axe was found in his wagon, it appeared certain that he had committed murder. When the news of McKane's death was received, the suspicion was verified. Wetherell was sent to the penitentiary on a life sentence eighteen years ago, for the murder of a sheep herder, but under the law passed two years ago, making twenty-five years the maximum imprisonment. Wetherell, with his commutation for good behavior, secured his release. He was taken to Canon City last night and placed in the penitentiary, as there was talk of lynching him.

Blaine addressed three large gatherings in Brooklyn.

The New York Press figures Harrison's plurality at 15,050.

Thurman addressed a large meeting at Nelsonville, O., on Saturday.

A negro at Blackshear. Ga., was lynched for assaulting a white woman.

May wheat opened in Chicago on Saturday $1 17½ and closed at $1 14.

Two young rowdies assaulted Marshal Brennan, of Hope, Ind., and in the encounter one was killed and the other mortally wounded.

The Republicans and Democrats paraded at Indianapolis, the rival displays passing one another at certain points on the line of march. The best of good feeling prevailed.

William Edgar Shepard and Miss Gettie Moore Guynne, the youngest sister of Mrs. Cornelius Vanderbilt, will be married on Wednesday at the house of Mrs. Vanderbilt.

The jury in the celebrated common-law marriagecase of Ida against Frank Bowman at Chicago, has returned a verdict granting Ida Bowman a divorce, which establishes the validity of the common-law marriage.

Captain Joshua Slocum of the wrecked bark Aquidneck, who is on his way in a thirty-foot canoe from Rio Grande del Sur to Washington, a distance of 4,500 miles, has been sighted off the South Carolina coast.

A match between the Right-weights McAuliffe, of Williamsburg, N. Y., and Myers, of Streator, Ill., has been arranged. The terms are that the men are to fight to a finish with skin-tight gloves, Marquis of Queensberry rules, for $2,500 a side.

FOREIGN.

Lord Tennyson is seriously ill.

Germany will strengthen her fleet.

The Prussian Minister at the Vatican has been recalled.

The Czar and Czarina were injured in the recent accident.

The Bank of England loses £70,000 on bills with forged indorsements.

It is rumored that Lord Sackville will be made Governor-General of Canada.

The Pope has received a gift of a million of dollars from India and Australia.

The Czar's visit to the Crimea has added significant interest to the Eastern question.

A French Court has ordered that the affairs of the American Exchange in Paris be wound up under the supervision of the Court.

Josephine Simon, a young Oakland girl, made her debut at a concert in Albert Hall on Wednesday. The critics consider her very promising.

Advices from Saigon say pirates attacked a post, consisting of forty men of the Foreign Legation, and seven pagodas in Tonquin, and killed but one man.

The Pope has named December 31st for special thanksgiving services in the Catholic churches throughout the world for grace during the year of the Papal Jubilee.

The marriage of Prince Alexander, of Battenberg, to Princess Victoria, of Germany, will probably take place at Windsor when Empress Victoria visits her mother during the latter part of this month.

Rain fell on Saturday at Santa Rosa, Marysville and Anderson.

Cornelius Driscoll fell off the steamer El Capitan and was drowned.

John Hutchinson shot and killed his brother at Blackfoot, Idaho.

The Prescott stage was stopped by a highwayman on Saturday and robbed.

The body of a tramp was found buried in a pile of lumber at Walla Walla.

Joseph Wostalle, a young man, was mysteriously murdered near Bonham, Tex.

At Stockton on Saturday the home club defeated the Haverlys by a score of 4 to 3.

Mrs. R. D. Butler has been appointed Deputy School Superintendent of San Diego county.

A. D. Calver tried to ride the cowcatcher of a locomotive at Coronado, Friday night, and was killed.

A Spanish land grant over 200 years old has been sprung on the people in a large area in New Mexico.

Heavy shipments of beans are being made from various parts of the State to Boston and other Eastern markets. The brown bread accompaniment is an Eastern production.

george-witherell-canyon-city-1888-11-03.A7:
SHOT WHILE ASLEEP.
Details of the Terrible Crime Near Canon City in Colorado.
City in Colorado.

From the Salt Lake "Tribune": A crime similar to Hopt's was committed near Canon City on October 26, the victim's body not being found for a week. Charles R McCain started from Pueblo with two teams, having George Witherell in company, who represented himself to be a mine foreman, and who engaged McCain to haul ore. The two camped near Canon City, and in the night Witherell shot McCain as the latter was lying asleep in his blankets, the ball going through his head and through the wagon bottom and flattened on a stone, with particles of bone, blood and blanket on it. As the victim's death was not as sudden as he expected, Witherell beat him over the head with an ax till the head was a mass of jelly. Then Witherell took McCain's body and buried it in a deep gully, burning hay over the spots of blood on the earth, to obliterate them.

Witherell took the teams next day and moved to another camp, from which he wrote a letter to his victim's wife, telling her to meet him at Grand Junction, as he had sold the teams and bought a ranch.

Mrs. McCain saw the writing was not her husband's, was alarmed, and asked the officers to look into the matter. The officers telegraphed all over that region, and Witherell was arrested in Denver with McCain's teams in his possession. They began a search for McCain's body, as by that time there was little doubt that he was murdered, the hole in the wagon bed and the bloody ax being strong witnesses, and officer Wellington McCandlass found the body buried as stated.

Witherell recently sold two teams at Pueblo, and it is now suspected that he got them also by murdering the own. The citizens of Canyon City were wild with excitement and took yossession of two trains on which they supposed Witherell was, with intent to lynch him, but he was held in Pueblo, whither he had been taken prior to the finding of McCain's body. Witherell has recently been released from the Colorado penitentiary after a service of sixteen years for the murder of an inoffensive sheepherder. ____

ELECTRIC STORM.
CONSIDERABLE DAMAGE BY LIGHTNING IN NORTH CAROLINA.
People Stunned and a Mouse Nearly Demolished-A Senseless Scare- Browned.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

News has been received of the drowning of Romulus Griggs, of Currituck county, by his falling overboard from a sloop.

A heavy electric storm struck the town of Southport yesterday. Several dwellings were badly damaged and a number of persons stunned. In one case the entire front of a dwelling was torn away.

Telegrams were received to-day by the Mayor of Raleigh and the Superintendent of Health of this county from the authorities of Goldsboro' stating that only one case of yellow-fever existed there and that it was far out of town and carefully isolated. A telegram to the authorities also confirmed my specials of yesterday to the Dispatch that there is no yellow-fever at Newberne or near it. This senseless scare about fever existing at Newberne has agitated thousands of people. There were also equally false rumors this morning that Wiggs, the man who is sick near Goldsboro', had died of black vomit, and that three more cases had developed there. The fact is that there are doubts whether Wiggs has yellow-fever at all, and if he has it is of a mild type.

The Republican organ to-day asserts that Charles Price, of Salisbury, who it was claimed would support Fowle and the Democratic ticket, will not only vote for Dockery but will take the stump for him. The same paper practically concedes the election of Simmons (Democrat) to Congress from the Second district.

The North Carolina Local Ministers' Conference begins at Rutherford College, Burke county, to-morrow, and ends on the 27th. It is a large and important gathering of the local Methodist preachers in the State. A large assembly hall has been built at the meeting-place for the use of the conference.

The authorities of Wilmington are taking prompt action both with regard to the cleansing of their city and of securing it against invasion by yellow fever. Passengers who are suspected are stopped at the railway "Y," about a mile from the city, and are then sent away. Detectives are on each train that passes Florence, S. C., north-bound, and these "spot" any cases which need looking after. The system appears to be complete and to be working well, and as a result there is no fear of fever at Wilmington.

The Independent Republicans of New Hanover county, who recently split off from the main branch of their party, will hold a regular convention next Saturday, and nominate a ticket for county offices and the Legislature. This movement is primarily dissatisfaction with Judge Russell and other white leaders. A negro preacher is actually to preach a sermon in reply to Judge Russell's assertion that the negroes are "savages."

The Democrats of Durham have taken the Third party by the throat. That party has developed much strength there in some way, and at last the action referred to became a necessity. The Democrats say very pointedly that a Democrat who votes for the Third party in effect casts half a vote for the Republican nominees, and is therefore half Republican. The Democrats have therefore cleared their decks for a straightout fight with Republicans, Third party people, and Independents.

The State Fruit Fair, which ended today, was an entire success, and its results greatly gratify the North Carolina Horticultural Association. It has strengthened the association. There is one matter which the officers of the association desire impressed upon the people of the State, and that is that every farmer should set out fruit trees. Such a course, they say, would greatly increase and add to home comforts. There is a ready market for all good fruit. The association will urge the people in an address to plant such trees and to give care to fruit. Hundreds of once fine orchards in the State have been worthless for years on account of inattention.

It is reported that in parts of Chatham county there has not been a good rain since June 1st.

It is said that a branch railway, thirty-five miles long, will be built by the Wilmington and Weldon road from Burgaw into Onslow county.

Robert Leeson Porter, the mysterious ex-prisoner, arrived here this morning at 7 o'clock from Weldon, where he was found last night. He was accompanied by a son of Solicitor Argo, of this city, was well dressed, and is in better spirits. As soon as possible he will be sent to his family in Ireland, which has so long searched for him.

Your correspondent had a long talk with Porter to-day. His mind is yet unsettled, but he can give some sort of an idea of his wanderings. He left here Friday night and went to Garner, eight miles southeast of Raleigh, then went to Eagle Rock, ten miles east of there. There he got under houses. The people who had seen him in jail recognized him and ran him out, threatening to kill him. He then fled to Rolesville, always keeping in the road. From Rolesville he got to Youngsville Monday.

Sheriff Hamilton, of Alamance county, received information night before last that an attempt would be made to lynch a prisoner in the jail at Graham. He has removed the man to Chatham county jail at Pittsboro'.

This week, at Moore County Superior Court, an interesting case comes up. It is that of St. Clair, the editor of the Sanford Express, for libelling Judge Fred. Philips.

Last night's session of the alliance was very interesting, as was also this morning's session. There was a very full discussion of the establishment of a State business agency. Some delegates were in favor of appointing a man outside of the alliance to have charge of this agency. The majority of the members strongly opposed this, and finally W. A. Darden, of Greene county, was chosen State agent. It will be his duty to make all purchases for the alliances. All sub-alliances will let him know their wants. He will purchase with the money furnished him by the State trustee. The alliance this morning elected William A. Graham, of Lincoln county, to the latter position. He is to be responsible for funds received from the sub-alliances and will pay them to the State agent, being aided in this part of the work

JOTTINGS AND CLIPPINGS FROM OUR STATE EXCHANGES.

The town of Liberty, in Randolph county, on the Cape Fear and Yadkin Valley railway, had a fire on Saturday. Five houses, four stores and a livery stable were burned.

John E. Kelley, a graduate of Davidson college of the class of 1874, and of late a very successful teacher in Moore county, has been elected Principal of the Centennial Graded School of Raleigh.

States, the Atlantic and North Carolina railroad defaulter, is making a fight in Chicago. He has sued out a writ of habeas corpus. Colonel Hinsdale has gone to Chicago to argue the case against him.

The Randolph county Democratic Convention nominated for the Senate J. J. White; for the House of Representatives, T. J. Redding and Mike Bradshaw; for sheriff, E. A. Moffitt; Register of Deeds, W. F. Craven.

Concord Standard: On last Monday Mr. Robert L. Smith killed a rattlesnake at Mr. Cal Roger's on the Mt. Pleasant road. His snakeship measured five and a half feet in length and was six inches in circumference and had twelve rattles and a button.

Greensboro Patriot: An attempt was on foot to lynch the negro jailed at Graham a few days since for a criminal assault on a white woman, but the matter reached Sheriff Hamilton's ears and he removed the prisoner to Chatham county jail at Pittsboro.

We are in receipt of the premium list of the 28th annual fair of the North Carolina State Agricultural Society. It is to pay over $5,000 in premiums. The exhibition will take place on the 16, 17, 18 and 19th of October. The secretary, Eugene Harrell, is full of activity and usually succeeds. We predict the fair will be one of the most satisfactory held for years.

Hillsboro Recorder; We were shown this morning by Mr. T. E. Hill, the builder of the Strudwick house a Spanish quarter of a dollar of the date of 1774 which he found while tearing down the cealing of the old Turner mansion, built 60 or 70 years ago, there is nothing remarkable about the coin except that every figure and letter is, as bright and plain as when it come from the Spanish Mint 118 years ago.

Charlotte Chronicle: As briefly indicted on the third page of this morning's Chronicle, the Charlotte public building bill has been signed by President Cleveland and has become a law. It is a settled fact at last that we are to have our public building. The building will be located on the Mint lot, corner of Trade and Mint streets, midway between Independence square and the Richmond & Danville passenger depot. The site is a beautiful one, though not as near the square as might have been desired. The appropriation is for the sum of $85,000, and every cent of this (and maybe more, too,) is to be expended on the building alone, the ground being already the property of the United States.

Charlotte Chronicle: Seven of the gang of railroad hands who marched under the red flag and who were brought back to the city last Saturday under military escort, will this morning commence working the public roads of Mecklenburg, and some of them will grace the county chain gang through the heat of three summers. * * * It was a pretty good haul, but had sheriff Cooper brought in the whole gang, Judge Meares would have given us a force of laborers sufficient to macadamize all our county roads in much less time than is now calculated on. The sheriff and his deputy, Mr. Clanton, went as far as Mount Mourne last Sunday in search of eight more offenders, but could not come up with them. The termination of this trouble is regarded with great satisfaction by our people, many of whom want to induce Judge Meares to come up and live with us all the time.

THE TWIN STATES.
NORTH CAROLINA.
Walter Alvis Thompson, who during the war with Mexico was color sergeant of Jeff Davis' regiment, the Mississippi Rifles, died at his home near Hillsboro, N. C. His age was 78.

There was a terrific storm at Raleigh Sunday night. The wind blew a gale, the rain fell in torrents and the electric display was brilliant and fearful.

Two prisoners broke jail at Pittsboro Friday night. Their names are Mack Miken and William Minter. One of them had been carried there from Alamance a few days before to escape lynching. He was in jail on the charge of rape.

Dixie Edwards, white, went to the house of Ben Glasgow, colo., in Vance county, calling him to the door shot him with a shotgun, breaking his legs. The negro had incurred Edward's displeasure because he held information against him that would probably convict him of violation of the revenue laws. Edwards has fled. One of Glasgow's legs will have to be amputated.

ARKANSAS STATE NEWS.
Hunley Royl, an aged negro, living near Newport, was assassinated by a party of masked men.

Mrs. Ellis, wife of Conductor H. C. Ellis, died at Texarkana a few evenings since, while sitting in her chair.

Hon. John M. Hewitt, ex-Speaker of the State House of Representatives, is reported dying.

Tax-payers throughout the State are reported as coming forward with the dust more promptly than usual. A good sign.

Several gentlemen from the great Northwest are visiting Camden and vicinity, looking for desirable investments.

Camden merchants have purchased a first-class boat to run in the river trade.

Sheriff Hargott recently captured and brought back from Hunt County, Tex., M. E. Dillard, who stole a lot of horses and mules near Little Rock. Dillard is a notorious horse-thief. He has confessed his guilt.

Governor S. P. Hughes, Prof. James Mitchell and Dr. C. M. Taylor, composing the agricultural committee of the board of trustees of the Arkansas Industrial University, together with Prof. Menke, held a meeting a few days ago for the purpose of discussing the best means of carrying into effect the provisions of the Hatch Agricultural Experiment Station bill. The committee did not decide upon any definite p'an.

The Pulaski County Bureau of Immigration has made arrangements with Mr. M. W. Manville to act as secretary. This gentleman is well known throughout the State as the agricultural editor of the Gazette. The sub-committees of the executive committee has been soliciting subscriptions and proved very successful and the probabilities are that Pulaski's pro rata of the $50,000 will soon be raised.

Squire John Coney, James Copeland and J. E. Malloy, prominent residents of Ashley County, have been lodged in the penitentiary to save them from mob violence. They are the men who waylaid and killed a sewing-machine agent, S. J. Echols, mistaking him for Wm. Duckworth. The latter had threatened to kill them on sight because they had him indicted. A reign of terror is reported in the neighborhood of the crime.

Abe Lafally, a brakeman, was run over and killed a few days ago at Little Rock.

Chairman Folsom, of the Northern District Press Association, has called a meeting of that body at Searcy on March 14.

George Anderson and George Edmonson, two notorious safe blowers, who tapped the Yell County safe last February, have been placed in the penitentiary to serve a term of seven years each.

H. T. Ahrens, night switchman, Thomas Suble and Mike Ryan were arrested at Little Rock a few days ago for stealing goods out of a freight car while standing in the Memphis & Little Rock yard, at that place. A lot of carpets, tobacco, cigars and dry goods were found in their possession.

B. F. Doughton, of Richmond. this State, married Jesse Boram at Stauanton, Ill., a few evenings since. At the depot the next morning the bride saw her husband enter a saloon near by and she straightway took her valise and left for home. A reconciliation followed and the couple left for their Arkansas home on an evening train.

Keep the immigration boom moving. Arkansas is a good field for the home seeker with its cheap and fertile lands, rich mines, valuable timber and a climate free from excessive cold. Come and see.

The Texarkana Board of Trade has filed articles of association in the office of Secretary of State. The authorized capital stock of this association is fixed at $20,-000 and limited to $50,000. J. Deutchman is president and G. A. Hays secretary.

It is understood that the murderers of Echols in Ashley County will plead guilty, and receive long terms of imprisonment in the penitentiary.

Governor Hughes has pardoned John Lockhart, of Lee County, who was fined fifty dollars and costs for carrying a pistol, and through his inability to pay the fine was sent to the county farm. He had almost served his time.

J. R. Berry, member of the State Bureau of Immigration for Madison County, has appointed the following persons as a county bureau of immigration, to-wit: W. H. Bolinger, J. T. Walker, W. C. Roberts, J. N. Bunch, H. H. Williams, S. M. Johnson and S. R. Reeves.

Mr. P. A. Smith, secretary and manager of the drill to be held at Nashville, Tenn., May 21 to 26, has written Adjutant-General Hughes extending a cordial invitation to all officers and members of military organizations in the State to attend and participate in the drill, and requesting the names and addresses of the officers of each military company.

A large petition was received by the Governor a few days ago asking for the remission of the fine of $200 assessed against J. D. Vick for giving away whisky on election day in the county of Pope. The county judge of Pope County stated in a letter to the Governor that Vick could pay as much as $25 of the fine, but that the full amount would ruin him. The Governor accordingly reduced the fine to $25.

The directors of the Southwest Arkansas fair, which is to be held in Hope next October, have purchased a beautiful forty-acre piece of prairie land just in the edge of town for the fair grounds, and are pusing right ahead, making arrangements for a grand display of stock and farm products of the southwest portion of the State.

It is said that a gentleman of Springdale last year raised a crop of early peas and after gathering them set it out in tomatoes, and on less than one-quarter acre he sold $65 worth of tomatoes. This is quite encouraging to farmers who desire to make a dollar.

The eighteenth annual session of the Arkansas Methodist Episcopal Conference assembled at Little Rock last week. It was presided over by Bishop H. W. Warren, of Denver, Col. A large number of ministers and lay delegates from all over the State were in attendance. Revs. J. H. Vincent and W. A. Spencer, of Philadelphia, were also there. Now see that the plows are bright. MACON GA. April 30—Sheriff Fountain, of WI
To Save Collins from Lynching.
MACON, GA., April 30.-Sheriff Fountain, of Wilkinson County, arrived here this morning with the negro Will Collins, who shot and instantly killed J. A. Sheffield, a prominent merchant at Irwinton, in that county, Saturday night. While Sheffield was on the way home, Collins, who stood in a corner of a fence on the roadside, killed him with a shotgun. He afterwards robbed him. The people of the town turned out and captured Collins, tracking him from the scene of the murder. He was brought here to prevent lynching.

GEORGIA.

The Gainesville Fair Association has purchased land on which to build houses and fix up a track.

The West Bros., of Rome, have established a broom factory at Dalton, and are turning out forty dozen brooms per diem.

Gainesville's electric light company is all organized, and preparations are going on to have the lights turned on by July 1.

The Indian Spring reserve has been leased for the season to Mr. Mercer for $100. All this fund will be placed on the reserve in improvements.

Dawson Journal: Primus Jones has at last been downed by a Terrell county man. Rev. M. B. L. Binion brought a bale of cotton to market last Monday.

The killing of two men in Atlanta, on Tuesday, by the trains, has again opened up the vexed question of what is best to be done to insure the public safety from trains in that city.

Rumph & James, of Fort Valley, made their first shipment of peaches Thursday, and expect fancy returns, as it is the first shipment yet reported in the State. They were shipped to New York.

O. H. B. Bloodworth, of Forsyth, has applied to Adjutant General Kell for permission to organize a military company of sixty at that place. Capt. Kell was unable to supply the guns and accoutrements.

Giles Shoot, of Calhoun county, has a steer 23 years old, with which he has made nineteen crops and is now under good headway with the twentyth. During all this time the steer has been Mr. Shoot's only plow animal.

At Maysville, Comer & Co. have purchased the old brick store, the old landmark, and are tearing it down to rebuild on its old site a large brick store. Carr & Bacon are building a handsome brick store on Athens street.

Dalton's annual postal receipts amount to $3,249, a sufficient sum to entitle her to a public edifice if the measure now before Congress for the "erection of government buildings in all towns where the postal receipts exceed $3,000" is adopted.

A force of hands is at work in the corporate limits of Fort Valley on the Atlanta and Florida railroad. The grading will be completed by June 15, and by July 1 the coal burners will be dashing into Fort Valley fresh from Georgia's capital.

Twenty-five fleet-footed Augusta boys have organized a strong team under the command of Assistant Chief F. A. Roulette, of the Augusta fire department, and they will enter the contest at Anderson, S. C., on June 12, 13 and 14. Big purses are offered.

A negro man and a negro woman were shot Tuesday night at Greenville by unknown parties. The man was shot in the hand and the wound is sight. Elbert Rosser is the man's name. The woman was a stranger in Greenville, and she is painfully hurt.

Rev. Thad Pickett, a Baptist preacher who is an independent candidate for Congress in the Ninth district, has been in Gainesville several days. His Baptist brethren would not consent for him to defile the pulpit with his electioneering scheme. He is trying to mix politics and religion.

Dr. Walter Cheatham, of Dawson, has a young Shepherd dog which makes a practice of catching and eating the common little grass sparrow. These birds rarely ever fly high when frightened up, and this dog simply outruns and catches them before they light. He not only eats the birds, but seems to enjoy the sport.

Miss Lorine Daniel, a charming young lady of Crawford, was in the midst of her preparations for her approaching marriage, when she became suddenly ill, and gradually grew worse. Wednesday her illness resulted in death. Capt. Plunkett, a popular conductor of the Georgia road, was to have been her husband.

A few weeks ago Jack Chapman, a negro who resides in Griffin, was married to Jennie Hall, of Atlanta. When the marriage took place the bride received a number of presents, which were worth probably $150. A few days ago the husband, while his wife was away, packed the bridal presents in a valise and carried them off, and he has not been seen since.

Wiley McGill, of Webster county, owns a mule which evidences his appetite for spring chicken by devouring all that come within his reach. He has eaten so many that for two or three years past it has been necessary to keep strict watch on him whenever he is in the lot, and especially at feeding time. When the chickens gather around the stable trough, as is usual with them, the mule will drop his corn and fodder any time to catch a nice tender chicken.

The sale of the Crump Park property, at Macon, was well attended Thursday, and was very satisfactory. This property of ninety-five acres, was purchased of Capt. W. S. Brantley by S. A. Crump four years ago for $9,000. Last year Mr. Horne paid $8,000 for a half interest in it. Ten acres were donated by them to the dummy line for a park. Thursday they sold off enough to realize over $11,000, and yet twenty-one acres of the prettiest part of the land left.

Will Collins, who murdered J. H. Sheffield several weeks ago, and who is now in the Bibb county jail, has written a letter to Sheriff Fountain, of Irwinton, in which he implicates another party. Collins says that on the afternoon preceding the murder, he was visited by a certain party, who gave him $20 for the loan of his gun and shoes for an hour. During the night they were returned to Collins. The Sheriff places no confidence in the letter, as the party whom Collins accuses wears a No. 10 shoe, and could not possibly have worn Collin's shoes, which are 7s.

An important case was disposed of in the Superior Court at Atlanta, Thursday, before Judge Marshall J. Clarke. It was a suit brought by M. C. & J. F. Kiser & Co. against the Liverpool, London and Globe Insurance Company. Some time ago the store of F. J. M. English, of Barnesville, was destroyed by fire. The Liverpool, London and Globe held the risk. Mr. English assigned the goods that were saved and also assigned the policy. Kiser & Co., were among the creditors, and the suit brought was to compel the company to pay the loss to that firm. The jury, after considering the case, found that the assignment was good.

A notable feature of the undertakers' convention, at Milledgeville, was the abatement of the superstitious "brother in black." It has been almost impossible to secure a bootblack or errand boy in the city since the convention met, and some terrible stories have been in circulation among the negroes about the delegates. A

NASHVILLE, Tenn., May 25.—A special to The American from Clarksville, Tenn., says: James Massey, who lives in Cheatham county, was arrested on a charge of attempting to rape Miss Weakley, a prominent young lady of that county. Since leaving Clarksville for Ashland City, the county seat of Cheatham, nothing has been heard of Massey, and it is believed indignant citizens have lynched him. Miss Weakley is completely prostrated and ill in consequence of her fearful experience.

Free Niagara. NIAGARA FAIRS, ONT., May 24.—The Queen's birthday was made the occasion of throwing open to the public the Queen Victoria Niagara Falls Park, the twin sister of the State Reservation on the American side, both of which are designed for the preservation of the great cataclysm. The first mark contains 118 acres, and is two hundred one-half miles long. The cost of the park to date is about $335,000. There were no formal ceremonies attending the opening to-day, but it is proposed to celebrate the event on Dominion Day—July 1—in a fitting manner. Mississippi Immigration Convention. JACKSON, MISS., May 24.—The Immigration Convention which assembled here today was the largest ever held, three hundred and fifty delegates being present, representing sixty-six counties. Speeches were made by Governor Lowry, Captain W. B. Hardy, General Miles and other prominent men, showing the resources of the State. Appropriate resolutions were adopted to induce immigration. Wisconsin Prohibitionists. MADISON, WIS., May 24.—The Prohibition State Convention started business to-day by securing $4,400 in pledges to a campaign fund. Eighteen delegates and as many alternates to the National Convention were chosen and also half a hundred so-called provisional delegates. At the afternoon session E.G. Durant, of Racine, was nominated for Governor by acclamation. Virginia Elections.
Virginia Elections.
RICHMOND, MAY 24—Returns from municipal elections throughout the State today show that the Democrats carried Petersburg, Lynchburg, Richmond and Danville.

NORFOLK, May 24—The election here today passed off quietly. The Republicans have probably elected their candidate for mayor, but the other officers on the ticket are still in doubt.

Woman Suffrage unconstitutional.
PORTLAND, ORE., May 24—The question of woman suffrage in Washington Territory came up to-day before Judge Nash, at Spokane Falls, on a test case. The Judge delivered a lengthy opinion, in which he decided that the act of the Legislature extending the franchise to women is unconstitutional.

A Mother's Vain Sacrifice.
ELGIN, ILL., May 24—Mrs. P. C. Kueger, living on North State street, was killed yesterday in trying to rescue her eight-month-old child from an approaching freight train on the Northwestera road. War of Extermination.
CINCINNATI, Jan. 24.—A special from Catlettsburg, Ky., says: "The war of extermination between the Hatfields and McCoys is still going on in the wilds of West Virginia. The steamer Frank Preston arrived from Pikeville yesterday afternoon and brought intelligence of the encounter between the pursuing party and the Hatfields on last Saturday. On Thursday last the capturing party, numbering twenty, left Pikeville for Tug River. After crossing the river, when nearing the residence of Capt. Hatfield, they came across a woman in the road who was standing picket and who immediately gave the alarm. The capturing party when turning a point in the road were fired upon by a squad of eight from the Hatfield gang. Bud McCoy was shot through the shoulder and dangerously wounded. Two of the posse were detailed to care for him and take him home. The capturing party immediately returned the fire, and Will Dempsey, of the Hatfield gang, fell to the ground shot through the bowels. At this juncture the Hatfields beat a hasty retreat, throwing away their blankets, overcoats &c. The posse went up to where Dempsey was and although he was in a dying condition and begged piteously to be saved as he would not live long, despite his cries for mercy, the man that killed Jim Vance on the first raid put his gun against Dempsey's head and almost blew it off. At this inhuman and sickening act one of the pursuing party became angry, left the posse and returned home. The Hatfields were organizing for a raid over on Peter Creek, in Kentucky, the scene of their new years night deeds, to murder people, burn property and kill stock. The Peter Creek Guards, twenty strong, have joined the capturing party, which now members forty odd, and are in hot pursuit of the Hatfields. The excitement throughout Pike county, though intense, is increasing daily, as the Hatfield's have warned the people that they propose to kill them and burn their property. They have sent word that they propose to burn Pikeville and extricate their six comrades now in jail there. The jail is strongly guarded day and night and pickets are set out in all directions from the town every night. Judge Waggoner, county judge of Pike county, and J. Lee Ferguson, attorney, came down on the Frank Preston from Pikesville en route to Frankfort, where they go to lay the case before the Governor and ask him for arms to protect themselves and their property.

THE HATFIELD SIDE OF THE LOGAN
COUNTY WAR.
The McCoys Again the Aggressors—A Letter from
the Seat of Trouble—How Dempsey Was
Killed—The Kentucky Gang
Was Resisting Arrest.
Special Telegram to the Register.
CHARLESTON, W. VA., January 25. — To-day's mail brings more information from Logan county concerning the trouble growing out of the Hatfield-McCoy trouble in Pike county, Ky., and Logan county, W. Va. Senator J. B. Floyd received a letter from Logan Court House this evening, from his brother, which fully explains the erroneous account of the last fight between the Kentucky outlaws and the West Virginia officers, which occurred Saturday last. It was not the Hatfield gang, as the Enquirer of the 24th has it, who was concerned in the fight, but a posse of men armed with the authority of the law, through the Sheriff of Logan county, who had made a raid on the Kentucky gang, who were known and charged with the late murder of old man Vance on West Virginia soil. It must be remembered those outlaws had

INVADED WEST VIRGINIA SOIL, bent upon murder and destruction.

The writer of the letter was a member of the posse of the Logan county officers, and knows what he is writing about. The letter is under date of January 22, 1888. Governor Wilson has been in telegraphic communication with Governer Buckner, of Kentucky, and it is likely if some steps are not taken by the Kentucky government to prevent further invasion by the crowd from Pike county, the Governor of this State will deem it necessary to adopt some means for the protection of the people of Logan county.
Mr. Floyd's Correspondent Says:
"We are about to get into a war with the Kentucky gang who killed James Vance some days ago. Warrants are issued for the arrest of some six of the gang who committed the murder and were placed in the hands of Constable J. R. Thompson to be executed and he summoned a guard of thirteen men to make the arrests. We were over the mouth of Grapevine, in this county, and there we were fired upon by about thirty men with Winchester rifles. We were in an open field and the balls just hailed around us until we charged on them. When the firing began Henry Thompson and I were in front on our horses. We all jumped from our horses and returned the fire with our Winchesters and the firing kept up for about thirty minutes, when we started for some trees about 175 yards away.
At this time they fired another volley and killed one of our men, Wm. Dempsey, shooting him three times. They were behind a fence all the time and we could see nothing but the heads of their gang.

BUD M'COY WAS KILLED
and another man was wounded whose name I do not know. They all had Winchester rifles and said they had started to Logan C. H. to take Elias Hatfield and burn the town. Three of their horses were killed during the fight. You must go and see the Governor at once and have a stop put to those desperadoes coming over here and killing men and robbing them after they are killed. The people of the county are going to hold a moss meeting here to marrow, asking the Governor to send men over to put a stop to this thing. If the State would furnish us a hundred Winchesters and plenty of ammunition we would not need the men. See the Governor as soon as you get this and let us know what can be done. I can tell you that I heard many a Winchester ball pass my head. It is almost a young war over here. People are laying out from their homes on account of those Kentucky desperadoes. See to this matter at once and let me hear from you. [Signed] W. P. FLOYD.

A DIFFERENT ACCOUNT.

A Charleston (W. Va.) dispatch gives a somewhat different history of the affair, as detailed by a reliable and leading citizen of Logan county. The report says:

J. B. Floyd, of this city, who has been a resident of Logan county and is well acquainted with the facts, gives the following history of the Hatfield-McCoy imbrogillo which has led to the recent murders in Logan county, W. Va.:

The accounts published in the papers of this State make the Hatfields outlaws and murderers. Now, I have known all of the Hatfields for fifteen or twenty years, and lived within eighteen miles of them the greater part of that time, and I never regarded them in the light of criminals or desperadoes, and they are not so regarded by the people of Logan county. On the contrary, some of these Hatfields are regarded as being of the very best and law abiding citizens of that county.

WHAT STARTED THE TROUBLE.

The trouble which has brought about the present state of affairs in Logan county, West Virginia, and Pike county, Kentucky, began during the war of secession. When the war ceased the differences between the Hatfields and McCoys seemed also to have practically come to an end, but in 1882 Ellisen Hatfield went from his home in West Virginia, across Tug river into Kentucky, only a few miles from his home, to an election over there, and during that day three of the McCoys deliberately laid their plans to assassinate Hatfield, and they carried them out by cutting and shooting him to pieces. Before the McCoys could get out of the reach they were themselves killed by some of the relations of Hatfield. This having taken place in Kentucky the Hatfields and several other citizens were indicted in Pike county, Kentucky, for the killing of the McCoys.

After the indictments were made no further steps were taken in the matter by the Kentucky authorities, and the matter rested for five years, because the authorities of Pike county regarded the McCoys as the aggressors, and they knew that the McCoys were just about as bad as men get to be.

A KENTUCKY JAILOR REBPENS THE FIGHT.

Every one thought the trouble was over; but a few months ago a man named P. A. Cline, a lawyer, and I am told the jailer of Pike county, concluded that he would stir up the thing again and make some money out of it, knowing that the Hatfields owned some good property in Logan county, West Virginia. He therefore looked up the old indictments and by misrepresentations induced the Governor of Kentucky to offer a reward of $2,700 for the capture of the Hatfields and to grant a requisition for them.

This done, he let the Hatfields know of the fact, and at the same time intimated that if he could get some $400 or $500 he would have the proceedings put an end to. Well, he agreed to take $220, and the money was placed in the hands of A. J. Auxier, a prominent lawyer at Pike Court House, for Cline, when he had fulfilled his agreement.

Cline made a pretense of having the reward and requisition recalled, but in the meantime his co-workers, John Kite, who is one of the most notorious murderers in West Virginia or Kentucky, and Frank Phillips have been making desperate efforts to get hold of the Hatfields so as to secure the reward.

The reinforced gang with volunteer followers have been bullying everybody along the border for the last two or three months, the Hatfields meanwhile keeping out of the way so as to avoid trouble.

The result of this marauding was the burning of McCoy's house and the killing of his son and daughter on the first of January, and an effort to kill old Randall McCoy himself. Everybody knew that McCoy had been way-laying the house of the Hatfields trying to kill them, and when this occurrence took place it was at once placed to the credit of the Hatfields by the men who were after them to better enable them to capture the Hatfields.

The circumstances surrounding the Hatfields may have been sufficient to justify them to try and kill McCoy, yet they did not, and knew nothing of the matter, as can and has been shown beyond all question. THE VENDETTA

OF PIKE COUNTY, KY., AND LOGAN COUNTY, W. VA.

The Affair Worked to Bring Dis- credit on This State.

Gross Ignorance of the Newspapers of Other States

Concerning the Geography of West Virginia and Kentucky,

Causes Them to Attribute the Lawlessness to This State.
Thus is West Virginia Getting a Bad Reputation Abroad.
Histories of the Feud as Told on Both Sides of the Line.
A dispatch from Louisville, Kentucky, received at the INTELLIGENCE office last night, says:

"Officials of Pike county have applied to the Governor for troops to defend the people against the Hatfield gang. Troops were refused, but the people were given permission to arm themselves. The Sheriff of Pike county has invaded West Virginia to capture the outlaws, but a West Virginia sheriff is out with a posse to drive him back to Kentucky."

This is the latest news concerning the Hatfield-McCoy Feud, which is attracting so much attention throughout the country. It should be stated that, with one or two exceptions, all the press dispatches relating to the matter which have appeared, have been sent from Kentucky towns. They contain a decided coloring in favor of the McCoy faction, and are evidently calculated to make it appear that the Hatfields are the aggressors. Pains are taken in the accounts sent out by these Kentucky correspondents, also, to create the impression that the affair is a case of "West Virginia outlawry," much to the discredit of the State. The truth of the matter is that it is a Kentucky feud, and is the result of a difficulty which occurred at a local election between rival factions in Pike county, Kentucky, some years ago.

There does not seem to be anything to warrant the

COURSE OF THE PRESS
in making it out a case of "West Virginia lawlessness," and charging the whole matter up to the account of this State. It will be observed that the reports of the depredations by both gangs show that the crimes have nearly all been committed in Kentucky. The unenviable reputation which West Virginia is gaining abroad by the reason of these inaccurate reports, and the gross ignorance of the geography of this State and Kentucky which exists in the minds of some editors, is illustrated by the following editorial, clipped from yesterday's Pittsburgh Times, under the caption, "West Virginia Barbarians:"

A DIZZY EDITORIAL.

"The latest reports from the seat of war in West Virginia left the Judge and Prosecuting Attorney of Lee county about starting to seek the aid of the Governor in suppressing the conflict between the Hatfield and McCoy factions. We shall be curious to hear what is the Governor's action.

"In one view refusing to interfere might be the better course, for the killing on both sides has been pretty lively of late. Kept up, the conflict would in time exterminate a lot of citizens of no earthly use and that had better be killed off for
"Something is due to the feelings of citizens of other States and the reputation of the country, and this may be the view the Governor will take. This might lead to the arrest of all who in any way have been engaged in the murderous raids of the Hatfields and McCoys, and to the summary hanging of the whole lot. That would go far towards redeeming the reputation of West Virginia, which, it must be confessed, is at a very low point, rather worse than Kentucky's.

"In the quarter of the State where the warring factions live law seems not to be operative. In some of the other States, where there is something to admire as well as much to condemn, the citizens of the rest of the State would gather at the seat of violence, set up Judge Lynch's Court and administer law which, although rude and unknown to the books, would yet be efficacious. Some such thing in West Virginia, which we do not wish to be understood as encouraging, would undoubtedly elevate the State in the estimation of intending settlers, who, as the case is, will go anywhere else.

"No one seems to think that the citizen will be safe in the quarter of the State in question until the Hatfields and McCoys and all their sympathizing friends are exterminated. This is the view the Governor may take and so not interfere, for the process of extermination was rather rapid at the last advices."
HISTORY OF THE FEUD.

A special dispatch from Frankfort, Ky., to the Louisville Commercial gives what purports to be an authentic history of the feud. It is, conservative, and the honors are divided between both States. Unlike most of the reports from Kentucky it does not leave West Virginia to bear all the odium. The dispatch is as follows:

Several years ago the first trouble originated between the Hatfields and McCoys. One of the latter, who was a Constable, arrested one of the former for some trifling offense. Subsequently, at an election in Pike county, a difficulty ensued between the parties, and Hatfield was shot. Four of the McCoys were arrested and were taken from the authorities by the Hatfield mob, who carried them, together with the wounded Hatfield, into Logan county, West Virginia. Here Hatfield died, and after his death the four McCoys were taken back to Pike county, tied to pawpaw bushes and shot to death. This ended the matter for a time.

Last September Governor Buckner of fered $500 reward for the murderers of the McCoys, but the Governor of West Virginia refused to recognize the requisition. Emboldened by this refusal, probably, the Hatfield gang made a raid into Pike county on New Year's eve of the present year, and burned old man McCoy's house. McCoy's young daughter attempted to quench the flames and was shot in the breast and killed.

CHARLESTON, W. Va., Jan. 31.—Col. W. L. Mahon, the emissary whom Governor Wilson sent to Logan county a week ago to inquire into and report upon the now famous Hatfields-McCoy vendetta, made his report to Governor Wilson to-day. While many depredations have been committed, and the whole surrounding country has been in a state of excitement and tumult bordering on genuine war, peace has again been restored, and the belligerent parties on both sides have disbanded, and no further trouble is anticipated. jas-vance-1888-01.A17:
HATFIELD-M'COY FEUD.
THE VIRGINIA CONTINGENT IN THE
LOUISVILLE JAIL.
Old Man Valentine Hatfield Tells a Straightforward Story About the Bloody War that Waged Between the Families.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., Feb. 17.—The nine West Virginians known as the "Hatfields" arrived here last night in charge of a deputy United States marshal and the jailer of Pike county. They will appear before Judge Barr, of the United States district court, Monday, when the habeas corpus application of the Governor of West Virginia will be further heard. Valentine Hatfield, the "old man" of the gang, after stating that they had been well treated while in the Pike county jail, gave the following account of the celebrated feud:

"The whole trouble, so far as I know, began about six or eight years ago. I had five brothers—Ellison, Elias, Anderson, Smith and Patterson. Ellison was the first one killed. Three of the McCoy boys shot and cut him on Blackberry creek, on the Kentucky side, and he died the next day. The trouble, I believe, was started by one of the McCoys attempting to arrest Anderson Hatfield's son Johnson, about eight years ago. There was a row, but I don't remember exactly what it was.
After Ellison Hatfield was killed, Talbert, Richard and Farmer McCoy, all young men, were killed by a crowd supposed to have come from West Virginia. The killing was done on the bridge between Blackberry and Mates creeks.

"The next Pike county grand jury indicted a lot of people in West Virginia. No one was arrested, however, and after that Jeff McCoy, who is Bill Daniel's brother-in-law, heard Daniels and Tom Wallace abusing the Hatfields, and a quarrel followed. McCoy attempted to arrest Wallace, and a fight took place. This resulted in Capt. Hatfield arresting McCoy, and when McCoy tried to get away he was killed by the men who were guarding him. Some time after this a squad of men went to Randolph McCoy's house and killed one of his sons and a daughter, and beat up his old woman. This was charged to the Hatfields, but I never knew anything about it until some time after the murders were committed.

"A short time after this, a company of Pike county men was formed to follow the Hatfields and kill them. They came into West Virginia and found Jim, Vance and Capt. Hatfield on a bridge near Thacker's creek. They shot Vance to death and wounded Capt. Hatfield. After that the Kentuckians came in and captured us while we were at work on our farms. None of us resisted and no injury was done us, but if there there was any authority for confining us in jail, I never heard of it."

County Attorney J. Lee, Ferguson, of Pike, was questioned concerning the claim of the prisoners that they were innocent. He laughed at the idea, and said that while the worst of the Hatfield crowd had not been captured, the men who are now in the Louisville jail are undoubtedly a part of the gang. He declared that the prisoners had not been unlawfully imprisoned, but after having crossed the border line between West Virginia and Kentucky, had been legally arrested and taken to jail by the proper officers. He did not deny that the West Virginians had been forcibly taken from their homes, but held that the Kentuckians were justified by the dangers threatening them in taking the matter into their own hands when the West Virginia authorities refused to assist in restraining and punishing the outlaws, who had only to cross a narrow stream to commit the most atrocious crimes and then cross back again to safety from the law. Mr. Ferguson asserted positively that he had creditable information that a State official of West Virginia had been retained with a fee of $500 to prevent Gov. Wilson from recognizing the requisition issued by Gov. Buckner. He charged also that the Hatfield crew had brought other influences to bear, and that the worst of the gang were now in comparative security.

Of the prisoners now in the Louisville jail, Mr. Ferguson says that Valentine Hatfield recently confessed to him that he had five living wives and thirty-three living children. Nine of his children have died. Mr. Ferguson states that Hatfield has peculiar ideas of polygamy and does not marry his wife according to law, but takes them and apportions his time out between them.

On the day of the August election, 1882, Ellison Hatfield, of Logan county, West Virginia, and Tolbert Macoy engaged in a fight at a county precinct in Pike county, contiguous to the West Virginia line. The fight was forced on Macoy, who was a small man, by Hatfield, who was a large and powerful man. Macoy, soon realizing that he was over-matched, drew his pocketknife and stabbed Hatfield, notwithstanding which, Hatfield forced him to the ground, and was in the act of braining him with a large stone, when Macoy's brother shot Hatfield with a pistol. The Hatfields, several of whom were present, fired several shots at the Macoy who did the shooting, but he escaped unhurt.

The Kentucky authorities arrested three of the Macoy brothers, yet a third one, some 14 years old, being charged by Hatfield's friends with having assisted in inflicting the knife wounds on the body of Ellison Hatfield, and were detaining them in custody to await the result of Hatfield's wounds, when a large band of Hatfields and their friends, heavily armed, crossed the Tug fork of the Big Sandy over into Kentucky, took the Macoy brothers away from the Kentucky authorities, carried them over into West Virginia, where they detained them until Ellison Hatfield died—some 36 or 48 hours, then brought them back to the Kentucky side of the Tug Fork of the Sandy, which is the dividing line between the States, and tying them up to pawpaw bushes, shot them to death. They first shot the two grown ones, and turned to go away, with the evident purpose of sparing the boy, but they had not gone far when Bad Andse Hatfield, the leader of the present Hatfield gang, said; "boys, dead men tell no tales," and turning, pointed to the little boy, who, with pallid face and bated breath, had just witnessed the murder of his two elder brothers, and in whose tender bosom hope for escape from their terrible doom was just beginning to rise. The suggestion of Bad Andse was sufficient to seal the poor boy's fate, for a number of the outlaws turned, and bringing their guns to bear upon the frail form of the pinioned youth, pulled their triggers and almost blew his head off.

For this triple murder, twenty-three of the Hatfield gang was indicted at the next term of the Pike Circuit Court, and while they frequently crossed over into Kentucky, they came in such numbers, and so well armed, as to defy arrest. Thus matters rested till last September Gov. Buckner was prevailed upon to issue his requisition upon the Governor of West Virginia, one E. W. Wilson, for the extradition of five of the worst of the gang. Governor Wilson did not respond till written to some several weeks after by Governor Buckner on the subject, when he replied that there was a law of West Virginia which required an affidavit in additim to the requirements of the law of Congress governing the extradition of fugitives. Governor Buckner not wishing to appear captious, complied with the technical requirement of the West Virginia Governor, and procured the additional affidavit and forwarded it to Governor Wilson.

Here the matter again rested for some weeks, when Governor Buckner again wrote to Governor Wilson, calling his attention to the matter, when Governor Wilson promptly responded, saying that sickness in his family and absence from his office had caused the delay, that he would promptly issue his warrant for the arrest of three of the men named in Gov. Buckner's requisition, but that he had grave doubt as to the guilt of the other two whose cases he would further investigate. He never complied with his promise to issue his warrants for three of the five parties required by Gov. Buckner.

Frank Phillips, former deputy Sheriff of Pike county, was designated by Gov. Buckner as the agent for Kentucky to receive the prisoners when arrested by Gov. Wilson's authority, and who, after waiting till sufficient time had elapsed to suppose that the warrants had been issued and the arrests made thereunder, when taking a couple of men with him, he went over into Logan county, West Virginia to receive his prisoners. When he got there he found that no warrants had been issued nor arrests made, but meeting with three of the indicted parties he arrested them and brought them back to Pike county with him, where the bench warrants were served on them by a deputy Sheriff of Pike county, and lodged in jail.

This was in the latter part of November last. To avenge that wrong, as some suppose, while others say for the purpose of destroying evidence, the Hatfield gang on New Year's night crossed over into Kentucky and proceeded seven miles into the interior till they reached the peaceful mountain home of old man Randolph Macoy, the father of the three murdered boys, on Briar fork of Peter Creek. Surrounding the house, they proclaim-

house. The family had retired for the night, but the approach of the raiders had been announced by the faithful watch dog, and old man Macoy and his son Calvin, aged about 27 years, had risen and hastily dressing themselves, and remembering the fate of their murdered kindred, who had in vain besought the same gang that their lives might be spared, prepared to make the best defense possible of the sanctity of their home, and for two hours or more returned a vigorous fire to the terrific volleys of the assaults.

Finally the Hatfields succeeded in firing the house, but still old man Macoy and his brave boy held the fort till it was evident that the house must soon fall in, when Calvin proposed that he would jump out and run to the corn crib, from which point, when gained, he could cover the retreat of his father to the same place, for said the young man, "father, if we both reach the crib we can whip them yet," saying which, Calvin leaped from the burning house and ran toward the crib, but when about half way he fell with his brain pierced with a ball from behind, and instantly expired. Old Randolph seeing his son fall, seized a double-barreled shot gun, and leaping from his burning dwelling, discharged both barrels in quick succession and at short range at the enemy and struck out to make the best retreat possible. Johns Hatfield Dead.
There is no doubt that the notorious Johnson Hatfield, of the well-known Hatfield gang, died last week at Granville Thompson's a few miles from this place. Some time since, a party passing through the country in a wagon was compelled to leave the deceased, owing to his serious sickness, at Mr. Thompson's. The sick man's name was given as Vance. After a few days some of the party returned for their comrade but found him too ill to be removed. He shortly afterward died and as there was a suspicion that it was Hatfield an investigation was made. He was identified by one or two parties who knew him and there is little doubt that it was Johns Hatfield. 'The remains were cared for by the county.

jeff-wilson-holbrook-1888-08-11.A1:
TELEGRAPHIC BREVITIES.
During a family riot in Castilla, Peru, ten persons were killed.

Fred Bade was drowned near Stockton yesterday while bathing.

James Stott and Jeff Wilson have been lynched by cowboys near Holbrook, A. T.

Yellow fever is committing ravages in Cuba. In one day twenty-four children died.

A large condor was lassoed at Puente, Los Angeles county, while struggling with a lamb.

Billie Scott killed Joseph Horn in a prize fight at Philadelphia on Tuesday, and was arrested.

The Sultan will not allow the opening of the transcontinental railroad to be celebrated in Turkey.

Albert Legault, fourteen years old, was carried over Chaudiere Falls, Canada, on Tuesday, and drowned.

The case against the men arrested by detective Bohen for the Kneebone murder does not seem to be a strong one.

L. Choard, a San Jose jeweler, paid $75 for a bag of gold dust last Wednesday, and got a bag of bronzed sand instead.

James Saultry, for many sessions an attache of the Legislature, and a State pensioner, died in San Rafael on Tuesday.

Charles Meyers, of Helena, M. T., got $4,000 from his affliance, Miss Minnie Long, and lit out. He is thought to be in California.

The Democratic State Convention of Texas has renominated Governor L. S. Ross and Lieutenant-Governor Wheeler by acclamation.

Madame Adam declares that Bismarck is the most impudent liar in the world. She forgets that diplomacy (or duplicity) is his regular business.

Winthrop, Me., had an earthquake shock on Tuesday night. Blaine's arrival in Maine may have had something to do with it, as the town is Democratic.

Hon. Ashbel P. Fitch, member of Congress from the Thirteenth New York Congressional District, has sent his formal resignation from the Republican party.

A crisis is reported in Turkey between the Sultan and Ministers, due to the refusal of the Sultan and Ministers, due to the refusal of the Sultan to saction the Grand Vizier's proposal to borrow £1,500,000 to pay the overdue wages of soldiers and sailors.

George Browning, while working with a refractory mule near Grimes' Landing, Colusa county, was kicked by it in the breast in the region of the heart, and instantly killed. Browning was an old resident of Grand Island.

A letter arrived from Crittenden, Ariz., on Sunday stating that two men had been killed between there and Huachucas, and that the deed was supposed to have been the work of Indians. The men killed were Mexican vaqueros.

Lizzie J. Byrnes, the 15-year-old daughter of J. E. Byrnes, was burned to death at her father's residence, San Antonio valley, last Monday. She was washing and had a fire near the house, when the wind blew the fire against her clothing.

John Robinson, the circus man, left an estate of $1,000,000. Boyd Robinson is given $10,000 in cash, James Robinson and Robert Stickney are given $15,000 each. The remainder is to be divided equally among his sons Charles, Gilbert and John.

Advices from Santiago de Cuba say: There were twenty deaths from yellow fever in this city up to the 28th of July, largely among the military. New food is furnished the disease by a lot of freshly arrived Spaniards. The weather is favorable for yellow fever. A report from the interior says many children and native Cubans are dying from yellow fever. At Sancti Espiritu twenty-four children were swept away in a single day. The steamer Ciiy of Baltimore cleared from this port a few days ago for Philadelphia. When six hours out the chief officer died of yellow fever. DOMESTIC.

Fred Blade, 30 years old, was drowned while bathing in the Stockton channel.

Colonel James L. D. Morrison, familiarly known as Don Morrison, somewhat noted as a Democratic politician and a very wealthy man, died at his residence in St. Louis, Tuesday. Mr. Morrison was a cousin to Interstate Commerce Commissioner Morrison.

A man living about two miles from Los Gatos, Cal, threw his wife out of bed and then jumped upon her, crushing her brains out and killing her. The man next attacked his son, but the boy escaped and ran to Los Gatos. The man was arrested, and it is believed he is insane.

One of the most severe earthquakes ever felt in the vicinity of Winthrop, Me., occurred at 8:30 Tuesday evening, continuing thirty seconds. It shook the earth violently, swaying buildings and rattling dishes and furniture. A second shock was felt at about midnight, somewhat lighter and of the same duration.

Dr. Jones and Rev. H. Sink, of Grass Valley, Cal., had a fearful experience Tuesday evening. While driving home from You-Bet they ran the gauntlet of a hot fire among the tall pines for two miles on both sides of the road. All the timber east of Greenhorn creek is on fire. B. Johnson's extensive shingle mill is reported destroyed.

A telegram was received at the office of Richard K. Fox yesterday from San Francisco, stating that Tom Meadows, the Australian champion pugilist, had signed articles to fight Billy Mahan, of that city. The will battle for the lightweight championship of the Pacific Slope and $500 a side. The mill will occur some time between the 20th and 30th inst.

The Chicago postoffice authorities, having in charge the box robbery affair, have completed a partial list of the checks, drafts, money orders and other negotiable papers found in Oberkampf's rooms. So far it foots up over two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. The Inspector is satisfied that the aggregate value of the stolen documents recovered will be fully a million dollars.

Advices from Cattlettsburg, Ky., say the Hatfield-McCoy feud has broken out again. The trouble was stirred up by the Sheriff, who went out to summon witnesses in the Hatfield case and was attacked. This was followed up by a meeting on Sunday between the Hatfield and McCoy gangs, since which three of the former have been killed and several of the latter badly wounded. More fighting is expected to follow very shortly.

Information has reached Holbrook, Arizona, of the lynching of James Scott and Jeff Wilson by outlaws, in the southwestern part of the county. The affair grew out of the recent war in the Tonto basin between sheep raisers and cattle raisers. Warrants were issued and arrests made by unauthorized persons and the prisoners were taken across the mountains into Gavapi county, where they were met by a prearranged mob of outlaws and hanged.

While entering the harbor at San Diego Tuesday afternoon the steamship City of Pueblo broke her rudder chain on the port side, causing her to become unmanageable. As she was running under a full head of steam, she veered and ran aground near La Playa. She was gotten off at high tide without any trouble. A large number of passengers were transferred to tugboats and brought to the city. The rudder chain has been repaired and the vessel sailed for San Francisco yesterday as usual.

A dispatch from Albuquerque, N. M., says: The fast-bound Atlantic and Pacific train due at Albuquerque at 1:30 Tuesday morning came in ten hours behind time. The delay was caused by the wreck which occured on the desert in California at the point known as Horse Snce Curve. The train was running very slowly, but the trucks of the express car it is claimed were not in good working order and refused to adjust themselves to the curves. In consequence the car was pulled off the track, and breaking away from the engine, which it left on the track, went tumbling down a thirty-foot embankment, pulling after it the baggage, mail and three emigrant coaches and two sleepers, well filled with passengers, all of whom suffered injuries more or less severe. It is asserted that the mail clerk, who was badly bruised, tried to telegraph to Albuquerque for assistance, and some of the wounded passengers tried to send dispatches to their friends, but the railway controlled the only wire and positively forbid the operator to send the messages. Twelve hours after the accident the passengers were picked up by a special train. The passengers were very indignant at their treatment, particularly in the matter of telegrams, and adopted resolutions condemning the company's action.
jeff-wilson-holbrook-1888-08-11.A9:
TONTO BASIN.
Serious Trouble Between the Cattlemen and Sheepmen There.
Serious Trouble Between the Cattlemen and Sheepmen There.

J. D. Houck, who has a ranch in Pleasant Valley known as Houck's Tanks, and is also Deputy Sheriff of Apache county, was in Flagstaff several days of the week.

Mr. Houck reports serious trouble in his section, growing out of the never-ending feud between the sheepmen and cattlemen. The first of the trouble took place about two weeks ago, when Jake Lauffer, whose ranch is in the southwestern portion of the valley, was fired at by unknown parties while out for his horses a few yards from his cabin. His arm was broken by one of the shots from the party in ambush, but he succeeded in reaching the cabin, when the attacking party left. On the same evening two men named Cody and Coleman, while coming into the valley near Lauffer's, were shot at a number of times from ambush, but they succeeded in making their escape, though the horse ridden by Cody was shot from under him.

It was supposed that the shooting was done by Jeff Wilson, Jim Stott and Jim Scott, and Mr. Houck and a posse succeeded in capturing them at Stott's ranch in the Mogollon mountains. While proceeding with the prisoners the posse was overpowered by a party of about forty masked men and the prisoners taken from them. It is stated that Stott was found the next day hanging to a tree, and a little later the bodies of the others were also found hanging, with their horses riderless and grazing near by.

Later advices from Holbrook confirm the report that the parties above named had been hung. This latter report says that the warrants were issued and the arrests made by unauthorized parties, and that the prisoners were taken for the purpose of being lynched.
jeff-wilson-holbrook-1888-08-11.A13:
"WAGING WAR" OUT WEST.
Murder and the Inevitable Lynching, and More to Come.
Murder and the Inevitable Lynching, and More to Come.

ALBUQUERQUE, N. M., Aug. 22.—Cattlemen and sheepmen living in the Tonto Basin, beyond the Arizona line, are again waging war against each other. About two weeks ago Jacob Lanffer, a prominent sheep raiser in the valley, while a few yards from his cabin, was shot by unknown parties, his assailants escaping. On the same evening two men named Cady and Coleman, while out on a hunt for stock, were also fired upon, Cady's horse being shot from under him.

Deputy Sheriff Houck and a posse started out to hunt down the perpetrators, and after a few days obtained sufficient evidence to place the crime on Jeff Wilson, James Scott and James Stott. They were pursued, and after a hot chase captured in the Mogollon mountains. While en route with the prisoners the officers were overpowered by forty masked men, who took charge of the prisoners. The next day Stott's body was found hanging to a tree. Wilson and Scott were also found hanging. Desperate trouble is expected to result from the lynching.
