Stott invited them also to get down and have some breakfast. While he was getting the meal ready for them, Stott asked Houck what he was arrested for and wanted him to read the warrant. Houck replied he did not have the warrant with him, that he had left it at Bear Spring. After eating breakfast the crowd sat around for an hour or so chatting and laughing before taking their departure. They then concluded to move, taking Stott, Scott and a man named Wilson, who had been in the employ of Stott for some seven or eight months, and went from Stott's residence to Phoenix Park, then took the trail for the old Verde road. When about five miles west of Phoenix Park they halted and hung the three—Stott, Scott and Wilson.

Jimmy Scott, as he is called by the cowboys of this section, has been in this county for two or three years, first in the employ of the Aztec Land and Cattle Company, and latterly with Messrs. Huning & Cooley, whom he left some two or three weeks ago. Those who have worked with him and know him best, speak well of him—say that he was quiet, sober and peaceable, and was never engaged in any questionable transactions to their knowledge.

Wilson, from what we can learn, is comparatively unknown. We could get no definite information in regard to him, as to where he was from or his antecedents. Stott is a man who has made enemies and friends. His enemies say that he was a bad man—that he was the head and brains of a desperate gang of rustlers; while his friends say that he was an honest, honorable and deserving man.

From what meagre information we have been able to gather, this appears to be rather a high handed move, to say the least. We could hear of no charge whatever against Scott, who had gone to Pleasant Valley after a horse he had loaned to Neglin Bros., while he was waiting to hear from parties to whom he had written seeking employment. Wilson is in a similar position—no charges against him that we could hear of. If the lynchers had any charge against either, they did not make them known.

We are informed there was bad blood existing between Stott and Houck, over some charges Houck had made against him, and at one time, in Holbrook, Stott had told Houck in pretty plain language what he thought of him, winding up by telling Houck that if he wanted to make a fight of it, "to go and heel himself."

These are the particulars of this strange affair, as we were told them by Mr. Willis, who obtained his information from a Mr. Clymer, who is in the employ of Wells, Fargo & Co., at Los Angeles, and who was at the house of Mr. Stott on the morning in question, taking care of a sick friend. This affair should be thoroughly investigated by our authorities and the matter sifted to the bottom. For a body of armed men to be scouring the country, picking up men against whom they may have a grudge, and hanging them without the semblance of a trial, or without even letting them or their friends know for what they were hung, is going a little too far,
jeff-wilson-holbrook-1888-08-11.A20:
Pleasant Valley Pastime.
Reports from Pleasant valley of the lynching by outlaws of James Stott, James Scott and Jeff Wilson, near Stott's ranch, on the afternoon of the 11th, received here up to the 16th, are as follows: The parties were arrested on alleged fictitious charges and were in charge of Jas. D. Houck, and five others. They were en route to Pleasant valley and when near the Canyon Creek trail were met by masked men who ordered Houck and his men to move on. The prisoners were found next morning hanging near the Verde road. Houck arrived in Holbrook on Monday, August 3rd, and the latest intelligence received from the scene was on Tuesday morning, when the bodies were reported as still hanging. From the best information to-day the county authorities are taking no action in the matter.

The most diligent inquiry among parties acquainted in the Tonto Basin country fails to elicit any information as to the identity of James Scott, the only one of that name known being the sheep man, and ex-member of the Legislature, who was not likely to have been found in the company of two such notorious characters as Stott and Wilson are alleged to be. The general impression is that the lynching party were not composed of outlaws either, as the man Stott, although arrested several times, had always managed to secure an acquittal to the disgust and annoyance of the better class of citizens, who were cognizant or his place being a rendezvous for horse thieves and bad characters, and who, as stated before had ordered him to leave the country.—Journal Miner.

A REIGN OF TERROR.

The women and children have been bunched and placed where they can better be protected from the death dealing rifles of freebooters who act upon the bushwhacking plan, shoot from concealment and make way with their plunder unseen.

The Governor, through the toe economical administration of the last Legislature, has no militia organization available to assist in the enforcement of the law, and it is questionable whether the Federal government would interfere in a matter that our laws provide the machinery of the county municipality to control. And as that fact has become so painfully apparent, threatened ranchers who have been driven from their homes have no recourse but the painful alternative of self-protection.

The reported hanging of James Scott. Jeff Wilson and James Stott has been confirmed by persons who some days after their execution saw them suspended to a tree at the foot of which their saddles were found, as left at the time of their being put to death. The story that they were arrested upon a fraudulent warrant is not true. At the time of their being taken by citizens, they were in custody of a deputy sheriff and posse, who were so numerously outnumbered that resistance was useless.

James Stott was no stranger in Globe. March 22nd and 23rd, 1887, he and a man named Thomas Tucker were given a preliminary hearing for the alleged larceny of a horse, the property of Jacob Lauffer, and discharged from custody by the justice upon the ground of insufficient testimony to establish guilt. The proof established the fact that the horse in question was found in the possession of Stott and that the animal was the property of Lauffer, but as then and now believed the bill of sale of the animal to Stott, produced in court, was simply a fraud and a trick to outweigh other convincing evidence. Mr. Tucker and others, it will be remembered, paid an unwelcome call at Newton's ranch, as is charged with evil intent; consequently the visit of himself and associates, such as could get away, was brief. Tucker while retreating upon a double quick was wounded by a far reaching rifle ball.

And now, most probably as a sequel to the lynching of Stott, Scott and Wilson, we are called upon to refer to a Holbrook dispatch, of August 18th, in which it is stated that "outlaws," in Pleasant valley, lynched William Nogler and Louis Nogler, stockmen, inoffensive citizens, and ordered W. H. McRaigy, an employee of the Aztec Land & Cattle Company to leave, and fired upon him.

This state of affairs suggests the question, have we a Governor clothed with power to see that laws are executed, that thrifty and law abiding citizens are not disturbed in the performance of legalized pursuits? From present appearances, in Pleasant valley, a negative answer might be expected. Nevertheless, we have a Governor and laws that afford all needful protection, but they are not executed.

These making war on settlers who have fled their homes for self-protection, so far as we are informed, are generally not identified with the section of the country where the demon of digcord has obtained a footing. Their continued presence there is attributed to the imbecility of executives of the law. When arrests are made and indictments had it is only the most sanguine who believe that conviction and punishment will follow. Quirks and quiddities of the law, alibies, changes of venue, hung juries and executive clemency will be invoked, and it is to this uncertainty in the administration of justice that the woods are full of outlaws whose chief reliance is in the virtue of gun powder, a protecting rock, a tree, a dense thicket. Such being the case, suggest the remedy.

On the 31st of July the people of Pleasant Valley and vicinity assembled at Perkins' store fearing an Indian raid, as they had been notified by some of John Dasin's Indians that a large party were out. After waiting until the 3d of August, two men were sent to Tento to find out what they could about the Indians. On their return next day they passed by Laffer's

UNLAWFUL HANGING.
Further Particulars of the Hanging of Stott, Scott and Wilson.
ranch, one hundred and fifty head of horses and some fifty head of cattle. Now sir, does it look reasonable that he should be engaged in stealing horses? If the parties who committed that lynching outrage, were justifiable, then why so much pains taken to disseminate false reports as to the standing and character of James Stott? Right needs no vindication; 'tis the wrong that requires a Nemesis. Right stands alone without support—like the sun, it shines unblushingly upon all. On the contrary, wrong must need apologists, and its agents run hither and thither, trying to make people think that black is white. If those outlaws had sufficient evidence against those unfortunate men to justify their hanging, surely they had enough to convict in the courts of law. Ah, my friends, there were other motives, not the least of which, was personal revenge.

I am ashamed at the attitude taken by the Prescott papers, that they should lend countenance to outlawry, and give their moral support to the worst of crimes. Yet, with my personal knowledge of John H. Marion, J. C. Martin Bucky O'Neil, I am sure neither of these gentlemen are guilty of such, through prejudice or spite, but have been basely deceived by persons guilty of the blackest of crimes, and done purposely, on the principle of stop thief.

The two gentlemen—one from New Hampshire and the other from Los Angeles—who are consumptive invalids and have resided at Mr. Stott's place for months past, both of whom testify to the honorable and gentlemanly character of Mr. Stott, say of their own knowledge, that Stott never has been absent over night since their sojournment with him, except when at Halbrook purchasing supplies. To see the gray-haired, armless old veteran, and his equally gray-haired wife, father and mother of Stott, who have come all the way from Boston to care for the last that remains of their son—to see this, and then read the scurrilous reports in the press, with not a scintilla of truth in their support, is really shocking to all honest citizens of this county. Who knew Stott better than his neighbors and daily associates? Surely not a gang of criminals, themselves outlaws by their own acts. If the friends, neighbors and acquaintances of Stott knew him to be an honorable man, (Brutus was said to have been "an honorable man," and upon the same hypothesis, every mother's son of that gang of assassins, were all honorable (?) men. "I had rather be a dog and bay the moon," than be classed with such.) how is it that a mob of concealed, unidentified, midnight assassins, know so much more of his business and character?

Mr. Alfred M. Ingham, one of the consumptive invalids, made a statement in which he says: "On the morning of the 11th of August, before daylight, and before any one had arisen, an armed party of 28 men, headed by James D. Houck, came to the house of Mr. Stott; I talked with Mr. Houck, and asked him it he had warrants for the parties; Houck seemed to hesitate, and finally said: 'Yes, but I left them in my coat pocket at the cabin where we stopped last night.' The weather was quite chilly, the altitude being high, and it struck me as being rather a strange procedure, that if he had warrants and had a coat, that he should leave both behind, and travel several miles during the coldest part of the night without a coat. I do not believe he, nor any one in the party, had a warrant for James Stott." The foregoing is the version of an eye witness, and of one who cannot be called a horse-thief, as he is unable to walk but little, nor can he speak above a whisper. Let the press do justice to the memory of the dead; if they cannot, do not do so much for the undeserving living.
jeff-wilson-holbrook-1888-08-11.A25:
TERRITORIAL TOPICS.
Condensed from Our Exchanges for "Silver Belt" Readers.
The public schools of Tucson opened with an attendance of 319 pupils as against 245 last year.

Troops of this department have received orders to engage in their annual sham skirmishes.

The season for deer does not begin till October 1st. and all persons buying venison this month are subject to a heavy penalty.

Our Republican brethren, says the Tucson Star, are busy registering Republican voters. They are putting in three to every one the Democrats are getting.

John T. Y. Smith, of Phoenix, has let a contract for the erection of a four-story brick flouring mill, to cost $35,000, and be completed about January 1st, 1889.

Hon. Patrick Hamilton and wife returned this morning from San Diego, While in that city Mr. Hamilton did not fail to do good work for Central Arizona.—Arizonan.

J. B. Blackwell met death by accidentally walking off the balcony of the Commercial Hotel, Phoenix. He was 75 years old, came to Arizona in '59, and for 22 years lived with King Woolsey.

The Enterprise says: There will be a free race and a fair fight among candidates for office in Pinal county this fall, and no party lines will be drawn over any of them.

The shipments of cattle from Arizona over the Atlantic & Pacific railroad the past summer, are said to have been larger than during any like period in the history of the road.

It is said there will be an independent political ticket nominated in Graham county upon which will be placed the names of the very best citizens of the county, irrespective of politics. Men and not party will be the controlling sentiment.

Stott, the gentleman who was so handy with a rope and branding iron, but used them too promiscuously to suit his neighbors and was in consequence lynched, left property valued at $2,000. An administrator is to be appointed, to close up the estate, on the 17th.

It is now alleged that the three proxies from Yavapai county who voted to sustain the administration of Arizona's chief executive were purchased. If this be true then the Governor's strikers appear to be getting down to the political ward business quite rapidly.—Star.

Eighteen cavalry horses from St. Louis, destined for San Carlos, were received here Monday. They were a fine lot of animals, and are the first consignment of one hundred and twenty-five to be received for distribution to San Carlos and Fort Grant and Thomas.—Wilcox Stockman.

Doc. Atkinson, the old trapper and hunter, well known all over the Pacific coast, was in Florence a few days this week. The venerable man is still hale and hearty notwithstanding his white hair and beard, and the ravages of time have made no serious inroads upon his general health. —Enterprise.

J. M. Slater, of libel notoriety, has gone to the Huachuca mountains to spy out parties cutting timber from Government land. The Prospector says: As there are no saw-mills in that vicinity it is to be presumed that some poor devil has built a house out of pine logs which a good Lord provided for his necessities, but which our great and just government says thou shalt not steal.

GEORGIA NEWS.
Told by the Constitution's State Correspondents
And Gathered from Our State Exchanges. A Mirror of the Happenings of the State for the Past Week.
The sentiment in favor of the extension of the road southward was unanimous, and a new route to the seacoast via the Atlanta and Florida is assured beyond a doubt.

The Leary Courier has the following advertisement: "Wanted—A teacher with plenty of gum, grit and intelligence to open a school at the academy in Leary. We believe such a person could succeed here."

Mr. Joseph Moore, of Walton county, was in Conyers Thursday. He is now about 93 years old, and moves real glibly, only his eyesight is failing. Few men have his strength at the extreme age to which he has attained.

Judge E. F. Lee is one of the first settlers of Dodge county. He came with his parents from North Carolina when a small child, in 1835, and the family located on the hill near where Eastman now stands, and the judge has lived there continuously ever since. That was long before Eastman or Dodge county was dreamed of.

S. B. Betton, of Cuthbort, is 82 years old, and he is vigorous and active yet, and frequently walks from his granddaughter's, Mrs. H. B. Mattox, to town, a distance of four miles, without complaint. Colonel Betton was a classmate of President Davis, and enjoys many other honorable distinctions. From appearance, he has several more years of usefulness and activity before him.

Charles Anderson, an old colored man in Pulaski county, was shot Monday night by Hilary Nelson, another colored man. They had had a quarrel Sunday. On Monday night Hilary and several other negroes went over to where Anderson lived and renewed the quarrel, and finally shot him in the back.

In the midst of local and state political excitement the stockholders of the Atlanta and Florida held a well attended and harmonious meeting yesterday in the basement of the courthouse. The very best of feeling prevailed and general satisfaction was expressed at the report of the road's present condition and future prospects.

There is one scuppernong vine in the garden of an Athens gentleman which several years ago produced one hundred gallons of wine. The owner thinks he will beat this record the coming season, as the vine is unusually full. It was planted about thirty years ago by Professor Rutherford, and now covers about a quarter of an acre of ground.

Mr. William Horace Cunningham, the well known vocalist of Macon, recently attended a praise and song service in the Hazard district and helped to swell the melody. The News refers to the event as follows: Whenever he inflated his lungs and let go, everything and everybody else had to stop. His voice was like unto the roar of a coming storm, and the waves of wind that he would emit at each note would raise the roof of the house about two feet.

George Walker, of Schley county, is experimenting in egg-plant culture this year, on rather an extensive scale. He has nearly three hundred plants, all of which are heavily fruited and growing vigorously. He sold nearly a buggy load here yesterday at satisfactory prices, but thinks of shipping the remainder of his crop to Atlanta and Savannah, where better prices can be obtained. The egg-plant is one of the finest vegetables grown here, and its culture could be made a profitable business, if properly conducted.

The Americus Republican says that a young lady aroused the whole household at her home, a few nights since, screaming and yelling that some one had kissed her while she was asleep. Her father rushed in with a pistol in one hand and a light in the other, but could not find the kisser, at first. The daughter declared that she felt the whiskers on her lips and the fellow's breath on her cheek and that it was "soft and nice." Just then her pet kitten slipped from behind her pillow, and she tried to kill it because it was not a man.

A few days ago Ebenezar Peck, a colored man living on the Harrison place, not far from Crawfordville, was out walking through his cotton patch when he discovered several silver coins on top of the ground. He procured a hoe and began digging, when he found three or four more pieces. He says he would have continued digging, but he didn't want to spoil his cotton. Some of the pieces were dated as follows: One 1722 and one 1773, both Spanish twenty-five cent pieces; one 1793, a Greek coin; one American half dollar, dated 1818.

The Eastman Times says: "Judge Rozar, ordinary of Dodge county, is one of the thrift-lest farmers of this section. He does some good farming on the intensive system, and says it pays. Says he makes every year on some of his acres fifty bushels of corn to the acre; has made as high as sixty-one. He made last year on a three mule farm 1,200 bushels of corn, 21 bales of cotton and 14 stacks of fodder, besides a variety of other smaller products. All this was done on common wiregrass land.

Mr. Osborn Watson, one of the most successful farmers of the Upper 11th district, Houston county, tells how he "tricked" two hawks not long since. Mrs. Watson felt great pride in 26 young turkeys that were growing finely. A couple of hawks took a fancy to these turkeys and killed all of them except nine. Mr. Watson then rubbed strychnine and syrup on the back part of the head and neck of each turkey. Next day two turkeys were missing, and a dead turkey and a dead hawk were found together in a field. The other hawk has not since been seen.
On Wednesday night a foul and most dastardly murder was committed on the plantation of Dr. L. D. Johnson. Early in the night a party of men rode up to the house of John Schley, a colored tenant of Dr. Johnson, and asked if Jim Thomas was in, and if so, for him to come out. The negro expecting no danger, answered their call, and when he got within five feet of the parties, he was shot to death. Jim had only recently come into the neighborhood, and was apparently a quiet, harmless man. Who were his murderers or their motive for the diabolical act are not yet known.

One day last week Mr. Rich Bowen, at Arabi, Dooly county, decided to try to blast a rock out of the bottom of his well and after trying dynamite a while sent a negro down in the well to try to dig it deeper. The negro remarked pretty soon that he could not stand it down there much longer, and preparations were made to draw him out. Several were standing looking down into the well waiting for the negro to give a signal when they saw his head drop over and he sank to the bottom; assistance was lowered as quick as possible, but when reached he was dead.

A little four-year-old negro boy whose parents live on Mr. Tank Carroll's place near Snow, says the Dooly Vindicator, killed his little brother last week by knocking him in the head with a piece of lightwood. No one knows the cause as the mother was off at the time. It is supposed that he became enraged with his little brother about something and struck him with the piece of wood, knocking his left eye entirely out of its socket, from the effects of which the child died in a few hours. This is the youngest murderer in the history of this country.

LYNCHED BY BALD-KNOBBERS. Friends of the Convicted Chief of the Gang Wreak Vengeance on Five Witnesses.
SPEINGFIELD, Mo., Nov. 15.—A rumor reached this city, this morning, from Christian county, the home of the famous Bald-knobber king, Dave Walker, to the effect that five of the witnesses who testified against him in his trial for murder have been lynched by ex-Bald-knobbers. It is said the friends of Walker waited until the Supreme Court had passed upon the case of Walker, and when it was announced that the ex-chief of the Bald-knobber regulators must hang, they wreaked vengeance on the five leading witnesses who brought him within the shadow of the gallows.

The lynching is said to have taken place on Tuesday night on the banks of Bull creek, in Christian county. Nothing authentic has been learned, however, the point at which it is said to have occurred being forty miles from a telegraph station and the only means of communication is by messenger.

Late last night a man by the name of Grant arrived here from Taney City, in Taney county, to see Joe Inman and Charles Graves, to give them warning not to return to their homes in Christian county. Inman and Graves were concerned in the Greene and Edens murders, and to save their necks they turned State's evidence. Both came here several days ago, and were about returning when Grant reached here and told them that five men had already all been lynched, and the mob was waiting for them. Grant knew nothing of the lynching himself. The information had been brought to him by one of Inman's relatives, who did not stop to give particulars, but continued his flight toward Arkansas, after begging Grant to warn Inman and Graves.

KANSAS CITY, Nov. 15.—A Times special from Springfield, Mo., says that a reliable gentleman who arrived there to-night from the Bull Creek neighborhood, in Christian county, reports everything quiet when he left. He does not think there is in any truth in the rumor that five Bald-knobber witnesses were killed, and thinks that the rumor arose from the fact that Joe Inman, one of the gang, who turned State's evidence, was warned not to go to that part of the country. Moreover, there were only three

of the gang who turned State's evidence, while the lynching-story places the number of victims at five.

THE WORK OF A SCHEMER.

Scott Ray Invents Grounds of Contest in the Hope of Getting a Seat in the Senate.

GREENSBURG, Nov. 15.—The first step is taken to steal the next United States Senator from Indiana. Scott Ray, by his attorney, J. S. Scobey, this evening filed in the clerk's office notice of contest against S. J. Carpenter. After alleging that Carpenter received 5,648 votes in the two counties, and Ray 5,566, showing a majority against Ray of 79, the notice alleges six reasons why Carpenter is not entitled to a seat as Senator, although he has received his certificate of election.

First—That Carpenter bribed electors in Shelby county.

Second—That he bribed voters in Shelby county.

Third—That Edward Speer, trustee and inspector in the northeast precinct of this township, is within the sixth degree of consanguinity with W. W. Lowe, who was elected surveyor of this county, and that the majority against Ray in the precinct was declared to be 245.

Fourth—That the board of election in the precinct was therefore illegal.

Fifth—Malconduct of the board of county canvassers in receiving the vote of said precinct.

Sixth—That the board of canvassers of this county, by reason of receiving said precinct's vote unlawfully declared that Carpenter received 312 majority in this county instead of 67, his rightful majority.

The injustice of the ground of contest is shown by the fact that three of the Democratic candidates for county offices are elected here if that precinct be not counted, yet not one of them has the hardihood to contest and try the case before the courts. Ray, well knowing that his case will be heard only by a Democratic Senate, hopes to secure a seat from which the people spurned him. The people of this county await patiently to see whether there are enough honest Democrats in the Senate to refuse his claim.

A Report That They Have Lynched Five of Their Enemies.
SPRINGFIELD, Mo., Nov. 15.—A thrilling piece of news that is yet to be confirmed floated down from the Ozark Mountains today. The story goes that late on Tuesday night the Bald Knobbers of Taney county assembled and started on a wholesale lynching campaign. They skirmished around the town of Chadwick and up Bull Creek and lynched five of the most active agents in the conviction of Dave Walker, the Bald Knobber Chief. On last Monday the Supreme Court passed on the case of Walker, and he was sentenced to be hanged on Dec. 28. This judgment, it is asserted, aroused all the hatred of the old band, and they lost no time in getting revenge.

Another act that incensed the lawless organization was the killing of Capt. Kinney, the head chief of the organization. After the conviction of Walker and others for the Edens murder, Kinney, although not implicated in these murders, was shot and killed by one of the State's witnesses, on the ground that Kinney attempted to draw a weapon when they met. The Knobbers asserted that he was hired to kill Kinney.

The particular crime for which Walker is condemned is the killing of two men, Green and Edens, in August, 1887. For more than a year previous a growing anti-Bald Knob sentiment spread through Christian and Taney counties which had for years been under the jurisdiction of the order. Men had been murdered, whipped, and run out of the county, and there was no redress. About twenty-five members took part in the crime which finally, by aid of the Federal authorities, resulted in breaking up the band. On that August night the Regulators visited the Edens homestead and, after forcing the door, killed Charles Edens and William Green, a son-in-law, and badly wounded Mrs. Edens and her husband. Four or five of the prisoners turned State's evidence, two of whom have since left the State. The others are supposed to be among the men reached.
joe-inman-springfield-1888-11-13.A9:
Five Men Dragged From Their Homes and Hempel Into the Hereafter.
Each Bore the Terrible Symbol of Death, Peculiar to the Banditti.
The Ozark Range Is Again Under a Reign of Terror.
Special to the Globe.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Nov. 15.—A special from Ozark, Christian county, this state, gives the following details of the quintuple lynching, last night, by Bald Knobbers of witnesses against Dave Walker and other leaders of that organization. James Wilson, a farmer living near Chadwick, on the Ozark range, came into Ozark this morning after five coffins, which were to be used to bury the victims of the vengeance of the Bald Knobbers. Far from the nearest town, in the shadow of the Ozark range, lived the men who had been instrumental in bringing justice to the murderous leaders of the organization, and since the trials, which resulted in the apparent demoralization of the band, these men have lived in the belief that their troubles were over. This morning's sun, however, shone on a sight that proved conclusively that the law defying organization still existed. From the limbs of a mighty oak tree on the banks of a creek, only a short distance from the place of the Green and Eden murder,

FIVE CORPSES WERE SWINGING in the breeze, and each one bore the dread symbol of death at the hands of the Bald Knobber—a knife-cut across the brow. A farmer who was early on his way to town was the first to see the horrible sight, and he quickly summoned his neighbors, who took down the bodies and found them to be those of Charles Green, James Eden, William Enders, Jonathan Wiley and Emmett Anderson. All these men had sworn to the facts of the killing of Green and Eden, brothers of the first named, and on their evidence Dave Walker was sentenced to pay the extreme penalty of the law. The bodies were placed in a wagon and carried to the homes of their families, and there the story of the latest Bald Knobber raid was heard. At the home of Green and Eden, who occupied jointly a long, double log house, all was terror and dismay. As soon as the wails of the bereaved women and children could be stilled, the following was told to the horrified listeners: At precisely 12 o'clock a knock was heard at the door, and in response to an inquiry the family were told that a neighbor had a stailed wagon near by, and requested assistance. Green and Eden immediately went out, and as they passed the gate, a single

PISTOL SHOT WAS HEARD and out into the moonlight, from the bushes rode about 200 Bald Knobbers with the disguise that a year ago was so well known in the Southwest. They surrounded the two unfortunate men, a slight struggle followed, and then all rode away with their victims. The terrorized family could do nothing and were afraid to stir out of doors until daylight. At the residence of Enders much the same story was told. At Wiley's house the demand for admittance was refused and the Bald Knobbers broke down the door and dragged the man from the house. During the melee several shots were fired at the assailing party by the members of the family, and they are confident that one of the raiders was wounded. Anderson was captured while on his way home from Chadwick. The whole country is again under a reign of terror, as no one knows who did the deed, and each is distrustful of his neighbor. Sheriff Williams has gone to the scene of the murders with a large posse of men, and says he will hunt down the perpetrators of the deed if it is possible. The only clue is the Bald Knobber, who is supposed to be wounded.

THE "BALD KNOBBER" LYNCHINGS A HOAX. To the Editor of The Tribune.
THE "BALD KNOBBER" LYNCHINGS A HOAX.
To the Editor of the Tribune.

Sir: In my copy of your paper dated the 21st instant I notice a telegram from Ozark, in this State, giving the details of the lynching of five witnesses against the "Bald Knobbers" by members of that organization. Will you permit me to have space to assure you that the statement of such lynching is an unmitigated hoax. Not only was there no such occurrence, but on the contrary, the news that the Supreme Court of the State had finally decided that the condemned "Bald Knobbers" must hang, which decision was the cause, according to your correspondent, of the terrible lynching he details, was greeted in every part of the county where the "Bald Knobbers" lived as a just and wise decision, and one well-merited by the condemned men.

This part of Missouri has suffered greatly by the publication of such misstatements as this. The whole "Bald Knob" organization and its outrages have been magnified to tenfold their rightful importance. It was never more than an association of ignorant country lads, who finally, under the lead of the more daring spirits among them, perpetrated a cowardly murder. The history of the "Order" since then is short and simple. With every participant in that crime in the clutch of the law, with tour of the most prominent under sentence of death, and with the whole outraged community around against them, there is not to-day in the southwest counties of Missouri a man bold or bad enough to avow himself a "Bald Knobber."

We have rolled up large Republican majorities through all this region, and we hope to prosper yet.

A. M. HASWELL

Springfield, Mo., Nov. 23, 1888.

The contractor, in obedience to demands from his laborers, has often asked for advances in the payments. Saturday morning he threatened to shoot Mr. McKee, superintendent of construction. Constable John Rucker interfered and saved trouble, but the latter lay in ambush and as Madden passed by shot and killed him in the most uncalled for and cowardly manner. He fled to a justice's office and in fifteen minutes was released on $1,000 bail and took to the woods. In the meantime the railroad hands organized for a lynching, and the last seen of Rucker was when flying through the woods, pursned by a howling mob. RAILROAD CONTRACTOR KILLED.

St. Louis, March 5.—An atrocious murder was committed Saturday morning at Winona, Mo., prominent railroad contractor named Madden, being the victim. He was in charge as sub-contractor of the construction part of the Current River branch of the Kansas City & Gulf railroad and had repeatedly asked for advance payments on his contract from the principal contractor, Mr. McKee, represented the original contractors as superintendent of constructions. On Saturday, Madden was drunk, and on McKee's refusal to advance him $150, a quarrel ensued. Constable John Rucker interfered and prevented trouble. Latter, as Madden was on his way to town, Rucker shot him from an ambush, riddling him with bullets. Rucker fled to a justices office and in fifteen minutes was released on $1,000 bail, and took to the woods, flying from a mob of laborers, who had organized to lynch him. There is no telegraph communications with Winona and it is not known whether the fugitive escaped or was overtaken and killed.

St. Louis, Mo., March 5—An atrocious murder was committed Saturday morning at Winona, Shannon county, Missouri. A prominent railroad conductor was the victim. The Current river branch of the Gulf Railroad is being constructed here under a contract sublet to George Madden. The contractor in obedience to a demand from the laborers asked for an advance in payments Saturday morning. He threatened to shoot Mr. McKee, superintendent of construction. Constable John Rucker interfered and saved trouble, but the latter lay in ambush and a Madden passed by shot and killed him in a most cowardly manner. He fled to the Justice's office and in fifteen minutes was released on $1000 ball and took to the woods. In the meantime the railroad hands organized for a lynching, and the last seen of Rucker was when flying through the woods pursued by howling mob.
murder was committed Saturday morning at Winona, Shannon county, Mo., a prominent railroad contractor named Madden being the victim. He was in charge of a sub-contract on the construction of a part of the Current river branch of the Kansas City and Gulf railroad, and had repeatedly asked for advance payments on this contract from the principal contractors. Mr. McKee represented the original contractors as superintendent of construction. On Saturday Madden was drunk, and on McKee's refusal to advance him $150 a quarrel ensued. Constable John Rucker interfered and prevented trouble. Later, as Madden was on his way to town, Rucker shot him from ambush, riddling him with bullets. Rucker fled to a justice's office, and in fifteen minutes was released on $1000 bail and took to the woods, fleeing from a mob of laborers who had organized to lynch him. There is no telegraphic communication with Winona, and it is not known whether the fugitive escaped or was captured and killed.

SANGUINARY AFFAIR.
SANGUINARY AFFAIR.
Bloody Deeds Done by Enraged Laborers in Missouri.
SPRINGFIELD (Mo.) March 6th — News
SPRINGFIELD (Mo.), March 6th.—News has reached here of wholesale shooting and lynching in Shannon county, which have been going on since Wednesday last. Geo. Madden is a sub-contractor working on the Current-river branches of the Gulf Railroad. At present the road has been extended to the little village of Winona. The village is at present filled with a rough crowd of day-laborers. For some time past these men have not received their pay, and many were showing signs of discontent. Madden and the other contractors succeeded in pacifying the men for a time by telling them that they, too, were out of funds, having received nothing from their employers—McTigh & Co., of Memphis, Tenn. This excuse satisfied them for some time, but only transferred their anger from their immediate superiors, with whom they were friendly, to the unknown moneyed men.

A CAPITALIST STRUNG UP.

On Wednesday, McKee, a member of the firm of McTigh & Co., arrived at Van Buren, Ark., having come to see how the work was progressing. The men, hearing he was coming to look at the work, stopped to receive him, and when he drove up the men, in excited, threatening tones, demanded the money due them. McKee, not understanding the demonstrations, refused to comply with their demand until he had seen the engineer of construction.

Anger had carried the men beyond the control of the bosses, and upon McKee's refusal they dragged him from his carriage to the Court-yard. A rope was placed around his neck and he was drawn from the ground. The men allowed him to hang until he became insensible, when they lowered him, and, throwing some water in his face to resuscitate him, allowed him to go.

McKee, thoroughly frightened, drove to Van Buren, and boarding the train was leaving the country. In the car in which he was seated he met George Madden, who demanded $1,500 with which to pay his men. McKee refused to give him the money. Madden at once drew a revolver and fired at McKee. The latter started to draw his pistol, but John Rucker, a constable, who had seen the trouble, interfered and tried to arrest Madden. A rough-and-tumble fight followed, which ended in Rucker being put off the train.

SHOOTING AND LYNCHING.

Hurrying to a house near by, he secured a Winchester rifle and waited for Madden at Winona as he left the train, and he had no sooner stepped on the platform than Rucker opened fire, sending nine bullets into the contractor's head and body. Madden's friends saw him fall, and hastening to him, found him dead. They then turned their attention to Rucker, who was endeavoring to make his escape. The angry mob of laborers, with whom Madden was a favorite, was soon following Rucker, with the avowed intention of lynching him. He struck out for the hills, turning every moment and firing at his pursuers, several of whom he killed.

A large portion of the mob kept up the chase after Rucker, while some returned to Winona, and collecting still more men, started out to revenge themselves upon the constable's friends. Two of them were caught and lynched by the infuriated rail-roaders, while another, who had barricaded himself in his house was shot. Additional forces moving for the hills to assist in the search for Rucker say they will not return until they have caught and lynched him. News of the terrible affair was sent to the nearest telegraph station by a special messenger.

A mother and her two children perished in their burning house at Cayuga, Canada, Monday night.

Most Rev. James Walshe, D. D., Roman Catholic Bishop of Kildare and Leighlin, Ireland, is dead.

Henricus Heetebrei, a 19-year-old lad of Holland, Mich., was exploring a cave near his home, when the roof fell in, killing him.

At Indianapolis, Ind., Monday the Prohibitionists filed remonstrances in commissioner's court against the granting of licenses for the sale of liquors.

Walter B. Lund obtained judgment for damages at Lebanon, Mo., Monday, against Sheriff Ehlus, who arrested him as W. B. Tascott. An appeal will be taken.

Morris Barron, a well-known sporting man, who was the backer of John Morrissey when he fought Heenan and Yankee Sullivan, died Monday at his home in New York.

Pleuro-pneumonia has broken out among the cattle in Middlesex County, N. J., and infected herds are being destroyed by order of the State authorities as a precautionary measure.

M. V. Dixon, formerly of Hancock County, Ill., has been sentenced to the California Penitentiary for life for the murder of William Hopkins, of Colusa, Cal., in November last.

Grocers at Madison, Wis., have been suffering from petty pilfering for some months, and Sunday the thief was caught in the act. He proved to be Willie Schulkamp, aged 10.

Sumner Hollander, 13 years old, of Somerville, Mass., seriously wounded his 11-year old cousin by trying to shoot an apple on the top of the latter's head while playing William Tell.

The Pennsylvania Railroad Company made a reduction of 226 men from its force at its car and machine shops at Fort Wayne, Ind., Monday, on account of the great falling off of freight business.

At St. Louis early Monday morning Fred Weiss, aged 15, while asleep, walked or jumped through the window of his room in the third story and fell to the sidewalk. He is in a critical condition from concussion of the brain.

At Winona, Mo., Saturday forenoon a man named Madden, a prominent railway contractor, was assaulted by Constable John Rucker, who took to the woods to escape lynchers. It is not known whether Rucker escaped or not.

The eastern part of Hodgeman county was the scene of a very singular murder last Friday: singular in as much as sufficient cause for such a deed is wanting. The murdered man, Thomas Andrews, lived about five miles west of Burdette and the other party, one Studebaker has his abode across the way. Report says that these two men, who had something of a partnership, fell into a difficulty in regard to the disposition of two mules, from which arose a series of quarrels, such as are common between uncongenial neighbors. Thursday Studebaker called Andrews out of his house and accused him of stealing a post from his premises. Andrews very imprudently appeared with a revolver in his hand and still more imprudently drew a line and dared his neighbor to cross it. Studebaker crossed the line, but owing to a quick retreat, it is supposed, was not shot. The difficulty ended with this. Friday about 11 o'clock Studebaker was seen approaching Andrews' house with a double-barreled shot gun. Andrews was alert and seizing his gun took refuge in the house. "His wife tumbled the children under the feather bed and then climbed in herself," says an exchange. Immediately afterward two shots were fired, the husband exclaimed that he was killed and fell bleeding on the bed. He was shot twice in the right breast and died a few hours later. As for Studebaker, he was found later in the day digging a grave for, as he stated it, "the d——n rascal I have just killed," and was arrested and taken into custody. The friends of Studebaker claim that he is insane.

LATE reports to the Kansas Farmer from eighty-five counties of the State showed that on June 1 wheat was in good condition, never better, probably, at this stage of its growth. If the average was as large as it was four years ago, the yield would be fully as large. Oats are doing well, heading short in some localities and in a few places hurt by chinch bugs, but there is very little complaint on that account. The season is backward and May was unusually cold, hence corn is not as far along as usual at this time of the year. Still it has received the last working in many parts of the southern counties. The stand is good, and a greatly increased acreage is reported in the western counties. A great deal of rice corn, sorghum and alfalfa is being grown. Millions of trees have been set out and they are growing well. Apples are favorably reported in most counties and so are small fruits. Grasses are doing well in most places. In the eastern counties there is some complaints of dry weather and bugs, but taking the State as a whole, the crops were never in better condition on June 1.

GOVERNOR MARTIN recently pardoned John W. Reed, who was sentenced in April last to serve one year in the Shawnee County jail for killing Rev. McIntyre, of Clay Center last September. Judge Gathrie, before whom he was tried, and County Attorney Curtis certified that the evidence on the trial showed that the faal blow was struck by the son of the prisoner and that there was no malice on the part of the convicted man. The son is a fugitive from justice.

ABOUT noon the other day a fire broke out in the Kansas City (Kan.) Ice Company's houses at Lawrence, and the buildings were soon in ruins. The loss was $14,000, on which the insurance was $8,000.

The body of May Mozley, one of the sisters drowned near Wyan lotte while boating, was found about a week after the accident just below Kansas City.

The Union Labor party of the Third Congressional district recently renominated Rev. W. H. Utley, of Labette County, for Congress.

A charter was recently filed with the Secretary of State of the Kansas River Improvement Company, of Quivera, the object being "to make the Kansas river navigable for boats for the carriage of freight and passengers from a point on the Kansas river near Quivera to Lawrence, and for the maintenance of facilities for skating, rowing, yachting and other innocent sport."

The report of the railroad assessors show an increase of over $10,000,000 in railway valuations since last year, and 2,000 miles additional road. In 1887 the report showed 6,211.70 miles of main track. This year the amount of mileage foots up 8,184.60 miles of main track, with 964 miles of side track. Such a record has never been made by any State in the Union.

J. RAILSBACK, a prominent attorney of Columbus, was placed under arrest the other day charged with the enbezzlement of about $9,000 from Jefferson Rainey, of Belleville, Ill., for whom he had been agent and attorney for the past five or six years for the purpose of loaning money.

The State Sunday School Association convention opened at Abilene on the 6th with about two hundred delegates and many visitors in attendance. A children's mass meeting was held in the afternoon. In the evening the convention listened to an able address of welcome by Rev. W. A. Welshe, D. D., of the Baptist Church. Hon. A. B. Jetmore, of Topeka, delivered an eloquent adress, the title of which was "Christianity More than Education the Sure Foundation of a Republic."

The Russell & Southeastern Railway Company, capital stock $500,000, recently filed its charter with the Secretary of State. The proposed line is from Russell to Hutchinson through Russell, Barton, Ellsworth, Rice and Reno Counties, a distance of eighty-one miles.

About four o'clock, the other afternoon three armed men entered the town of Hugoton and attempted to murder County Commissioner J. B. Chamberlain, the city marshal and Deputy United States Marshal Samuel Robinson. Some thirty shots were fired, but fortunately no one was wounded. The Hugoton people immediately turned on and were in hot pursuit when the would-be assasin left their buggies, mounted their horses and made good their escape.

A year ago the county attorney o'Sevens County began proceedings against Governor Martin to enjoin him from organizing Grant County, which had been attached to Stevens County for judicial purposes. The case was brought in the Shownee district court and Judge Gathre rendered a judgment making the injunction perpetual. From this an appeal was taken to the Supreme Court, which tribunal recently dissolved the injunction, holding that a county attorney had no authority to sue in the district court beyond the limits of his own county in any matter in which his own county was not especially interested.

KANRAS continues to boom.

John Studebaker, a farmer living near Jetmore, recently went from his field to the home of Thomas Andrews and shot him dead in his own house. Studebaker was arrested and there was strong talk of lynching, although he had for some time been regarded as crazy. An old time feud caused the crime.

The ten-year-old son of C. W. Knapp recently attempted to jump on a moving train at Iuka, when he fell under the wheels and was killed.

Senator Plumb has secured favorable action on the applications for pension of Joseph Allstrom, of Clay Center, and George Farmer, of Fredonia.
A LATE fire damaged the large planing mills of E. E. Sprague, at Emporia, to the amount of $5,000. Fully insured.

When Mrs. Crocker, a widow residing in Sedwick County, returned home from a visit the other day she found the doors open with every indication that robbers had been about. George Dennis, a thirteen-year-old boy who had been left in charge could not be found and valuables were missing, but her money, about $200, was found where left. Two days later she heard a noise in the cellar, and the boy was found bound and gagged, where he had been thrown by a tramp who had applied for and received a meal and maltreated the boy because he refused to tell where the money was. The little fellow died soon after discovery.

OUTLAWRY IN KANSAS. A Negro Tarred and Feathered-A Mob Looked For.
JETEARE, Kan., June 17.—Tuesday night a negro was taken from his home in the southeast part of this, Hodgeman, county a mile or more into the country by some ten or a dozen white men who proceeded to treat him to a full and unstinted coat of tar and feathers. John and Mike Gleason were arrested and brought to this city last night upon the charge of having participated in the mob. It is claimed that the negro was a notorious thief and neighborhood pilferer.

The most intense excitement still prevails in this city and the entire east half of the county over the killing by John Studebaker of Thomas Andrews. Every night for more than a week a mob of over 100 men from the neighborhood of the killing has been expected in Jetmore, determined on lynching Studebaker. Sheriff Gilland is determined to protect him at all hazards, and last night some 200 citizens gathered at the court house in this city and expressed themselves as fully determined to stand by the sheriff in protecting the prisoner from mob violence. It looks now as though more blood would be shed before the trouble ends.

Those who know most about the facts in the case are divided in opinion as to the degree of Studebaker's guilt, as it is believed by some that he is insane, while justification is claimed by others.

Some forty of the best citizens, armed with Winchester rifles and shotguns, guarded over the jail all last night. The same number will be on guard to-night.

Captain Tumbridge's Tweaked Nose.

New York, June 17.—Special Telegram

Captain Tumbridge's tweaked Nose.

New York, June 17.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Almost the sole topic of conversation on the street yesterday was the nose tweaking episode in which Ed Stokes and Captain Tumbridge were the principals. A complaint has been drawn against Ed Stokes for assault and battery. He will be tried in the Kings county supreme court Monday. Captain Tumbridge will sue for $10,000. Immediately after the fracas Captain Tumbridge sent for his family physician to discover to what extent he had been injured. To a reporter the doctor said: "His face presented a pitiful aspect. On the right side of the head is a swelling nearly as large as a base ball. His right cheek is terribly cut and so is the left. The left eye is swollen as if Stokes had tried to gouge it out. His nose is also swollen and contused." At the Hoffman cafe the men in charge laughed at the complaint as a huge joke. Stokes is not at all concerned about it but said: "Let them go on with it. I wont run away."

An Alleged Missouri Murderer.

LEAVENWORTH, Kan., June 17.—Sheriff Hack, of Platte county, Missouri, has succeeded in arresting John A. Gamble, the man who is charged with killing Jeff Cluck near Union Mills, Mo., August 6, 1887. Since that time Gamble has been almost continually on the move, living in one place never over a few months, and then moving in a direction opposite to that in which he started out. Gamble is now in jail at Platte City, awaiting his preliminary trial.

Good Work by White Caps.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., April 15.—A band of "White Caps" made a raid last night in the country back of New Albany, Ind. They visited the house of a Mrs. Jones, a widow woman, and whipped soundly her three boys because they would not work, but left their mother to support the family. Then they visited William Wright, whom they warned to leave the state, and a lawyer from Leavenworth, who had been paying attention to Mrs. Jones' daughter. They threatened him with tar and feathers unless he left for home within half an hour. He went at once.

NEW ALBANY, IND., April 17.—The "White Caps" have become unusually daring. Saturday night a band of fifty-seven of these regulators rode into the suburbs of this place, a city of 25,000 inhabitants, took from their beds three stalwart men, the sons of a widow named Jones, tied them to trees and gave them a severe whipping with switches and sticks. After the whippings all the men were told that if they did not go to work and earn a living they would be whipped again. The White Caps then visited the house of William Wright, and warned him under pain of death to get out of Harrison County. What Wright has done is not known, as he is apparently a law-abiding citizen. REFORM A LA WHITE-CAP.
TWO MEN AND A WOMAN GIVEN A SEVERE WHIPPING.
NEW ALBANY, Ind., April 19.—The Crawford county "White Caps" were again on the warpath Tuesday night. Ten days ago they notified James Seebers, Robert Broomfield, and Mrs. Nancy Wilson that unless they ceased their bad practices, reformed, and went to work within ten days they would be given 100 lashes each. The notices were in writing and were left on the door-steps of the individuals notified, together with a bundle of long hickory switches. Broomfield and Seebers treated the warnings with contempt, swearing they would fill the bodies of the "White Caps" with bullets should they attempt to carry out their warning, and vowing also to defend Mrs. Wilson. These persons all reside in the country a few miles distant from English, Crawford county, and forty miles west of this city. They are all very tough characters, and are charged by the people with a number of offenses.

About midnight of the 17th the "White Caps," fifty strong, rode up to Mrs. Wilson's house, where Broomfield and Seebers were spending the night. Both men and the woman were seized, and, in spite of their piteous pleas not to be whipped, taken to the woods, stripped, and tied to trees. The men were given 125 lashes each, the elastic switches cutting into the flesh and drawing blood at every stroke. The men fainted several times,
were merciless.
“You have kept a den of thieves and vagabonds, and led a life of harlotry,” they answered, “and we will make you suffer for it.”
At the end of twenty five lashes the wretched woman was apparently in a dead faint, and she was spared further torture. When the victims were untied they fell to the ground and were left there. The “White Caps” then rode away to the residences of several other disreputables to notify them to leave the country or take the consequences.
Jake and Bill Wright, whom the “White Caps” sought to hang on the 13th inst., have fled to Tennessee. Several other toughs have taken refuge in Kentucky or Tennessee. Every one of the Crawford county men recently whipped by the “White Caps” was a desperado, and the organization is determined to rid the county of the last one of these bad characters. The organization is composed, is is understood, of reputable farmers.

LYNCH LAW IN NORTH CAROLINA.
Three Negro Prisoners Taken From Jail, Tied to Trees, and Riddled with Bullets.
PLYMOUTH, N. C., Jan. 28.—Lynch law ran riot here Thursday night, and yesterday morning the people were horrified to find that three negro prisoners had been taken from the county jail by masked men, conveyed to the woods on the outskirts of the town, tied to trees, and then shot to death. Their bodies were found in the positions in which the lynchers left them, securely bound to the trees and riddled with bullets. The lynching party gathered at the jail shortly before midnight and demanded that the jailor should deliver to them Jack Blount, his brother, Matthew Blount, and Patterson Spruitt, all colored, who had been placed in jail charged with the murder of John Dawson, a peddler, on New Year's day last. The jailer refused, but was overpowered and was forced to permit the men to be taken away. When the woods were reached, the victims begged for mercy, but no attention was paid to their outcries, except the stern reply that they would be given a moment to pray, when the lynchers, who were armed with shot-guns, muskets and pistols, began their bloody work, and fired volley after volley, until the wretches were dead. Matthew Blunt was a preacher of some local notoriety, and had previously lost an arm.

Night before last a large party of masked men went to the jail at Plymouth and took therefrom three negroes charged with murder. The lynchers carried the negroes, whose names were John Blount, Matthew Blount, and Patterson Spruill, to a point some half a mile from the jail and, after tying them to trees, shot them to death. The murder with which they were charged was that of Edward Dawman, a travelling jeweller, who was passing through the neighborhood of Cresswell, Washington county. He was decoyed into some dense woods by four negroes on the afternoon of December 23d last. While the negroes were walking along with him one, with an axe, slipped up behind him and crushed his skull. Another blow was given, and then Dawman lay dead, with both temples broken, back of head crushed in, and a shoulder broken. The murderers dug a hole and hastily put him in it. They only partially covered the body, and a negro who was driving through the woods saw his knees sticking out of the shallow pit. The murderers were arrested Christmas day. The Plymouth massacre or lynching is one of those atrocious deeds which can find apologists nowhere. It was a deed done in cold blood without the ordinary provocations which sometimes justify popular violence. There was no pretense that justice would not be meted out to the guilty; the murder though an atrocious one, did not involve as a victim one who drew to his character or associations the fury of popular vengeance. That vengeance could patiently await the course of the law. There is only one crime for the punishment of which lynch law is excusable. In this Plymouth case, the lynchers were murderers, and if detected, should be punished as such.

WHITE MEN SHOULD THINK.

The District of Columbia, though it has no vote, is allowed to send delegates to the National Republican convention which names the candidates of that party for President and Vice-President. In the District, as elsewhere in the South, the negroes constitute the bulk of the Republican party. The other day a convention was held in Washington to select delegates to the next National Republican convention. The negroes, representing both Blaine and Sherman, raised such a row that the police had to interfere, and the convention adjourned without choosing delegates. In a communication to the National Republican Fred Douglass, a negro leader, says:

"I hardly need say in this I was sorely disappointed and greatly humiliated. The proceedings of that convention far transcended in treachery, baseness, brutality and violence any description which I have seen in the most malignant of the papers which have noticed it."

And yet the delegates chosen by this people may decide who shall be the candidate of the party for the high office of President of this great country, and who, through such agencies as such and their allies may put in operation may be declared to be elected.

Do white men of this country want their government controlled by such elements and such agencies.

And yet it is just such that Republicans say shall again have control of not only the nation, but of the Southern States. If this party has any hopes whatever of again getting control of the State of North Carolina it is through votes three-fourths of which will be cast by this same ignorant, irresponsible negro. In their demand that the present system of county government be repealed it is with the knowledge that the tax assessing, tax collecting and tax spending control of nearly one-third the counties of this State will again pass into the hands of negroes. While the negroes in these counties pay no taxes, comparatively, they are to be entrusted with the assessment of the property of white people, the levying and collection and expending of taxes. Can white men think of such propositions with patience or indifference?

The Raleigh Index Appeal correspondent says: R. G. Dunn, a wealthy resident of this city, has made public an offer to furnish free of charge for rent, any reasonable number of acres of land, in Wake county, for two years, to any person known to be a practical tobacco grower, who will agree to plant and raise a crop on the same. He also agrees to furnish all the necessary timber for barn building, &c. Of course none other but a reliable person in all particulars will be selected. It is an opportunity rarely presented, and no doubt a number of offers will be made.

The supreme court has just made public a decision which may be of service to the legal profession and which to some extent puts a check to the almost innumerable cases appealed from the lower courts. It decides that the only ground on which an application to the supreme court for a new trial below can be based in the discovery of such new evidence as was proper to be heard below, and the supreme court will not interfere because of irregularities occurring in the trial below, its jurisdiction as a court of appeal for the correction of errors not extending to such cases.

The question of what shall be done with the governor's mansion, now in an unfinished condition, will come before the next legislature, and there is a great diversity of opinion concerning it. It is evident that the building is of too grand proportions, and planned in too extravagant a style to suit the meagre salary of $3,000 per annum, now allowed the governor. It was rumord last spring that the Baptist denomination of the state desired to buy it and remodel the building for a female school, but the board of public buildings did not feel authorized to sell it, withou

legislative sanction. It is hardly probable, in the present financial condition of the state, that either party will brave public opinion so far as to vote a sufficient sum for its completion, and it will either stand for some years in its present unfinished condition or be used for some other department of the state government. The general tendency of opinion is that it should be turned over to the judicial department, and that the building just finished for the supreme court be devoted entirely to the state library and museum. This is a good idea and will, in all probability, be carried out by the general assembly.

A fire in the town of Malone, Western New York, on the 29th, destroyed property to the amount of $200,000, on which was insurance of $75,000.

Judge Schenck, of Greensboro, has completed the manuscript of the revolutionary history of North Carolina, embracing principally the years 1780-'81.
