The colonels of the four regiments of State Guard are called to meet here Saturday to confer with regard to the place of holding the encampment and on other matters looking to the welfare of the force.

Wilmington cotton receipts to this date are almost 160,000 bales—an increase of 32,000 bales. Raleigh has thus far received something over 28,000 bales.

At Rich Square Jacob Bryan (colored) was shot and killed after a quarrel by a white man named Charles Bush. Both had been drinking. Bryan attacked Bush and knocked him down. While down Bush shot Bryan.

A couple of Mormon elders have gone to Davie county to begin the work of making converts to their faith. It is reported that many Mormon missionaries will arrive in various sections of the South in the next few months, and that the Church of the Latter-Day Saints will seek to make proselytes in this section of the country.

At Mountain island cotton-mills, at Mount Holly, Gaston county, a sensation has been caused by an order issued by the supernumerary promoter use of tobacco and snuff in the mills. Some of the operatives, it is stated, have quit work, refusing to submit to this order.

The road-workers in Alexander county day before yesterday dug up the skeleton of a man in a sitting posture. It is believed to be that of a man who twenty years ago lived in that section who mysteriously disappeared.

Yesterday Angus McNeill, a prominent farmer of Robeson county, was riding in a buggy. His horse ran away and threw him under the vehicle and killed him instantly.

At Henderson at 8:30 o'clock this evening Mr. Thaddeus R. Manning, editor of the Gold Leaf, and one of the sprightliest writers in the State, was married to Mrs. Fanny L. Porter, a very engaging lady of Henderson, a sister of Mrs. A. R. Wortham. The marriage ceremony was performed at the Presbyterian church. Both bride and groom are very highly esteemed by the people of Henderson and all that fine section of country.

The demand on the part of the people for the passage of the Blair bill does not abate, but the feeling is growing that there is no chance for its passage. Private letters from members of Congress state that many northern members are bitterly opposed to it, and that no amount of argument in its favor appears to affect them or modify their views.

The new Washington graded school for colored pupils in this city has been occupied. It is handsomely fitted and is pronounced the finest colored public-school building in North Carolina.

Near Washington, Beaufort county, R. W. Walker and his young son, Engene Walker, were set upon by three negroes after a quarrel. A negro named C. W. Howard threw a brick at young Walker, which missed him. He then threw another at the elder Walker, which struck the latter in the forehead, inflicting what is regarded as a fatal wound. Howard has made his escape.

No clue to the identity of the men who composed the mob which shot to death the negroes who murdered the peddler in Washington county has yet been found. It is now improbable that any further attempts in that direction will be made, though there are rumors that the grand jury will take action in the matter in some way. There have been some false rumors of anticipated race troubles at Plymouth. There is no disturbance.

The petition of Lucien Rowe, of Durham for a commutation of his death sentence to imprisonment for life has been prepared and will be laid before Governor Scales in a day or two. March 6th is the date set for Rowe's execution for burglary.

Rev. G. P. Bostick, the new pastor of the First Baptist church at Durham, will preach his first sermon next Sunday.

Work on the Wilkeston extension of the Greensboro'-Winsboro' railway is expected to begin actively in a few days.

At Plymouth yesterday there was an incendiary fire which burned the Episcopal rectory and Harrison's Hotel, causing a loss of $3,000, with $1,500 insurance.
matthew-blount-plymouth-1888-01-26.A25:
JUDGE LYNCH.
A FEARFUL CRIME COMMITTED AT PLYMOUTH, N. C.
Some two or three weeks since, as stated before in this paper, a clock peddler was found murdered, in Washington county, near Creswell, N. C. Three negroes by the names of Jack Blount, Mathew Blount and Patterson Spruill, were charged with the crime and arrested and taken to the jail at Plymouth, N. C., to await the action of the Superior Court.

On Thursday night, January 26th, about mid-night, they were taken from the jail, by a gang of masked men, carried about one mile from Plymouth, lashed to trees and riddled with bullets. When found, the morning afterwards, we hear, the clothes of one of them was on fire, supposed to have caught from the powder when shot.

It is also reported that lynching was talked of for some time.
matthew-blount-plymouth-1888-01-26.A32:
MEDICINE-MEN.
ANNUAL MEETING OF THE NORTH CAROLINA ASSOCIATION.
A Brutal Murder—Struck by Lightning— Searching for Miss Foe's Assailant— Other Notes.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
annual session of the North Carolina Medical Society began this morning at Williams's Hall, Fayetteville—Dr. T. D. Haigh, of Fayetteville, presiding, and Dr. Julian E. Baker, of Tarboro', secretary. The attendance is up to the secretary. This afternoon President Haligh delivered the annual address. To-morrow evening the people of the town will give a banquet and ball to the society. On Thursday the society will participate in the memorial-day exercises, and on the evening of that day the annual oration before the society will be delivered.

Near Davidson College lightning struck the warehouse of John Caldwell and burned it with its contents, causing a loss of $1,200.

The municipal election at Durham yesterday was quite exciting. There were three tickets in the field, headed by John F. Freeland, W. J. Christian, and Thomas C. Oakley respectively for mayor. Oakley was the labor candidate, but many of his pledged friends deserted him and voted for Christian, who was elected.

The people of Monroe are greatly excited by the brutal murder of Policeman John Pearce by a negro named Bill Weddington. There was a row at a negro festival, and Pearce arrested the leader in the disturbance and started to the guard-house with him. A mob of negroes gathered and decided that they would rescue the negro who was under arrest. Weddington with a heavy iron bar in his hand was in the rear of Pearce. Frank Thomas, another negro, armed with a bludgeon, cried out, "Kill him!" Whereupon Weddington with one stroke crushed the skull of Pearce, who soon died, never having regained consciousness. Weddington was arrested at once, and Thomas, who had fled to Charlotte, was also captured. Both are in jail at Monroe. Thomas was tried for murder two years ago and got off. Pearce leaves a wife and four children.

The French corvette Brisson has arrived at Wilmington, whose people are showing her officers many courtesies.

It has been found that there are not enough legal signatures to the petition for the local-option election at Charlotte, and the county commissioners have withdrawn the order for the election.

The Federal Court began to-day at Asheville—Judge Dick presiding.

Reports to the Department of Agriculture from Durham and Orange counties state that the wheat and oats crops are being ruined by the prolonged and unusual drought. The same report says the tobacco-plants look well, and that large crops will be planted.

Mr. Hasten Poe, whose sister, Miss Ida Poe, was shot at Carthage by Robert L. McNeill, returned here to-day. He reports that her wound is not at present regarded as dangerous. No tidings of McNeill can be heard. This morning before daylight the town of Carthage, and particularly the house of McNeill's father, was strongly guarded, if having been rumored that McNeill was back in town in hiding. Search for him continued all last night, with the avowed intention of lynching. There is a belief this afternoon that he has after all gone safely away, and is now in Texas or on his way there for refuge.

North Carolina is rather coming towards the front in the matter of lynching. There has not been a legal execution this year, yet there have been five persons lynched. On the 27th of January Matthew Blouat, John Blount, and Patterson Spruill (all colored) were disposed of at Plymouth by his Honor Judge Lynch, and the same judge had another victim at Washington March 12th in the person of a white man, who boasted that he was the assassin of General Bryan Grimes. The last victim at this date is Frazier, who was disposed of at Washington last Saturday night for the murder of Cox. Of the persons sentenced legally to be hanged there have been the following, the commutations being in every case save one to life imprisonment: Charles F. Jones, Newberne; Lucien Rowe, Durham; James Thomas, Hendersonville; Allen McCarter, Statesville, and Daniel Biggs, Wilmington.

The Wake county Grape-Growers' Association met to-day and beard reports. It is discovered that vineyards west of the city and in this township were not hurt by the frosts of late April, while vineyards east of the city have suffered much damage.

Rev. Dr. C. H. Strickland, of Nashville, Tenn., was this evening called to the pastorate of the First Baptist church of this city. He is a very able man and will receive a $3,000 salary.

Captain E. R. Stamps, president of the Board of Directors of the penitentiary, and Mr. W. J. Hieks, warden of that institution, are now in the Blue-Ridge country inspecting the convict quarters in that section. The penitentiary is greatly cramped for funds and may have to remove from railways some of the convicts whose labor has been furnished free.

Major John Gatling, once so prominent as a lawyer, and who died yesterday morning, was buried this afternoon from Christ church, Rev. Dr. M. M. Marshall conducting the services.

The unfortunate white woman who drowned herself some days ago in Robeson county was a native of Robeson county. She ran away from her husband some months ago, and the greater part of the time wandered here and there.

There has been some dispute as to whether the names of the signers of the petition for a local-option election in Barton's-Creek township, Wake county, were or were not those of bona-fide voters, and so the county commissioners have been considering the matter.

The pea crop in the Goldsboro' section is about all picked. It has been quite remunerative. Next week the land now in peas will be planted in corn or cotton.

The Cape-Fear and Yadkin-Valley railroad make a fine showing in the matter of net earnings for the year ended April 30th. They were $31,188 in excess of those during the previous year.

A great revival is in progress in the Baptist church at Fayetteville. There have been many converts.

It is rather noticeable that the Democratic Convention of Cumberland county did not instruct its delegates as to the man they should support for Governor.

Mrs. Rebecca Long's house, in Richmond county, was burned a night or two ago, causing a loss of $1,500, with no insurance. Raleigh is well represented at the session of the Grand Lodge of Independent Order Odd-Fellows, which met at Greensboro' this morning in the hall of Buena Vista lodge. Grand Representatives Charles M. Busbee and C. B. Edwards are present. Captain W. A. Bobbitt, of Oxford, is grand master.

There were elections yesterday at several towns. At Shelby the Democrats were successful and W. L. Damson was reelected mayor. At Newberne the "Coalition party" carried the day. This is the "Reform party," composed of Democrats and the better class of Republicans which figured so extensively in the campaign of 1886. At Goldsboro' the Democrats were again winners, electing eight of the nine aldermen. At Greensboro' John A. Barringer was elected mayor.

Great fires have raged through the forests in Caldwell and Watauga counties, in a district covering some fifty or sixty square miles. The damage is immense. A great deal of the timber burned is chestnut.

ALEXANDRIA.

morgan-healdton-1888-04.A2:
HORSE THIEVES HANGED.
Some of their Supposed Executioners Under Arrest.
St. Louis, April 11.—A special to the Post-Dispatch from Gainesville, Tex., says: "News was received here last night from Healdton, Indian Territory, that thieves who lived in that vicinity and were believed to be connected with a bold band of horse thieves, who have been stealing large numbers of horses in the Chicasaw Nation during the past winter, were seized Monday night by a mob who live near Healdton and hanged. One of the executed thieves was Bill Morgan. Some of the parties connected with the mob who did the hanging have been arrested by Deputy United States Marshals.
morgan-healdton-1888-04.A5:
Horse-Thieves Hanged.
Horse-Thieves Hanged.
GAINESVILLE, Tex., April 11.—News was received here, late last night, from Healdton, I. T., a small village twenty miles northwest of Gainesville, that the thieves who lived in that vicinity, and who are believed to be connected with a bold band of horse-thieves who have been stealing large numbers of horses in the Chickasaw Nation during the past winter, running them into Texas and selling them, were seized, Monday night, by a mob of enraged citizens, who live near Healdton, and hanged. One of the executed thieves was Bill Morgan. Some of the parties accused of being connected with the mob who did the hanging have been arrested by deputy United States marshals.
morgan-healdton-1888-04.A7:
JUDGE LYNCH.
He Holds Court in the Indian Territory. Three Thieves Hanged. Special Telegram to the Statesman.
He Holds Court in the Indian Territory. Three Thieves Hanged. Special Telegram to the Statesman.

GAINESVILLE, April 12.—A report reached the city last night that three men living in the vicinity of Headton, I. T., had been arrested by a mob of citizens and hanged within a short distance of that place. The parties hanged were accused of being connected with a gang of horse thieves who have been stealing horses in that part of the territory for several months. The gentleman who brought the information learned of the incident while on the way to Gainesville, having met with two United States marshals who had a man under arrest charged with being one of the mob who did the hanging. These officials informed the gentleman who brought the news here of the mob's triple execution. He stated, that one of the parties who met his doom was named, Morgan, but had forgotten the names of the other two victims. A number of citizens of the territory were in the city today, and confirmed the report. They gave the name of one of the parties, but failed to learn the names of the other two. They say hangings will continue in that country, until horse thieves and other criminals are convinced that the nation is no longer a harbor for outlaws.

bank of Raleigh, N. C., have returned from Canada to stand trial.

Several miners were killed by an explosion of gas near Albuquerque, N. M., on the 10th inst.

George Baueria, Louisville 13-year old boy, committed suicide after being punished for truancy.

Ex-Attorney-General Brewster's will bequeaths his entire property, valued at $100,000, to his only son.

The United States supreme court has rendered a decision sustaining the oleomargarine law of Pennsylvania.

James A. Bailey, a miner at Shamokin, Pa., went out on the recent strike, and was recently compelled to ask for help from the poor authorities. A few days ago he received notice that an uncle had died in England, leaving him $1,600,000.

The assembly sub-committee of the whole of the New York legislature has reported adversely on the woman's suffrage bill.

Cattle de-horned are dying by the hundred near Bloomington, Ill.

Eight moonshiners and their stills were captured near Huntsville, Ala., the other night.

The Pope's thanks have been conveyed to President Cleveland for that gentleman's jubilee gift to His Holiness.

The normal school at Terra Haute, Ind., was destroyed by fire a few days ago. Loss $180,000.

About $40,000 worth of smuggled opium was seized by customs officials in San Francisco a few days ago.

The report that Mr. Blaine is a very sick man is emphatically denied by that gentleman's friends.

R. F. Berger, special agent investigating the Redwood land frauds in California, reports that a Scotch syndicate was organized for the purpose of obtaining control of all the valuable redwood lands in Humbolt county, and they had in their employ a brother of the register of the land office at Humbolt. The agents of the syndicate secured men to make timber entries for which the latter received $50 on the completion of the entry. Special agent Bergen submits that the evidence is sufficient to warrant the cancellation of patents issued to the syndicate by devious ways.

John Roach's will, which has only just been filed, provides that his business shall be continued not exceeding ten years. Mrs. Roach is to have an annuity of $5,000. The remainder is divided among the children and grandchildren.

In the supreme court the other morning Attorney-General Garland presented the resolutions on the death of Chief Justice Waite, adopted by the supreme court bar, and delivered a touching eulogy on the late chief justice. Justice Miller, who presided, received the resolutions and in doing so delivered an eloquent address. "The oldest members of this court," he said, "know of no man who was better fitted to discharge the administrative duties of the office of its chief justice, or who ever did so with more acceptability to his associates and to the public at large."

The bills forfeiting unearned railroad lands cover about 50,000,000 acres.

Rumored in political circles that Secretary Whitney is to succeed Minister Phelps at the court of St. James.

Twenty-three buildings in Orlando, Florida, were destroyed by fire on the 10th inst., resulting in a loss of $200,000.

The house military committee has authorized Mr. Ford of Michigan to report favorably the senate bill authorizing the secretary of war to detail 50 army and navy officers to give military and naval instructions in educational institutions. The bill was amended, authorizing the issuance of arms and ordinance to colleges where retired officers are assigned as instructors.

S. M. Weir, treasurer of New Albany, Ind., is short in his accounts $70,000. Weir had engaged in "margin speculations."

Gen. Terry, recently retired, is talked of as a candidate for governor of Connecticut, of which state he is a citizen.

Senator Leland Stanford of California, wants to be president.

G. H. Griffith, the well-known actor died in Philadelphia a few days ago. He had been connected with the American stage for 28 years.

Gen. Ashbel Wells Riley died at Rochester, N. Y., recently, aged 93. He was well known as a leading temperance and anti-slavery lecturer before the war. At the time of the nullification troubles in South Carolina he was in command of the Twenty-third New York regiment, state militia, and tendered Gen. Jackson the use of his "troops," for which he was afterward personally thanked by the president.

May Emily Bird, a colored woman, has just died at Centreville, Tenn. She was for a long time a missionary in Liberia and once entertained there the great explorer Livingstone, when on one of his expeditions. She spoke with fluency many of the native languages.

Josephus Sooy, ex-state treasurer of New Jersey, is dead

The case against John Coughlin, who was on trial at Ravenna, Ohio, for the second time, for the murder of Detective William Hulligan of Cleveland, has been dismissed.

Six inches of snow fell at Bellows Falls, Vt., on the 12th inst.

Supreme court sustains prohibition law of Kansas, and the last brewery has been closed.

Four horse-thieves near Healdton, I. T., were strung up by vigilants the other day.

Over 2,000 immigrants have reached

HAVOC AT MADISONVILLE.
Four Men Lynched By an Unmasked Vigilance Committee.
Special to the Gazette.

Special to the Gazette.

HUNTSVILLE, Tex., Jan. 4.—Reliable news reaches here from Madison county, thirty miles west of here, that a mob of two or three hundred went to the town of Madisonville yesterday and shot down one Will Bobo on the public square in the presence of the Sheriff.

The mob went from there to the house of one Red Page and took him out and hanged him; also shot Alf Whtiing, supposedly fatally and killed one other party, name unknown. The county has been in a state of terror for years by a band of horse and cattle thieves, committing depredations, and recently two witnesses against certain parties were foully murdered. The lives of others were threatened, and people became almost afraid to be seen out. To offset this the best citizens of the county organized themselves into a mob to clean out the set. It is stated they are not half through their work. The Governor has been appealed to for troops. The parties composing the mob were unmasked.

SITUATION AT MADISONVILLE.
The Trouble Believed to Be at an End. Only Two People Killed.
HUNTSVILLE, TEX, Jan. 6 — Reports from Madison county to-day are conflicting. Some state that the mob has dispersed, while others report directly to the contrary. It is definitely learned, however, that only two persons have been killed outright, though others have been shot at and some made to leave the country. Judge Kittrell arrived from the scene of action this afternoon and thinks the trouble at an end. It is learned that the Navasota Guard detachment stacked arms and went into town unarmed, acting under the advice of the District Judge and others. The mob is said to be gathering strength, now numbering 500.

NEVASOTA, Tex., Jan. 6.—No further particulars have been received regarding the disturbance at Madisonville, beyond the fact that the vigilantes had killed another member of the Bolo gang, making five in all. The Nevasota guards left for Madisonville last night, but it is thought the mob dispersed before they arrived.
reu-page-madisonville-1888-01-03.A11:
NO RANGERS WANTED.
A Review of the Lawlessness in Madison County Which Led to the Uprising of the Citizens.
Two Bad Characters Lynched, a Third Fired Upon, but Escaped-Others Warned to Obey the Laws.
Correspondence of the Gazette. MADISONVILLE

Correspondence of the Gazette.

MADISONVILLE, TEX., Jan. 5.—For many months the people of this county have been in quite a state of excitement over the numerous crimes that have been committed and the ineffectuality of the law in reaching the criminals. Theft, arson, robbery and murder have been committed. Men have been murdered because they were witnesses for the state in prosecutions for theft and the like. The finger of suspicion has been for months pointed to some five or six persons as being the guilty ones. Not longer than the 7th day of November last, the first day of our District court, two men, a Dutchman by the name of Keifer and a gentleman by the name of F. M. Gafford, were murdered near here in cold blood at night. Gafford was a citizen of Williamson county and was brought here by attachment to testify for the state in a cow stealing case. Several arrests were made for the murder of these men and some others have been suspected as being connected with the same. Peacher, a brother-in-law of Gafford's, and against whom Gafford was an important witness in a cow stealing case, was on examining trial before the justice of the peace here for over a week, and all the evidence against him being circumstantial, was admitted to bond in the sum of $2500. His wife, who was Gafford's sister and who was constantly in attendance upon the trial, from the first to the last of the examination, went home, and during the first night of her stay at home committed suicide, and it is believed that from her knowledge of the parties and all the evidence she was firmly convinced that her husband had murdered her brother. The people have been at fever heat over the case, and public prejudice has been running very high against Peacher and others who are suspected as being implicated in Gafford's murder. The people have grown furious over other crimes. A number of citizens some months ago organized a law and order society, and have met and resolved time and again, to no avail. It has been difficult it is claimed to secure convictions. Juries have often disagreed, and many times the guilty ones have gone scot free. The lawless element defied those who would enforce the law, and have even threatened the lives of men who have always lived peaceably, and simply because they wanted the laws enforced. Tuesday the whole thing came to a head. The Gafford and Keifer murders were fresh on the minds of the people. Some parties fired into the dwelling house of Alf Whitten, a notorious person, last Friday night, and he was swearing vengeance afterwards against certain parties whom he suspected as having done the firing. Many of his friends, most of whom are known to be toughs, were in town Saturday buying up all the ammunition and cartridges. Some 200 or more citizens, composed of the best element of the county, held a meeting a few miles distant from here Tuesday and organized in squads of about thirty men each and came to this place armed with shotguns and Winchester rifles. Here they found William Bobo, a man of desperate character and the one who has furnished the backbone to most all our lawless element and who has frequently indulged in threats against good citizens of this county, and killed him on the streets in open daylight in the presence of the public. From here they went to Whitten's and made war upon him. He was on horseback and made for the bushes. They fired some twenty shots at him, and it is believed wounded him, but nothing definite has been learned. Whitten was regarded as a leader of the lawless. They then went to the home of Reden S. Page's and carried him to a tree in the woods near by and hung him. Page was a notorious sneak thief and shrewd scoundrel. Newton J. Williams of the east, Clay Roberts of the west, Joice Wooley of the north and J. L. Connor of the south part of the county, all first-class men, were the leaders in this crowd. It is believed generally that lawlessness in this county is now broken up. Several other persons than those named were visited and told what must be done. Public sentiment sustains the conduct of the citizens.

Sheriff Block took time by the forelock and on Monday night had all the prisoners in the county jail taken out and sent to the penitentiary for safe keeping. This was wise for had the prisoners been here the crowd would have had them or torn down the new $8000 jail. It is rumored everywhere that rangers are to be brought here, but now everything is quiet. Whitten has no doubt left the country Page, the hanged man, was once a County Commissioner of this county, and it is said made a good officer. Bobo was shot twice—one shot in the head, the other in the breast. He died without a struggle, and was buried in the town cemetery. Texas Citizens Organize and Kill Two of a Murderous Gang. The Governor Interferes and the Citizens, After Exacting a Promise of Speedy Justice, Disperse. [Correspondence of the Courier-Journal.]
[Correspondence of the Courier-Journal.]

BEDIAS, GRIMES Co., TEX., Jan. 17.—The citizens of this section lately organized and took the first steps toward breaking up a band of horse-thieves. They killed two desperadoes in their effort and this brought them in collision with State authority.

For three or four years Grimes. Madison and adjoining counties have been infested by this gang of horse and cattle thieves. Horses were traced by their owners, the thieves arrested and indicted by the grand juries, but when brought to trial nothing could be proved, for the desperadoes had their witnesses ready to prove anything that was necessary. Trials were put off or the accused acquitted.

Citizens, finding that they could not get justice through the courts become more and more indignant and finally were out of all patience. On the night of November 6 last, the first week of the District Court of Madison county, two of the witnesses against the thieves were brutally murdered a short distance from Madisonville. One was shot to death in the presence of his wife and child. The other was murdered and buried, and his body was found three weeks later. Suspected parties were arrested and placed in the county jail at Madisonville. But popular feeling was so strong against them that they had to be placed in the penitentiary at Huntsville to save them from lynching.

On the night of January 2, three others of the same gang were arrested and placed in jail at Anderson, this county. Sheriff Grimes made the arrest. On January 3 the citizens rose in a body, entered the town of Madisonville, shot and killed "Bill" Boba, captain of the band to which the men under arrest belonged, hung "Reu" Page and gave several others orders to leave. Gov. Ross at once ordered a detachment of the Navasota Guards to Madisonville to quell the disturbance. The militia after a new days stay returned to Navasota, the citizens having promised Judge Ketsell to return to their homes. The judge promised to have the prisoners at Madisonville brought before the next term of the District Court.

The so-called mob was composed of the oldest and best citizens of the county, staunch brave men who do not uphold lynch law, but who could no longer leave their property at the mercy of a band of thieves and murderers.

Hidden Treasure Found.
KW Orleans, Jan. 25.—Confidderable te-

citement was created yesterday at Pass Christian by the discovery of a pot of buried treasure. Colita Narcisse, a colored man, was plowing in a vacant lot owned by Nicholas Buchert, when the plow point struck a hidden object, breaking it off. On looking to see what he had struck he found a curiously shaped jar, such as are still used in Mexico and South American countries to hold water. The jar was broken and found to be nearly full of silver coin. They examined and counted the coin, and found 209 silver half-dollars of American coinage and two quarter pieces, ranging in date from 1789 to 1826. The remaining contents consisted of Spanish and Mexican plasters and small coins, the dates from 1879 to 1820. The value of the whole is estimated at $235. As to how it got there, the most plausible theory is that it was buried by an old negro named Charlo, who was a slave of Mme. Azmar, one of the first settlers of the place. His cabin stood near the spot, and being a miser it is naturally supposed that he hid his hoard in the ground about the year 1830.

LATEST EXODUS SCHEME.

Liberal-Hearted Philanthropists to Ship the Colored Brother to South America to Save His Life.

Indianapolis, Ind., Jan. 26.—Col. A. A. Jones, of the State Auditor's office, who is connected with the latest proposed exodus of negroes from the Southern States to South America, talks freely about the scheme. He is an active friend of all movements for the improvement of the condition of the race and was engaged in the first exodus in 1879. He accompanied Gov. Chamberlain, together with several other young colored men, to South Carolina from Massachusetts, and entered heartily into that movement.

"This exodus," he said, "will be effectually pushed, and by May 1 we expect to get our first party on the road. There are no headquarters as yet; the movement is very young, less than a month old; so far as active work is concerned, headquarters will be established probably in New York. We shall have three agents in Cincinnati, one at St. Louis, and one at Chicago. I am agent at this point. We have some of the best people in the country interested; men who are willing to go down into their poekts for the relief of their oppressed brethren. We have some colored people in this country pretty well fixed, and they are committed to the work. There is no fixed amount of capital. We hope to accomplish by the exodus, first and foremost, protection. There is not a question of politics at the bottom, although it will, of course, have some political bearing. Why, do you know that in the last fifteen years 18,000 black people have been killed in the South for their political opinions, and nothing has been done to remedy the matter? It is life or death with us, primarily. We are tired of having representatives in Congress upon a voting population that has no representation. There is no other remedy; so we propose to pull out. The colored man has developed and made the South what it is, and the white laborer could not and does not do the work that our people do. The Southerners will find the difference when they have to use white labor. We have selected South America for the location because of its climate and the adaptability of the soil to produce such articles as the colored people are accustomed to raising. We have investigated the country and received favorable reports. Our people do not want to come North and West because of the climatic conditions and because the prejudice against a black face follows them even there. In South America, as well as in other parts of the world, the color of the skin does not bar a man out of the race for the best. We shall start our emigrants from Eastern points. I cannot speak any more definitely than to say that a Boston line running to Brazil will carry passengers at $14 per head. That certainly is cheap enough. We have agents at work in the South now, and we shall get as many emigrants as possible out of Mississippi, Louisiana and Alabama, while not neglecting Missouri and Kentucky, and if there is not a big emigration before next summer then I miss my guess."

Anarchy in Texas---Two of its Late Exhibitions.
Governor Ross has done himself himself credit by publishing a strong protest against mob law in Texas, which he justly brands as anarchy. We copy from the Huntsville Item a summary of the case which called forth the Governor's manifesto:

Tom Forsyth, the confessed murderer of county treasurer Hill of Panola county, was hanged by the indignant citizens of Carthage shortly after his capture. The particulars of the lynching are revolting. With his arms pinioned behind him, young Forsyth was led to the foot of a ladder placed against a tree whereon he was to be hanged by unmasked men, friends and neighbors. One of the two sons of the murdered treasurer adjusted the rope on the boy's neck. Nearly all the details of the hanging were known to the lynched boys friends, who said as death was deserved and must inevitably come, the sooner the end was reached the better. Clasped in each others arms the mother and sister of the doomed son and brother prayed with streaming eyes and moans of anguish to the God of Mercy for their loved, while he, with stoical nonchalance, climbed the ladder, received a drink of water from the hand of the son of his victim and leaped into eternity. Those who saw the leap say it seemed as if the neck was stretched to the distance of a foot. Death came rapidly and then the body was cut down, taken to the late treasurer's office and laid in the blood of his victim. Far better than that had been the trial of the culprit by law and his execution in a legal manner.

We copy from an exchange a summary of the facts in the other case which transpired about the same time as the above:

In Wharton county is a village called Spanish Camp. It is a retired and isolated spot in the edge of a dense forest. Here some negroes had gained possession of some land which they were quietly tilling and from which they had raised a crop. Some white men coveted the ground and ordered the negroes to vacate. This they refused to do. The matter came to a trial in a court of justice and the negroes won the suit, the court sustaining their legal claim to the property. This was about one month ago. Finding that threats could not intimidate, nor law dispossess these colored men, their white antagonists, in the dead of night, gathered a posse of their own diabolical breed, who armed themselves with winchesters and shotguns, surrounded the house while eight negroes were asleep inside, saturated the outside of the building with kerosene, while the inmates to whom the law had given possession were within, fired it, and as the roasting victims attempted to escape shot them down in cold blood, killing seven out of the eight and wounding the sole survivor.

The Governor scarcely alluded to this latter outrage, which he ought to have denounced quite as strongly as the other. He however justly adds:

The people of the world will seize hold of these casual or incidental acts of violence occurring in Madison, Wharton and Panola counties to blacken whole communities, and to misrepresent the entire state as well as baptize our people anew in a perfect stream of calumny. Hence, as the executive charged with the care for these public interests, and jealous of the honor and fair name of the state, I record my utter condemnation of mob violence of every character, and urge the people to a prompt and fearless vindication of the supremacy of the laws wherever and by whomsoever they may be assailed.

Frances B. Willard, pres., and Caroline B. Buel, sec., of the National W. C. T. U. have appointed a week of prayer from the 18th to the 25th inst. for the National, state and local organizations of the Union, and earnestly urge its observance. We make the following extract:

Seek God. Seek Him alone for a great awakening of the church and nation. The liquor traffic is here with its abominations legalized because of spiritual death. We need conscience aroused and made true. Sisters of the W. C. T. U., set the week apart, hold at least one meeting a day for the quiet, unostentations seeking of God herein suggested. Two public evening meetings, with sermons, gospel talks or conferences would be of great value. The evening of March 25 might be made effective by union services where these can be secured. When churches cannot give way for this, hold such a meeting in the afternoon of that day.

No topics are suggested lest they lead from the one central thought of all the days. Many things you will remember: our own work, our country's needs and perils, the workers who must go out into the coming contest, the pleaders at the fireside, the voters at the ballot box, but this one thing seek and find—God's touch of power upon our own spiritual life, and the spiritual life of the nation.

Assistance Nent to Burning Suffolk—
Personals and Briefs.
[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]
NORFOLK, Va., August 1, 1888.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

NORFOLK, Va., August 1, 1888.

Last night about 11 o'clock the large barn and various out-houses on the Green Ridge farm of Mr. George A. Wilson, in Butt's road District, took fire and were totally consumed, together with a considerable quantity of corn and provender, farming utensils, wagons, carts, a number of valuable mules and several fine horses, involving a loss of between $7,000 and $8,000. The buildings are supposed to have been fired by an incendary. The loss is very nearly covered by insurance.

About 10 o'clock to-day Mayor R. G. Banks received the following startling telegram from Suffolk:

SUFFOLK, VA., August 1, 1888.

Mayor Banks, Norfolk, Va.:

Send a steam fire engine at once. A large fire is raging, and the whole town will go, I fear.

BENJAMIN RIDDICK, Mayor.

One of the engines of the Norfolk department with a working detachment of men left about 11 o'clock under command of Chief-Engineer Kevill, and was on the scene of the fire in Suffolk in about thirty minutes.

Later, about 12 o'clock, Mayor J. Thompson Baird, of Portsmouth, received a similar telegram from Mayor Riddick.

The Chambers Fire Company, with the steamer Palmer, was at once ordered to the assistance of the imperilled town, and left within thirty minutes on a special fast train furnished by the Seaboard and Roanoke Railroad Company, under command of Chief-Engineer W. T. Robinson. The Superintendent of the Portsmouth Water-Works also promptly telegraphed to the pump-works at Lake Kilby to fill the mains and fire-plugs they have in Suffolk with water, although the town refuses to take water from the company.

Fourteen vessels cleared from this port during the month of July, carrying cargoes valued at $387,243—an increase of $75,765 as compared with last year.

During the month of July there were twenty marriages in Norfolk, eighteen in the county, and thirteen in Portsmouth.

The new Police Justice is endeavoring to break up the practice of liquor-selling on Sunday and selling to minors.

John F. Evans, who killed Peter J. McLean, has thirty visitors a day to call on him in his cell at the city jail. The friends of the murdered man have means, and will use every effort to assist the prosecution.

The County Court adjourned last night until September, and judge, sheriff, and clerk of the court all left with their families to-day for the mountains of Virginia. Judge Parker and Countv-Clerk A. H. Martin have gone to Orkney Springs.

Rev. W. V. Tudor, D. D., Rev. John T. Basman, and Rev. J. D. Hank leave to-morrow for the camp-meetings on the Eastern Shore.

Rev. A. J. Witherspoon, D. D., of New Orleans, is the guest of Rev. Dr. George D. Armstrong. Dr. Witherspoon was for many years minister to the seamen in this city.

Sheriff Bunting, of the county, and guard left for the penitentiary with a large batch of convicts this morning.

A few nights ago Mrs. Reuben Bright (colored), of Great Bridge, Norfolk county, gave birth to four live and well-developed children—two boys and two girls.

Great Excitement—Threats of Lynching. [Special Correspondence.]

Portsmouth, September 20.—On the 31st of July the barn of George A. Wilson, Esq., one of the largest of landholders of Norfolk county, together with its contents, consisting of all the latest improved farming implements, nine head of mules and horses, was burned by an incendiary.

The J. W. Southward Detective Agency were employed, and sent two operatives to Green Ridge, the scene of the crime. After prompt, diligent and earnest work they succeeded in arresting Sampson Dey (colored), a tenant on Mr. Wilson's plantation. Dey was taken before Justice Jordon, and after an examination was sent on to the October term of the Norfolk County Court.

Considerable excitement exists in the community, and serious threats of lynching the prisoner were made, but he was spirited away by the detectives and safely landed in the Portsmouth jail.

ANOTHER LYNCHING IN THE OLD NORTH STATE.
A Negro Brute Hanged-Critically Ill-
The Freshet in the Cape Fear-
Briefs.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
RALEIGH, N. C., September 14.—News was received here to-night of another lynching, which is the thirteenth this year. It occurred at Whiteville, Columbus county, night before last. A body of masked men, a hundred or more, entered the jail and demanded the keys from the jailer. With a score of revolvers pointed at him he surrendered the keys, and the lynchers went to the cell where Sherman Farrier (colored) was confined for an outrage committed on an aged white woman, took him and departed. Yesterday, suspended to the limb of a large oak about one mile from the jail, the body of Sherman Farrier was found with a placard pinned on his breast bearing the words: "We protect the virtue of our women. Beware." Farrier was a man of bad character, and had repeatedly been engaged in robbery. He was given a preliminary hearing before two magistrates last Monday, and was committed to jail to await trial. The evidence against him was conclusive.

William C. Lamb, son of ex-Mayor Lamb, of Norfolk, died yesterday at Newberne. He had recently engaged extensively in business in Jones county.

Ex-Secretary-of-the-State Rufus H. Page is critically sick with cancer at his home here.

The freshet in Cape Fear river below Fayetteville is said to be approaching in magnitude to the famous one of 1865, which was the highest ever known. All the bottom lands are to-day completely submerged.

RALEIGH N. C. September 15
A Negro Hung by Colored Men.

RALEIGH, N. C., September 15.—A mob composed of a hundred negroes entered the jail at Whiteville, Columbus county, Wednesday night, having forced the jailer at the point of revolvers to give up the keys, and took out Sherman Farrier, colored, and hanged him. He was accused of outraging Mrs. Sasser, an aged white woman on the 26th of August. On his breast was a card with the words: "We will protect our women. Beware men." J. C. Parrish of this county was brought here to-day very quietly in order to prevent his being lynched, and was tried before a magistrate upon the charge of outraging his own daughter, aged 12 years. The girl, her mother and brother were witnesses, and the evidence was direct and positive. Parrish was held for trial. His crime is a capital one in this State.

A BRUTE LYNCHED. "We Protect the Virtue of Our Women. Beware." [From Wilmington Messenger.] WHITEVILLE, N. C., Sept. 13 — A body of masked men, supposed to number a hundred or more, entered Whiteville, Columbus county, jail last night and demanded the keys from the jailer. At the point of arms he surrendered the keys to them, and they proceeded at once to the cell where Sherman Farrior, colored, was confined for an outrage committed on an aged white lady of this county, and took him and departed with him into the night. This morning, suspended to the limb of a large oak, about one mile from the jail, was found the body of Sherman Farrior with a placard pinned on his breast, bearing this inscription: WE PROTECT THE VIRTUE OF OUR WOMEN. BEWARE! The negro was a man of bad character and had repeatedly been engaged in robbery. The crime that cost him his life was the outraging of Mrs. E. A. Sasser on the 29th of August. He was given a preliminary hearing before Justices G. W. Fleim and Thos. Barefoot on Monday last, and was committed to jail to await his trial at the next term of the Columbus county Superior Court. The evidence was conclusive. From Wake Forest.

"Hard Times in the Confederacy."

Under the above title A. C. Gordon contributes to the September Century an anecdotal article, from which we quote as follows: "The traditional rebel soldier in the persimmon tree, who told his captain that he was eating the green persimmons in order to fit his mouth to the size of his rations, epitomized in his epigramatical speech the history of the economic conditions of the Southern States, both in the field and at home, during the war of the Rebellion. After the seaports of the South had once become thoroughly blockaded, it was a continuous, and in the end unavailing, struggle on the part of the people of the Confederacy to accommodate the status of supply to that of demand.

"After the war ended, a monthly magazine dedicated to perpetinating the records of the war from a Southern standpoint, and soon perishing in the vain endeavor, published a rude wood cut, which, with its concomitant inscription, expressed with great pith and point the extremities to which soldiers and homefolk alike were reduced in the late days of the contest. It represented two lank, lean, lantern-jawed Confederates in a blackberry patch. One of them, on his knees, the more readily to reach the palatable fruit, is looking upward at his comrade with a grim smile, and saying:

"They can't starve us, nohow, as long as blackberries last."

"The vein of his self-gratulation and assurance is readily acquised in and reinforced by the other, who responds in a spirit of apt commendation, and with an even larger and more catholic faith:

"Naw, sir! and not as long as that's huckleberries, nuther. And when there're gone, come 'simmons!"

"To the uninitiated stranger who saw and read, the rude cut and its underwritten legend, if considered at all, doubtless were held coarse and witless, but to him who knew the bitter meaning thereof, through his own harsh experience, they spoke with the emphasis of a stern and powerful significance."

sherman-farrier-whiteville-1888-09-12.A10:
Several lynchings have occurred in this State and elsewhere within the past two months—men taken from Jail or from the law officers and hanged or shot. That should not be so, and every good citizen should do all he can to prevent it. It is a terrible thing to execute a man without trial. The matter of an injured person identifying a criminal is an uncertain as well as a difficult thing to do—there have been many fatal and serious mistakes in that regard. Every man should have a fair trial, and courts and juries should act more promptly than they have been doing. We agree with the Wilmington Star in its remarks on this subject, copied below:

"Another case of mob law has occurred, this time in this section of the State. A negro was hanged for an assault upon a respectable white woman. What makes the case peculiar is that it was the work of negroes. We again say that such lynchings are to be deplored. If continued it will end in destroying the courts and returning society into a condition of lawlessness, when the strong will persecute the weak and the darkness of the Dark Ages will return. Let the criminal laws be improved and strengthened. Give society a chance against criminals on trial. Do not let all of the technicalities be on the side of villainy and violence. Let the Courts be prompt. Change the trial by jury so as to make nine men convict."

warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A1:
FLOGGED TO DEATH.
Outrages Perpetrated on Convict Laborers in Missouri.
St. Louis, Mo., March 12.—A report says that startling developments have just been brought to light at Coal Hill, one of the mining towns where the mines are worked with convict labor, near Fort Smith, Ark.. A negro convict by the name of Williams was flogged to death, and further inquiry developed the fact that Mose Harvey, a white man, aged thirty-five years, had been kicked to death by a fellow convict who had been egged on to do the desperate deed by Warden Grafford, and it was learned that he was in the habit of making the prisoners fight. The body of Mark Elder was exhumed, and the bruises and gashes on the body indicated a violent death. It was also developed that a prisoner by name of Hummel was tied up to a post in the mines last summer and beaten to death. As the investigation continues the more horrible details are revealed, and the citizens of Coal Hill are much excited and threaten to hang Grafford and tear down the prison barracks.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A2:
A Brutal Arkansas Prison Overseer Murders With Stripes.
It Is Supposed He Has Made His Escape to Memphis.
Two Sons Kill Their Respective Fathers in Arkansas.
A Bloody Day for Our Neighboring State-Particulars of the Horrible Affairs Over Which Communities Are Very Much Excited.
Special Dispatch to The Appeal.
LITTLE ROCK, Ark., March 12.—Considerable agitation was created in this city on its becoming known that Charles Williams, a convict in the mines at Coal Hill, this State, had been whipped to death by a camp warden named J. A. Gafford. The man was flogged to death last week, but for some cause the news was kept from the public till today. Regular court proceedings have been under way up at Coal Hill for the past several days and the revelations of the coroner's jury are revolting in the extreme. Gafford resigned as soon as he heard that an examination was being made and jumped the country, going, it is believed, from here to Memphis. The Governor today offered a reward of $200 for his apprehension. It is alleged that Williams is not the only one suffering death at the hands of this cruel brute.

The convict question is one that seems to be beyond the capacity of the citizens of this State to fathom, and what to do with these unfortunate human beings is a problem. The convicts at the camp are afraid when put on the stand to give testimony against the overseers, being fearful for their existence after the court adjourns.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A6:
INHUMAN BARBARITY.
Revelations That Forced a Convict Overseer to Seek Safety in Flight.
St. Louis, March 13.—Last Tuesday and Wednesday a coroner's jury began an investigation at Coal Hill, Ark., of the cause of the death of a convict, one Charles Williams. Warden Gafford hindered the investigation in every way in his power, but the facts of such horrible brutality were revealed that he was compelled to seek safety in flight, as it appears that punishment was the cause of Williams's death. The shoulders of the convict had been completely stripped of their cuticle by the lash. The skull near the right temple was fractured, the result, it is supposed, of a kick. The right side of the body contained a series of bruises, being the imprints of boots. In the back, in the vicinity of the kidneys, there was a bruise about six inches square, an evidence of further application of the boot. The testimony given by witnesses and the examination of the body showed that the man had received about 400 lashes, any ten of which would have been considered severe punishment. This was not all the testimony obtained by the coroner's jury concerning the cruelties practiced in the Coal Hill camp. Witnesses testified that about a week ago Gafford permitted two negro convicts, Mose Harney and Marsh Bailey, to engage in a desperate fight. The result is too shocking to admit of any extended description. The lower part of Harney's spinal column was broken by a terrible kick that Bailey gave him, and by the same means he crushed into a jelly the genital organs of his antagonist, who lay upon the ground writhing in pain. He was kicked in the head and in the stomach, one-fourth of which punishment was sufficient to cause his death. Harney was not killed outright, but died last Friday, after a week of terrible suffering.

Another case of brutal treatment was that of Mose Elder, a white convict, who recently died at the camp. It was over the body of this man that the warden refused to permit the coroner to hold an investigation. His remains were buried in a marsh a quarter of a mile from the camp. An examination of his body revealed thirty-four scars which caused the prisoner
to hold an investigation. His remains were buried in a marsh a quarter of a mile from the camp. An examination of his body revealed thirty-four scars, which caused the prisoner great suffering, but not sufficient of itself to have caused death. During the investigation J. B. Walker, a guard at the camp, was put on the stand. He was asked if a convict was not chained to a post, last summer, and whipped to death. The witness said he had not been summoned to testify in that case, and refused to give any evidence about it. The belief at Coal Hill is that last summer a convict was chained to a post, soundly lashed, and left there two hours. When the warden returned he gave him another whipping. When the chains were taken off the convict was dead. Another man was at that time warden of the camp. After he resigned Gafford was appointed his successor, and the latter held the position for about three months. There are ten or twelve new graves in the camp-yard, and no one seems to know anything about them, as no inquests were held on the bodies buried there.

Among the other 'charges preferred against the managers of the camp is that the colored convicts were compelled to work during the winter without shoes. Coal Hill is in a prohibition community, but a "trusty" was indicted not long ago by the grand jury for selling liquor, and was acquitted because he was a convict. The coroner arrived in Little Rock to-day and informed Governor Hughes of the result of the investigation at Coal Hill, and at his request his Excellency offered a reward of $200 for the arrest and delivery of Gafford to the sheriff of Johnson county. The condition of affairs at the camp appeared to the Governor to be in such bad shape that he called a special meeting of the penitentiary commissioners, and it was nearly 10 o'clock when the meeting adjourned.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A9:
WORSE THAN SLAVERY.
Shocking Developments of Inbuman Treatment of Convicts at the Coal Hill Conv Treatment of Camp in Arkansas. Fort Smith Ark March 13 The
Shocking Developments of Inhuman Treatment of Convicts at the Coal Hill Convict Camp in Arkansas.

FORT SMITH, Ark., March 13.—The startling developments brought to light at Coal Hill, in the case of Williams, the negro convict whipped to death, served to bring out the most revolting details of cruelty and death among the convicts. Suspicions were aroused by the developments in the Williams' case that others had suffered a like death. Mose Harvey, a white man aged thirty-five, died on the 9th inst.

The coroner had the body examine and found it in a terrible condition with the marks of kicks and bruises. The stomach was torn open and the entrails hanging out and unmentionable injury had been made. It was developed at the inquest that Warden Grafford, the same who whipped Williams to death, was in the habit of making the prisoners fight. He had put a convict named Mat Bailey up to giving Harvey, who was a small, weak man a beating and stood by urging him to kick and beat his victim until he was senseless. The guards were all afraid to testify.

The body of Mark Elder was exhumed and found terribly blackened, and it was also found that there were whip gashes on his back as deep as a man's finger. The jury could not determine if the wounds caused death, but think it highly probable. A number of prisoners testified, upon being assured that they would be kept from punishment.

It was also developed that a prisoner named Hummel was tied up to a post in the mines last summer and beaten to death by the brutal warden. The list of the cruelties told by the prisoners, now that their tongues are loosened, is almost incredible in point of human treatment. Investigations are still in progress, and other cases are expected to develope.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A11:
PRISON REFORM NEEDED.
The following account of the cruel and horrible treatment of convicts at Coal Hill mining camp, proves what we have heretofore said, Arkansas needs prison reform and needs it badly, this from the Gazette:

On February 22 J. A. Gafford, the warden, had whipped Williams, who, being unable to do as much work as his partner (convicts are worked in pairs), had been punished and had run off and hid in the mines. He was found by the guard and brought out one morning at breakfast time. He was stripped naked and chained to the whipping post, and during the day 400 lashes were laid on his naked back, that night he was taken to the hospital chained hand and foot and died the next day. When the body was exhumed it was found in a pine box, filled with mud and water. It was wrapped in a piece of old blanket and the only garment was a fragment of a shirt. Every particle of fiesh had been whipped off of the back from the shoulders down. The right temple of the skull had been fractured with a pick axe or some other similar tool. On the right side just over the kidneys was a hole six inches square which had been kicked in there. The doctors said ten of the blows were enough to kill him. The physician, Dr. W. Hunt, had been informed by the steward that the man died of a congestive chill and signed a certificate to that effect without ever seeing the body. The coroner's jury rendered the following verdict: "We the jury find that Charles Williams came to his death from cruel treatment inflicted by J. A. Gafford, which consisted of whipping, violence and neglect. "Coroner Blythe immediately swore out a warrant for Gafford's arrest but it was found he had gone to Little Rock the day before. He telegraphed here, but the wretch had gone on to Memphis.

The guards testified that Gafford was very brutal and delighted in seeing the convicts fight. He would go off and get drunk and come to the stockade and make two of them fight until one or the other was so badly bruised he could fight no longer. There are now no less than thirty convicts in the camp who bear marks and bruises received in these forced encounters.

When the coroner and the jury came back to Coal Hill they heard that another negro had just died at the stockade through violence. After hesitating some time and squabbling over the matter, Waller permitted Mr. Blythe to go in, but it was found the negro had been buried. After another long squabble they induced Waller to have the body exhumed. The coroner's jury examined it and then examined a number of witnesses and brought out the fact that the negro's name was Mose Harvey and that he had been killed by another convict named Mat Bailey. Altogether there were forty distinct severe kicks and bruises, any one of which might have produced death. The head had been punched out of shape and was unrecognizable. The eyes had been burst from the sockets and hung down over the face, looking like a black pulp or some raw, spoiled beef. A more revolting sight than that presented by the remains could not be imagined. The man had been kicked and bruised on March 1st, and lay in the hospital and suffered until March 8—one week.

While Waller was on the stand in the Harvey case the question was asked him if some time last summer a convict had not been chained to the post and whipped to death. Waller replied: "I am not called here to tell about that: I am a witness in the present (Harvey) case, and refuse to answer any questions outside of the case proper." The reporter found, though, that last summer a warden whose name was Hudson had had a negro chained to the post and stripped. Hudson hit him 150 licks making the back raw and causing the negro to yell so that his shrieks were heard at Coal Hill, more than a mile away. When he had whipped that way he then took salt and water and threw upon the lacerated and bleeding back. He then left the negro standing in the hot sun while he went down town and attended to some business. He then came back after two hours and whipped the negro until he died, at least he was found dead chained to the post.

Max Elder a white man, died about a month ago. Mr. Blythe had the body exhumed. It was somewhat decomposed on account of the stuff in which it was buried, but it could be seen that he died from injuries inflicted by the prison authorities, or they had been instrumental in it at least. On the back were thirty-four gashes, in any one of which a man's two fingers could be placed. There were other bruises, but it was impossible to tell which one of them caused the man's death.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A12:
A HANGING BEE
Expected When Two Brutal Murderers Reach Coal Hill.
Expected When Two Brutal Murderers Reach Coal Hill.

St. Louis, March 21.—A Post-Dispatch special says: The people of Coal Hill, Ark., are worked up to a furore over a series of outrages, that have given that peaceful mining camp a criminal notoriety that is disgusting, and there is promise of a double lynching very soon. Clifford, the penitentiary warden, who so brutally served the prisoners under him, is in the hands of the sheriff, and will be taken to the Coal Hill jail at once. While waiting for him, the people clamor for George Crispi, who is now in the Ozark jail, and had been arrested by the sheriff yesterday, charged with the criminal assault of the eight-year-old daughter of Rev. Mr. Turner, of Coal Hill. Both prisoners are hourly expected at Coal Hill, and a hanging bee is anticipated.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A16:
TERRIBLE BRUTALITY.
Sickening Details of the Arkansas Coal Mine Prison Pen.
Coal Hill, Ark., March 22.—Gov. Hughes and the penitentiary board arrived at 3 o'clock this afternoon to further investigate the brutalities to convicts in the coal mines. They found that another warden, who preceded fugitive Gafford, named J.B. Scott, has proven even more brutal. He whipped as many as fifteen men in one night, until blood ran in streams from their bodies. The place where convicts were confined was so filthy that a sickening stench rose from them. Beds and blankets were dirty and many were covered with vermin. The whole place was overhauled and whitewashed last week. Yesterday a box of shoes and clothing arrived and men were provided who had gone borefooted all winter. Physicians to-day examined a large number of convicts whom Gafford had whipped, and found their bodies almost solid sores. The men feared to complain while Gafford was here, for fear of being beaten again. It was proved that Frank Tellbert (colored) ran off, hid in the mines, and refused to come out, and Warden Schott ordered Tom Gaddis, pitt boss, to go down and shoot him. He did so and reported to Schott, but nobody knew anything then about the murder. Things are changed now, but the details of the past acts are sickening and horrible.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A22:
THE COAL HILL INVESTIGATION. LITTLE ROCK Ark. March 26 - Governor
LITTLE ROCK, Ark., March 26.—Governor Hughes, Attorney General Jones and Secretary of State Moore, comprising the state penitentiary board,' who recently investigated the charge of brutality and other mistreatment of convicts employed by the penitentiary lessees, in the Coal Hill mines, made their report today. It charges violation by the lessees of rules and regulations prescribed by the board, in nine particulars. The report orders dismissal of the chief warden of the penitentiary and a return of the convicts to the penitentiary. refusing permission to work them in Coal Hill mines or anywhere beyond the immediate supervision of "pen" physicians.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A25:
MURDERER CAPTURED.
Arrest of a Man Charged With Killing Three Convicts.
Arrest of a Man Charged With Killing Three Convicts.

LITTLE Rock, November 17.—News is just received of the capture, at Cumberland Gap, Tenn., of J. A. Gafford, fugitive from justice since last March and under indictment for murdering, or being accessory to the murder, of three convicts at Coal Hill mine, Ark., of which he was a warden. A reward of $500 was offered for his arrest and last summer he murdered a detective named Provost, who had followed him into Florida. His brutalities to convicts at Coal Hill furnished a great sensation at the time and entered largely into the political canvass for state officers that followed. J. A. Hugo, another warden, accused of beating a convict to death while chained to a post in camp, was arrested a few days ago in Arkansas county where, under an assumed name, he was practicing medicine, and lodged in Johnson county jail.
warden-grafford-coal-hill-1888-03.A26: J. A. Gafford, the inhuman wretch who, as warden, it is claimed murdered several convicts at Coal Hill and other places, has been caught and lodged in the Johnson county jail, to await trial. He was captured at Cumberland Ga, Tenn., and brought back in irons. It will be no surprise if Judge Lynch gets in his work.

A quarrel between John Dunn and John Culverson in Lee County, Ala., a few evinings since, culminated in a duel with pocket-knives, in which Culverson's throat was cut, resulting in his death in a short time. Dunn was badly cut about the ace, and may not recover.

The cotton product of the levee district in Mississippi last year was 140,930 bales.

A family quarrel resulted in the murder of Jesse J. Marlow at Ocala, Fla., a few days ago, by a neighbor named Green Hodge.

W. T. Wilson, a well-known business man of Atlanta, Ga., committed suicide a few days ago by taking strychnine.

Charles Murphy, a fisherman, while drawing in his net near Louisville, Ky., a few days ago, was dragged under the water and drowned.

The strawberry season in Tennessee is over.

The city of Columbus, Miss., by an almost unanimous vote favored a subscription of $80,000 to the Memphis, Oxford & Columbus railroad. Work is in progress at Columbus on the western extension of the Georgia Pacific railway.

W. A. Elliott, aged twenty-one, and Miss Maggie Stewart, aged eighteen, were out driving at Childersburg, Ala., a few days ago, when the horse took fright and ran into the river, drowning both the young man and young lady.

Convicts to the number of eighteen, employed on the Versailles, Midway & Georgetown railroad, escaped from their camp, near Georgetown, Ky., a few nights ago, and at last accounts were still at large. A reward of $50 each is offered for their capture.

Captain John J. Brown, a well-known steamboat man, died at New Orleans a few days since.

J. B. Friedman, a merchant of Boutte, La., and railroad express agent at that place, which is on the Morgan railroad, was shot in the back, a few nights ago, by an unknown person and died a few hours later. The assassin escaped.

The National organization of the colored Y. M. C. A. was completed at Louisville, Ky., by the election of Chas. S. Morris president; W. H. Goodall, Albert Mack, L. W. Cross and W. C. Duson, vicepresidents; Albert White, secretary, and G. W. Talbott, treasurer. Morris is only thirty-eight years old. He has been a teacher in the Louisville public schools, has just finished a course at Howard College, Washington, D. C., and intends to go to Harvard. His mother is a public-school teacher in Louisville.

J. T. Shepherd, a railroad post-office clerk of the New Orleans & Marshall railroad post-office, was arrested a few days ago charged with embezzling registered mail letters. The arrest is considered one of the most important made in some time, as the theft involves something over $1,000. There were five packages taken, one alone containing $515. This package was a remittance from the postmaster at Donaldsonville, La., to the New Orleans post-office.

Governor Buckner of Kentucky has refused to commute the sentence of Wm. Patterson, who is to be hanged in Louisville on the 22d for participation in the murder of Jennie Bowman.

As Turnkey James Turner of the Henderson (Ky.) jail was entering the building with the dinner of the prisoners a few days ago, one of them, named Baxter, jumped upon him and tried to knock him down. Turner drew his revolver and shot Baxter fatally, but in the meantime three of the prisoners had made good their escape.

The negro miners at Warrior, Ala., for some supposed offense of the white bosses, recently armed themselves with the intention of killing the first white man who molests them. The white men decided on the same course, and blood-shed seemed imminent.

Wm. J. Palmer died at the Morgantown (N. C.) Insane Asylum a few days since from injuries inflicted by an inmate of the institution. Mr. Palmer was a graduate of Columbia College and had been super-intendent of a number of insane asylums until he went insane himself.

A special train on the East Tennessee, Virginia & Georgia railway, carrying Jay Gould and party, made the fastest time on record in the South a few days since. The distance from Chattanooga to Knoxville, 112 miles, was made in two hours and seventeen minutes, which included two stops of five minutes each.

The trustees of the University of Tennessee have elected Charles E. Wait, of Rolla, Mo., to the chair of chemistry and metallurgy; Thomas L. Norwood, of Bingham School, N. C., professor of modern languages; Wm. W. Carson, professor of mathematics, and Thomas C. Karns, associate professor of the English language.

Alfred Blackwell, of Barclaysville, N. C., was found dead at his saw-mill, a few nights ago, being most fearfully mutilated! He had been trying to run his saw-mill alone, and it is supposed accidentally fell on the saw, when he suffered a most shocking death. His left arm was severed in two places, and his body was completely cut in twain except at the spinal column.

The Louisiana Senate confirmed the nomination of ex-Governor McEnery to be Associate Justice of the Supreme Court for the term of twelve years, in place of Robert B. Todd, whose term has just expired.

Oscar Searcy was killed at Greenville, Ala., a few nights ago, by a shot accidentally fired by Webb Perdue, who was flourishing a weapon in a reckless manner while under the influence of liquor.

W. H. Remert, a wealthy planter, residing in Sumter County, S. C., was recently sentenced to two years' hard labor for persisting in consorting with a negress to the utter neglect of his young and beautiful wife. His colored companion received a like sentence.

Dennis Williams, colored, was lynched at Ellaville, Fla., a few days since the crime of shooting at a white man. His body was found in the Suwannee river, perforated with bullets and having a rope around the neck.

Sam Jones' brother has eloped.

A sensation was created at Holly Springs, Miss., recently, by the conversion of Thomas F. Seligman, a saloon-keeper, who displayed a sign across his door "Closed for Good." This is one of the results of a Methodist revival, conducted by Rev. George S. Inge, under which many conversions have been made.

An Americus (Ga.) gentleman has a lot of young 'possums and kittens which he is raising together as a "happy family."

Two large bears have been committing depredations in Whitefield County, Ga., recently, and have thus far managed to elude the hunting parties organized for their destruction.

Birmingham (Ala.) bootblacks pay a license of ten dollars a year.

Robert Bratcher was recently tried at Abbeville, S. C., for enticing away a laborer under contract, a serious offense in that State. He wooed and won Miss Hamilton, the laborer in question, and married her, taking her to his home, hence the suit. The jury was disposed to be lenient, however, and returned a verdict of not guilty.

The first National convention of the Colore | Young Men's Christian Association met in Louisville, Ky. on the 10th

william-lewis-1888-09-04.A1:
News Summary. last week 584 (Chi)
During last week 584 Chinamen arrived at Vancouver, British Columbia, their ultimate destination evidently being the United States. It is estimated that during the present year the Chinese population of British Columbia has sent 5000 persons to the American side of the line.

The schooner Colonel Cook, in tow, at Cleveland. Ohio, yesterday morning, sprang a leak, and Captain Henderson and his wife were lowered into the yawl. At the same moment the tow line was cut and the schooner, swinging around rapidly, capsized the yawl. Henderson and his wife were drowned.

William Miller, a private officer of Allegheny City, Penna., was shot and killed by John Demmy, a negro, early yesterday morning. Demmy was on his way home from a ball and claims that Miller assaulted him with a blackjack and that he shot him in self defence.

There were indications at Havana on Monday of the approach of a cyclone, moving across the island in the direction of Florida. The edge of the storm reached Key West yesterday, with frequent rain squalls and a north wind, having a velocity of 55 miles an hour.

B Frank Faker, aged 19 years, was killed in Norristown, Penna, early yesterday morning, while sleep-walking. He climbed out of a window to a fourth-story roof and walked along the gutter, a distance of 60 feet, when he fell to an awning below, a distance of 25 feet.

J. C. Payne, of Covington, New York, committed suicide on Monday by shooting himself in the head. He was a member of the Assembly from Wyoming county several years ago. He had suffered from mental troubles for three years past.

It has been discovered that Jules List, Secretary of the Duckworth Building Association in Cincinnati, has stolen $20,000 of the the money of members. List used the money in fast living, and is now in hiding.

While a freight train was crossing a bridge at Halifax, yesterday, a brakeman named Cummings accidentally ran against another named Christie, and both fell into the trestle work and were killed.

The five Anarchist rioters in Cleveland, Ohio, were arraigned yesterday on the charge of disturbing the peace. All except one pleaded not guilty, and their trials were set for Thursday.

It has been decided by the Treasury Department that bicycle lamps which resemble carriage lamps in their character and use are dutiable at the rate of 35 per cent. ad valorem.

The body of William Lewis, colored, was found hanging to a tree, near Durant, Mississippi, yesterday morning. The lynchers are unknown.

The body of Maggie Rice, aged 23 years, was found in the river near Harrisburg, Penna., yesterday. It is supposed she committed suicide.

The suspension of W. L. Williams, a cotton broker, was announced on the floor of the Cotton exchange, in New York, yesterday.

James Shaw, 73 years of age, a well known citizen of Paterson. New Jersey, committed suicide on Monday night by taking laudanum

At Jacksonville, Florida, yesterday there were 23 new cases of yellow fever and one death.

The police of Milwaukee, Wisconsin, have closed every gambling house in the city.

Lynched Very Quietly.
NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 5.—The body of William Lewis (colored) was found hanging to a tree near Durant, Miss., and the man is supposed to have been lynched by unknown persons.
william-lewis-1888-09-04.A3:
A Negro Found Hanged.
NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 4. A dispatch from Durant, Miss., says: "The body of William Lewis (colored) was discovered hanging to a tree five miles from here this morning. He was evidently hanged last night. The perpetrators of the deed are unknown. No cause is assigned."
